CRIMINAL LAW 1: COMPLETE 275 LANDMARK CASE DIGESTS

PART: I. GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF CRIMINAL LAW

Topic: Theories of Criminal Law (Classical vs. Positivist)

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):General Principles of Criminal Law; Classical & Positivist Theories; R.A. 9262 (Anti-VAWC Act) • Total Cases: 2Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the foundational philosophical paradigms of Philippine criminal jurisprudence, contrasting the Classical school (free will, retributive justice, and moral responsibility) with the Positivist school (determinism, social defense, rehabilitation, and victimology/psychological trauma such as Battered Woman Syndrome).

CASE 1

People v. Marivic Genosa

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 135981, 29 September 2000 & 15 January 2004 | Topic: Theories of Criminal Law (Classical vs. Positivist)

Statutory Anchor:General Principles; Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 13, pars. 6 & 9, RPC; RA 9262.- Applicability:Applicable because the positivist school considers the offender's psychological mindset and victimology, allowing BWS to be treated as mitigating factors analogous to psychological illness and passion/obfuscation under Article 13.

Facts:Marivic Genosa, an 8-month pregnant wife who had endured repeated physical violence and psychological torture by her alcoholic husband Ben, shot him in the head while he was sleeping in their bedroom following an assault.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked self-defense based on Battered Woman Syndrome (BWS), arguing under the Positivist theory that chronic trauma altered her psychological perception, making her genuinely believe she was in imminent, inescapable danger of death.

Issue:Can Battered Woman Syndrome (BWS) be recognized under Philippine criminal law to establish complete self-defense or mitigate liability for parricide?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (as mitigating circumstances). The Supreme Court recognized BWS under the positivist theory, holding that while complete self-defense failed because the victim was asleep (no actual imminent aggression at the exact moment of shooting), BWS constituted two mitigating circumstances.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1, RPC (Self-Defense); Art. 13, pars. 6 & 9, RPC (Mitigating Circumstances - Passion/Obfuscation and Illness diminishing willpower); Positivist Theory of Criminal Law. Applicability: Applicable because the positivist school considers the offender's psychological mindset and victimology, allowing BWS to be treated as mitigating factors analogous to psychological illness and passion/obfuscation under Article 13.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Complete self-defense requires unlawful aggression at the time of the fatal act. Because the husband was sleeping, aggression had ceased. However, pursuant to the positivist approach and Art. 13(9) & (6), the cumulative psychological trauma and acute panic entitled Genosa to two mitigating circumstances without aggravating circumstances.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for parricide AFFIRMED with MODIFIED penalty (penalty reduced to 6 years and 1 day of prision mayor to 14 years, 8 months and 1 day of reclusion temporal; accused ordered released due to time served). DOCTRINE: BWS is recognized as a mitigating circumstance under the Positivist theory of criminal law.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:General Principles; Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 13, pars. 6 & 9, RPC; RA 9262.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 2

Norma de Joya v. Jail Warden of Batangas

CITATION Citation: G.R. Nos. 15948-19, 10 December 2003 | Topic: Theories of Criminal Law (Classical vs. Positivist)

Statutory Anchor:General Principles; Art. III, Sec. 19(2), 1987 Constitution; RPC Book I Title Three.- Applicability:Applicable because penal detention cannot be administered solely as punitive retribution; statutory and constitutional mandates require correctional standards focused on rehabilitation.

Facts:Petitioners challenged the custodial detention procedures, subhuman living conditions, and punitive segregation in the Batangas City Jail, demanding humane treatment and proper classification.

Accused's Defense:Petitioners contended that correctional administration must adhere to the Positivist philosophy focusing on offender rehabilitation and human dignity rather than the Classical theory of purely retributive punishment and cruel isolation.

Issue:Are custodial detention facilities and penal execution governed by the positivist/rehabilitative theory and constitutional standards of human dignity?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The Supreme Court ruled that modern penal administration in the Philippines synthesizes the classical retribution theory with the positivist philosophy prioritizing offender reformation, human dignity, and rehabilitation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Philippine Constitution, Art. III, Sec. 19(2) (Humane penal facilities); RPC penal execution principles; Positivist and Eclectic Penal Theories. Applicability: Applicable because penal detention cannot be administered solely as punitive retribution; statutory and constitutional mandates require correctional standards focused on rehabilitation.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Supreme Court underscored that the Revised Penal Code adopts an eclectic/mixed philosophy. While the classical school governs liability and deterrence, the positivist school governs penal execution, custodial welfare, and reformative rehabilitation of detainees.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Custodial guidelines ordered enforced and humane detention conditions mandated. DOCTRINE: Philippine penal law embraces an eclectic philosophy: retributive classical deterrence in culpability, and positivist reformation in penal execution and correctional custody.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:General Principles; Art. III, Sec. 19(2), 1987 Constitution; RPC Book I Title Three.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).

Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 14, Civil Code; 1987 Constitution (Art. VI, Sec. 11); Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations; Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA); R.A. 7055 • Total Cases: 18Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the territorial reach and universal binding force of Philippine penal statutes over all persons within national borders, while governing recognized sovereign, diplomatic, and treaty-based jurisdictional immunities and parliamentary speech privileges.

CASE 3

People v. Santiago

CITATION Citation: 43 Phil. 120 (1922) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. 2, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because territorial penal jurisdiction binds all individuals present within national borders regardless of their nationality or political status.

Facts:Santiago was charged with a statutory offense committed within the territory of the Philippine Islands. He demurred to the information, questioning the jurisdiction of the trial court.

Accused's Defense:The accused contended that the Philippine courts lacked jurisdiction because the information was brought in the name of the 'People of the Philippine Islands' rather than the sovereign United States Government.

Issue:Do Philippine courts possess criminal jurisdiction over all offenses committed within the territory pursuant to the Generality Principle?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Penal laws are obligatory upon all persons who live or sojourn in Philippine territory, and criminal prosecutions are properly instituted by the territorial sovereign authority.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, Civil Code; Principle of Generality and Territorial Sovereignty. Applicability: Applicable because territorial penal jurisdiction binds all individuals present within national borders regardless of their nationality or political status.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Generality Principle dictates that criminal laws apply universally within the state's territory. Prosecuting crimes in the name of the territorial sovereign fulfills the state's police power and territorial jurisdiction.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Demurrer OVERRULED and jurisdiction AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: The Generality Principle subjects every individual within Philippine territory to the command and punitive reach of domestic penal statutes.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. 2, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 4

United States v. Pablo

CITATION Citation: 35 Phil. 94 (1916) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. 208, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because official status or badge provides no immunity from criminal prosecution when a public officer violates or intentionally omits penal mandates.

Facts:Pablo, a municipal policeman, failed to report and apprehend individuals running an illegal gambling ('jueteng') operation occurring right in his presence and jurisdiction.

Accused's Defense:The accused claimed that he was acting within discretionary police authority and was exempt from strict penal enforcement because no formal written complaint had been lodged by private citizens.

Issue:Is a public law enforcement officer exempt from the general application of penal laws for intentional omission of official duty?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The Generality Principle applies equally to public officers and private citizens alike; no individual is above or exempt from penal liability.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, Civil Code; RPC provisions on dereliction of duty; Generality of Penal Law. Applicability: Applicable because official status or badge provides no immunity from criminal prosecution when a public officer violates or intentionally omits penal mandates.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The law operates equally on all individuals within the state's territory. A police officer who tolerates crimes or commits dereliction cannot invoke official status as a shield against criminal liability.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for dereliction of duty AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Public officers possess no personal immunity from criminal laws; the generality principle subjects all individuals equally to statutory penal duties.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. 208, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 5

In re: Kay Villegas Kami, Inc.

CITATION Citation: 35 SCRA 429 (1970) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. III, Sec. 22, 1987 Constitution; Art. 21, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because constitutional limitations test whether a penal law operates retrospectively or targets specific persons without judicial trial.

Facts:A civic non-profit organization challenged Section 12 of RA 6132 (Constitutional Convention Act), which prohibited any corporation, association, or group from giving campaign contributions or conducting partisan election propaganda.

Accused's Defense:Petitioner corporation argued that the penal statute was an unconstitutional ex post facto law, a bill of attainder, and an unlawful curtailment of constitutional rights that should not generally bind civic organizations.

Issue:Does Section 12 of RA 6132 violate the constitutional prohibitions against ex post facto laws, bills of attainder, and the generality principle?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The statute operates purely prospectively during the election period and applies generally and equally to all associations within the state.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 22 (Ex Post Facto / Bill of Attainder Clause); Art. 14, Civil Code (Generality). Applicability: Applicable because constitutional limitations test whether a penal law operates retrospectively or targets specific persons without judicial trial.
•
[A] APPLICATION:An ex post facto law penalizes acts committed before its enactment, whereas RA 6132 punished only future conduct committed after its effectivity. It applies generally to all groups without singling out named individuals as a bill of attainder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition DISMISSED; constitutionality and general binding effect of the statute UPHELD. DOCTRINE: Prospective penal laws applying equally to all entities within the jurisdiction satisfy the Generality Principle and do not violate the ex post facto ban.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. III, Sec. 22, 1987 Constitution; Art. 21, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 6

People v. Villaraza

CITATION Citation: 81 SCRA 95 (1978) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 21, RPC; Art. 14, Civil Code; PD 818.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 21 strictly prohibits retroactive application of harsher penal sanctions, but mandates enforcement of laws in force at the time of the offense.

Facts:The accused was prosecuted for issuing a bouncing check under the provisions of Presidential Decree No. 818 (which increased penalties for estafa by issuing bouncing checks). The crime was committed after PD 818 took effect.

Accused's Defense:The accused contended that the heavier penalties under PD 818 should not apply to him because check issuance was traditionally punished by lesser penalties under Article 315 of the RPC.

Issue:Does the application of increased statutory penalties to acts committed after the decree's effectivity violate the prospectivity or generality principle?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. PD 818 took effect prior to the commission of the act, and criminal laws apply to all offenses committed subsequent to their promulgation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 21, RPC (No felony shall be punishable by any penalty not prescribed by law prior to its commission); Art. 14, Civil Code. Applicability: Applicable because Article 21 strictly prohibits retroactive application of harsher penal sanctions, but mandates enforcement of laws in force at the time of the offense.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the check was issued after the promulgation of PD 818, the accused had statutory notice of the enhanced penalty. The principle of prospectivity was fully respected.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Jurisdiction of trial court SUSTAINED and application of PD 818 AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Penal laws and decree amendments imposing heavier penalties apply to all acts committed after their promulgation.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 21, RPC; Art. 14, Civil Code; PD 818.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 7

U.S. v. Diaz-Conde

CITATION Citation: 42 Phil. 766 (1922) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 21, 22, RPC; 1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 22; Act No. 2655.- Applicability:Applicable because the constitutional ban on ex post facto legislation directly protects individuals from being punished for acts that did not constitute crimes when committed.

Facts:Diaz-Conde executed a loan contract stipulating an interest rate that was lawful at the time of execution. Later, the Usury Law (Act No. 2655) was enacted, making such interest rates criminal. Diaz-Conde was prosecuted for collecting interest after the new law's passage.

Accused's Defense:The accused argued that prosecuting them under a new law for a loan agreement lawfully perfected prior to the statute's enactment was an unconstitutional ex post facto application.

Issue:Can a penal statute penalize the enforcement of a contract that was completely lawful when entered into before the enactment of the law?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Applying a penal law to acts or contracts that were innocent and lawful when made constitutes a prohibited ex post facto law.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. III, Sec. 22, Constitution (Ex Post Facto Law Prohibition); Art. 21 & 22, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the constitutional ban on ex post facto legislation directly protects individuals from being punished for acts that did not constitute crimes when committed.
•
[A] APPLICATION:A statute cannot retroactively criminalize an act that was innocent when done, nor can it impair vested contractual rights by attaching criminal liability to prior lawful agreements.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment of conviction REVERSED and accused ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: A penal law cannot be applied retroactively to punish acts or contracts that were lawful at the time of their execution.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 21, 22, RPC; 1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 22; Act No. 2655.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 8

People of the Philippines vs. Roman Derilo et al.

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 117818, April 18, 1997 | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 22, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 22, 1987 Constitution; RA 7659.- Applicability:Applicable because penal statutes that increase punishment or impose the death penalty can never be applied retroactively against an accused.

Facts:Roman Derilo and co-accused were charged with murder committed during the effectivity of the 1987 Constitution when the death penalty was suspended. During trial, RA 7659 (Death Penalty Law) took effect.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that RA 7659 could not be retroactively applied to impose the capital penalty on them for an offense committed before its enactment.

Issue:Can the newly restored death penalty under RA 7659 be applied retroactively to offenses committed prior to its effectivity?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Retroactive application of an unfavorable or harsher penal statute violates the constitutional prohibition against ex post facto laws and Article 22 of the RPC.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 22, RPC (Retroactive effect of penal laws only when favorable to the accused); 1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 22. Applicability: Applicable because penal statutes that increase punishment or impose the death penalty can never be applied retroactively against an accused.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the murder was committed while the 1987 Constitution suspended the death penalty, the maximum penalty imposable at the time of the crime was reclusion perpetua. RA 7659, being unfavorable, cannot be applied retroactively.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for murder AFFIRMED, but penalty MODIFIED from death to reclusion perpetua. DOCTRINE: Penal laws that increase penalties or restore capital punishment cannot be applied retroactively.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 22, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 22, 1987 Constitution; RA 7659.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 9

People v. Ferrer

CITATION Citation: 48 SCRA 382 (1972) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 22, 1987 Constitution; RA 1700.- Applicability:Applicable because a bill of attainder is a legislative act inflicting punishment without judicial trial, whereas RA 1700 required full judicial proceedings and proof of criminal intent.

Facts:The constitutionality of the Anti-Subversion Act (RA 1700), which outlawed the Communist Party of the Philippines (CPP) and similar subversive organizations, was challenged in criminal proceedings against accused subversives.

Accused's Defense:The accused argued that RA 1700 was a prohibited bill of attainder because it named the CPP directly, and an ex post facto law that penalized mere political affiliation and association.

Issue:Does the Anti-Subversion Act constitute an unconstitutional bill of attainder or an ex post facto law?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The statute does not automatically punish members by legislative fiat; it defines subversive acts and requires judicial trial and proof of knowing, willful membership and overt acts.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 22 (Bill of Attainder & Ex Post Facto Clauses); RA 1700. Applicability: Applicable because a bill of attainder is a legislative act inflicting punishment without judicial trial, whereas RA 1700 required full judicial proceedings and proof of criminal intent.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Supreme Court held that the legislative naming of the organization was merely descriptive. To convict, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the accused actively and knowingly affiliated with the illegal aims of the conspiracy.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Trial court order dismissing informations REVERSED and cases REMANDED for trial. DOCTRINE: A statute is not a bill of attainder if it requires full judicial trial and proof of specific criminal overt acts and intent.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 22, 1987 Constitution; RA 1700.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 10

Pesigan v. Angeles

CITATION Citation: 129 SCRA 174 (1984) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, Civil Code; Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 1, 1987 Constitution.- Applicability:Applicable because penal laws must be published to give the public adequate notice before any person can be subjected to criminal liability or forfeiture.

Facts:Pesigan was transporting carabaos from Camarines Sur to Batangas on April 2, 1982. The carabaos were confiscated pursuant to Executive Order No. 626-A (banning inter-provincial transport of carabaos), which was signed in October 1980 but published in the Official Gazette only on June 14, 1982.

Accused's Defense:Pesigan argued that EO 626-A could not penalize his conduct or justify confiscation on April 2, 1982 because the executive order had not yet been published and had no legal effect.

Issue:Can an executive order penalizing conduct be enforced prior to its publication in the Official Gazette?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Penal laws and executive orders with punitive sanctions have no binding force or effect until they are duly published in full.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, Civil Code; Art. 21, RPC; Due Process Clause (1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 1). Applicability: Applicable because penal laws must be published to give the public adequate notice before any person can be subjected to criminal liability or forfeiture.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the transport occurred on April 2, 1982 and EO 626-A was published only on June 14, 1982, the order was legally non-existent and unenforceable at the time of the incident.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Confiscation declared NULL AND VOID; carabaos or their value ordered returned. DOCTRINE: Publication is an indispensable requirement of due process for penal statutes and executive orders to become effective.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, Civil Code; Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 1, 1987 Constitution.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 11

Tañada v. Tuvera

CITATION Citation: 136 SCRA 27 (1985) & 146 SCRA 446 (1986) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, Civil Code; Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 1, 1987 Constitution.- Applicability:Applicable because without publication, the people have no notice of penal laws, violating the fundamental due process guarantee that no person shall be punished for an act not previously made known as a crime.

Facts:Petitioners filed a writ of mandamus to compel public officials to publish in the Official Gazette various presidential decrees, letters of instructions, and general orders that carried penal sanctions.

Accused's Defense:Respondents claimed that presidential issuances stating they take effect 'immediately upon approval' dispensed with the requirement of publication.

Issue:Is publication in full in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation indispensable before presidential decrees and penal statutes acquire legal force?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. All statutes, including presidential decrees and executive issuances of general application and penal nature, must be published in full to become effective.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, Civil Code; Due Process Clause (1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 1); Art. 21, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because without publication, the people have no notice of penal laws, violating the fundamental due process guarantee that no person shall be punished for an act not previously made known as a crime.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The phrase 'unless it is otherwise provided' refers solely to the date of effectivity, not to the requirement of publication itself, which is absolute and non-negotiable.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for mandamus GRANTED; full publication ordered for all unpublished presidential decrees and general penal issuances. DOCTRINE: Publication of penal laws is an absolute due process prerequisite for their legal validity and enforceability.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, Civil Code; Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 1, 1987 Constitution.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 12

Alfredo Romualdez v. Sandiganbayan

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 152259, 29 July 2004 | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 1, 1987 Constitution; Sec. 5, RA 3019.- Applicability:Applicable because penal statutes must define criminal acts with sufficient clarity so that a person of ordinary intelligence can understand what conduct is forbidden.

Facts:Alfredo Romualdez was charged with violating Section 5 of RA 3019 (Anti-Graft and Corrupt Practices Act) for intervening in a contract between a private corporation and a government agency during the presidency of his brother-in-law.

Accused's Defense:The accused argued that Section 5 of RA 3019 was unconstitutionally vague and overbroad, failing to provide fair notice of prohibited conduct.

Issue:Is Section 5 of RA 3019 void for vagueness under the constitutional due process clause?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The statute is valid; the void-for-vagueness doctrine applies only when a statute is utterly devoid of any comprehensible standard, not to penal provisions whose terms can be understood by ordinary persons.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 1 (Due Process Clause); RA 3019, Sec. 5; Void-for-Vagueness Doctrine. Applicability: Applicable because penal statutes must define criminal acts with sufficient clarity so that a person of ordinary intelligence can understand what conduct is forbidden.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Section 5 clearly defines the prohibited act of intervening in government business by close relatives of the President. The statute provides fair warning and adequate guidelines for law enforcement.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition DISMISSED; constitutionality of Section 5 UPHELD and criminal proceedings continued. DOCTRINE: A criminal statute is not void for vagueness if ordinary citizens can understand its terms and determine what acts are prohibited.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 21, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 1, 1987 Constitution; Sec. 5, RA 3019.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 13

SPARK v. Quezon City

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 225442, 8 August 2017 | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. III, Sec. 1 & 6, 1987 Constitution; RA 9344; Art. 14, Civil Code.- Applicability:Applicable because penal sanctions and curfew restrictions targeting minors must withstand strict scrutiny and cannot impose criminal penalties prohibited by RA 9344.

Facts:Samahan ng mga Progresibong Kabataan (SPARK) and several student petitioners challenged the curfew ordinances for minors enacted by the local governments of Quezon City, Manila, and Navotas.

Accused's Defense:Petitioners argued that the curfew ordinances were unconstitutionally vague, overbroad, violated minors' right to travel, and improperly imposed penal sanctions on minors and their parents.

Issue:Are curfew ordinances imposing criminal penalties on minors constitutional and compliant with the juvenile justice system?

•
[A] ANSWER:PARTIALLY UNCONSTITUTIONAL. The Supreme Court struck down the Manila and Navotas ordinances for failing the strict scrutiny test, while upholding the Quezon City ordinance which provided adequate exceptions and complied with the Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act (RA 9344).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 1 & Sec. 6 (Liberty of Abode and Travel); RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006). Applicability: Applicable because penal sanctions and curfew restrictions targeting minors must withstand strict scrutiny and cannot impose criminal penalties prohibited by RA 9344.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Under RA 9344, no penalty may be imposed on children for status offenses like curfew violations; they may only be subjected to intervention programs. Curfew ordinances lacking sufficient exceptions impermissibly infringe upon fundamental constitutional rights.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Manila and Navotas curfew ordinances declared UNCONSTITUTIONAL; Quezon City curfew ordinance UPHELD with directives to eliminate penal sanctions against minors. DOCTRINE: Penal ordinances affecting fundamental rights must withstand strict scrutiny and cannot impose criminal penalties on minors contrary to RA 9344.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. III, Sec. 1 & 6, 1987 Constitution; RA 9344; Art. 14, Civil Code.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 14

United States v. Sweet

CITATION Citation: 1 Phil. 18 (1901) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. 2, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because all individuals within Philippine territory, including military personnel, are subject to the general jurisdiction of domestic criminal courts in the absence of explicit treaty exemptions.

Facts:Sweet, an employee of the United States military forces in the Philippines, assaulted a prisoner of war on Philippine territory. He was charged with physical injuries before the civil court.

Accused's Defense:Sweet challenged the court's jurisdiction, arguing that as a military employee committing an act during military operations, he was exempt from the jurisdiction of domestic civil courts.

Issue:Does the Generality Principle subject foreign military employees to the criminal jurisdiction of civil courts for offenses committed against individuals within Philippine territory?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Civil courts have general criminal jurisdiction over all crimes committed within Philippine territory, even by military personnel, unless an express treaty or statute provides an exception.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, Civil Code; Generality Principle of Penal Law. Applicability: Applicable because all individuals within Philippine territory, including military personnel, are subject to the general jurisdiction of domestic criminal courts in the absence of explicit treaty exemptions.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Military personnel and civilian employees of armed forces do not enjoy general extraterritorial immunity from domestic penal statutes for non-combat crimes committed on local soil.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Jurisdiction of civil courts AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Under the Generality Principle, military personnel committing ordinary crimes within Philippine territory are amenable to domestic civil criminal jurisdiction.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. 2, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 15

Raquiza v. Bradford

CITATION Citation: 75 Phil. 50 (1945) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Treaty & International Law Exceptions.- Applicability:Applicable because international law recognizes an exception to generality when foreign troops are present by sovereign invitation/consent during active war operations.

Facts:Petitioners were detained by US Army military authorities during the liberation of the Philippines for alleged collaboration with the Japanese enemy. They filed a petition for habeas corpus before Philippine civil courts against US military commanders.

Accused's Defense:Respondents (US military officers) argued that foreign armed forces operating in the territory of an ally with its consent are exempt from domestic civil court jurisdiction regarding military security actions during active warfare.

Issue:Are foreign military forces permitted within national territory during wartime exempt from the jurisdiction of domestic civil courts?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Treaty/War Exception to Generality). Foreign armed forces stationed in or passing through the territory of an ally with consent enjoy immunity from local civil and criminal jurisdiction regarding military security measures.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Principles of International Law (Public International Law Exception to Generality under Art. 14, Civil Code). Applicability: Applicable because international law recognizes an exception to generality when foreign troops are present by sovereign invitation/consent during active war operations.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Supreme Court recognized that the presence of allied military forces carrying out military operations constitutes an established sovereign exception to territorial jurisdiction.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for habeas corpus DISMISSED. DOCTRINE: Foreign military forces operating within the country by sovereign consent enjoy immunity from domestic civil court jurisdiction for acts related to military security.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Treaty & International Law Exceptions.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 16

Liang v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 125865, 28 January 2000 & 26 March 2001 | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Treaty Exceptions to Generality.- Applicability:Applicable because treaty exceptions to the generality principle cover only official acts; private offenses and slander are outside the scope of diplomatic functions.

Facts:Jeffrey Liang, an economist with the Asian Development Bank (ADB), was charged with grave oral defamation for allegedly uttering defamatory words against a fellow ADB employee.

Accused's Defense:Liang invoked diplomatic immunity under the ADB Headquarters Agreement, claiming absolute immunity from criminal prosecution for all acts performed while employed at ADB.

Issue:Does diplomatic immunity of international organization officials extend to acts of oral defamation committed against individuals?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Immunity granted to international organization officials is functional (restricted to acts performed in an official capacity) and does not cover commission of crimes such as oral defamation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, Civil Code; ADB Headquarters Agreement; Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations; Functional Immunity Doctrine. Applicability: Applicable because treaty exceptions to the generality principle cover only official acts; private offenses and slander are outside the scope of diplomatic functions.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Defaming a co-worker cannot be considered part of the official functions of an international economist. Immunity cannot be used as a license to commit crimes in the host state.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for dismissal DENIED and trial court directed to proceed with criminal trial. DOCTRINE: International organization officials enjoy functional immunity, which does not cover personal criminal offenses such as defamation.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Treaty Exceptions to Generality.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 17

Minucher v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 142399, 11 February 2003 | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Principles of International Law.- Applicability:Applicable because foreign agents acting within the scope of authorized official state duties represent a recognized exception to domestic generality jurisdiction under international law.

Facts:Minucher filed a damages suit against Arthur Scalzo, an agent of the US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) assigned to the US Embassy in Manila, arising from an anti-narcotics buy-bust operation conducted with Philippine police.

Accused's Defense:Scalzo claimed diplomatic immunity and state immunity, asserting he was a diplomatic agent performing official sovereign functions authorized by the US Government in coordination with Philippine law enforcement.

Issue:Does a foreign law enforcement agent conducting official operations with host government consent enjoy state immunity from domestic suit and penal liability?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Foreign agents performing official state functions with the consent and coordination of the host government enjoy immunity for official acts.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Principle of Sovereign State Immunity; Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations; Art. 14, Civil Code. Applicability: Applicable because foreign agents acting within the scope of authorized official state duties represent a recognized exception to domestic generality jurisdiction under international law.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because Scalzo conducted the narcotics operation in his official capacity as a DEA agent with the knowledge and participation of the Philippine government, his actions were acts of state protected by immunity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Complaint against Scalzo DISMISSED based on state immunity. DOCTRINE: Foreign state agents acting within the authorized scope of official sovereign duties with host government consent are immune from domestic jurisdiction.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Principles of International Law.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 18

Vinuya v. Romulo

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 162230, 28 April 2010 | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Treaty & International Law Principles.- Applicability:Applicable because the enforcement of international penal reparations through diplomatic channels is an executive foreign policy function outside the realm of judicial mandamus.

Facts:Filipino comfort women (Malaya Lolas) filed a petition for certiorari and mandamus to compel the Executive Department to espouse their claims for official apology and war reparations against the Japanese Government before the International Court of Justice.

Accused's Defense:The Executive Branch contended that foreign relations, treaty negotiations, and diplomatic espousal are non-justiciable political questions committed exclusively to the President's discretion under the Constitution.

Issue:Can the judiciary compel the Executive Department by mandamus to prosecute international claims and espouse crimes against humanity against a foreign sovereign?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The conduct of foreign relations and diplomatic espousal of claims are political questions within the exclusive constitutional prerogative of the Executive Department.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Const. Art. VII; Political Question Doctrine; Principles of International Law & Treaties (1951 San Francisco Peñace Treaty). Applicability: Applicable because the enforcement of international penal reparations through diplomatic channels is an executive foreign policy function outside the realm of judicial mandamus.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Supreme Court ruled that foreign policy decisions, including whether to waive or espouse war crime claims against foreign nations, belong exclusively to the Executive branch.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for mandamus DISMISSED. DOCTRINE: Espousal of claims for war crimes and international atrocities against foreign sovereigns is a non-justiciable political question reserved to the Executive.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Treaty & International Law Principles.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 19

Osmeña v. Pendatun

CITATION Citation: 109 Phil. 863 (1960) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. VI, Sec. 11, 1987 Constitution.- Applicability:Applicable because parliamentary immunity is a constitutional exception to the Generality Principle, protecting lawmakers from external suits, but reserving internal disciplinary authority to Congress itself.

Facts:Congressman Sergio Osmeña Jr. delivered a privilege speech on the floor of the House of Representatives accusing President Carlos P. Garcia of bribery. The House created a committee to investigate him for disorderly behavior and subsequently suspended him.

Accused's Defense:Osmeña filed a petition for declaratory relief and prohibition, claiming constitutional parliamentary immunity from questioning and discipline for speech made in Congress.

Issue:Does parliamentary immunity protect a legislator from internal disciplinary sanctions imposed by his own legislative chamber for disorderly behavior?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Parliamentary immunity protects legislators from outside criminal and civil prosecution, but does not shield them from disciplinary power exercised by their own house.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Const. Art. VI, Sec. 11 & Sec. 16(3); Constitutional Parliamentary Immunity. Applicability: Applicable because parliamentary immunity is a constitutional exception to the Generality Principle, protecting lawmakers from external suits, but reserving internal disciplinary authority to Congress itself.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Speech and Debate clause prevents judicial courts and executive agencies from prosecuting a member for speech delivered in Congress, but each legislative house retains inherent power to discipline its own members.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for prohibition DISMISSED; legislative suspension UPHELD. DOCTRINE: Parliamentary immunity is an exception to general criminal liability protecting legislators from outside prosecution, but not from internal congressional discipline.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. VI, Sec. 11, 1987 Constitution.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 20

People v. Jalosjos

CITATION Citation: 324 SCRA 689 (2000) | Topic: Characteristics: Generality Principle (Constitutional & Treaty Exceptions)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. VI, Sec. 11, 1987 Constitution; Art. 335, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because constitutional parliamentary privilege explicitly excludes offenses punishable by imprisonment of more than six years, and penal laws apply equally to elected officials.

Facts:Romeo Jalosjos, an elected member of the House of Representatives, was convicted of statutory rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. While his appeal was pending, he filed a motion requesting permission to attend legislative sessions in Congress.

Accused's Defense:Jalosjos claimed that parliamentary immunity, mandate of the electorate, and official legislative duties entitled him to temporary release to attend congressional deliberations.

Issue:Does parliamentary immunity or election to Congress exempt a convicted legislator from custodial confinement and the general application of penal detention?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Parliamentary immunity applies only to offenses punishable by not more than 6 years imprisonment; it provides no immunity for serious crimes, nor does popular election override the generality of penal confinement.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:1987 Const. Art. VI, Sec. 11; Art. 14, Civil Code (Generality Principle). Applicability: Applicable because constitutional parliamentary privilege explicitly excludes offenses punishable by imprisonment of more than six years, and penal laws apply equally to elected officials.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Rape is a heinous crime carrying reclusion perpetua. The mandate of the electorate cannot place an official above the law or negate the general enforcement of penal sentences.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Motion for temporary release DENIED. DOCTRINE: Under the Generality Principle, election to Congress does not confer immunity from detention for serious crimes carrying penalties over 6 years.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. VI, Sec. 11, 1987 Constitution; Art. 335, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).

Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 2, Paragraphs 1 through 5, Revised Penal Code; UNCLOS; Section 15, Rule 110, Rules of Court • Total Cases: 7Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the sovereign authority of Philippine courts over offenses committed within the Philippine archipelago, its atmosphere, and its territorial waters (under the English Rule of maritime jurisdiction), as well as the 5 exceptional extraterritorial categories under Article 2 (Philippine ships/airships, forgery of currency/securities, public officer offenses, and crimes against national security/law of nations).

CASE 21

United States v. Bull

CITATION Citation: 15 Phil. 7 (1910) | Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 55.- Applicability:Applicable because the offense affected the public policy, trade, and animal welfare regulations of the host state upon the vessel's entry into Philippine territorial waters.

Facts:Bull, master of a Norwegian vessel, transported cattle and carabaos from Formosa to Manila. The vessel failed to provide suitable stalls and care for the animals, causing injury and death while sailing within Philippine territorial waters.

Accused's Defense:The accused master argued that Philippine courts lacked jurisdiction because the vessel was of foreign registry and the voyage originated in a foreign port.

Issue:Do Philippine courts have jurisdiction over crimes committed on board foreign merchant vessels entering Philippine territorial waters?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (French vs. English Rule / English Rule Adopted). Under the English Rule, crimes committed on board foreign merchant vessels within territorial waters are triable in local courts unless they involve merely the internal order of the ship.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, RPC (Territoriality Principle); English Rule on Maritime Jurisdiction. Applicability: Applicable because the offense affected the public policy, trade, and animal welfare regulations of the host state upon the vessel's entry into Philippine territorial waters.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Philippine legal system follows the English Rule: foreign merchant vessels entering domestic waters subject themselves to local criminal jurisdiction for offenses affecting public order and statutory regulations.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for violation of animal welfare statute AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Philippine courts follow the English Rule; foreign merchant vessels in Philippine territorial waters are subject to domestic criminal jurisdiction.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 55.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 22

People v. Look Chaw

CITATION Citation: 18 Phil. 573 (1910) | Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 1761.- Applicability:Applicable because unloading or offering contraband for sale on domestic territory breaches the peace and violates the host state's penal laws.

Facts:Look Chaw, a passenger on a foreign steamship anchored in the port of Cebu, carried cans of opium which he offered for sale and attempted to land on Philippine territory.

Accused's Defense:The accused claimed that the opium remained on a foreign merchant vessel and was intended for transit, meaning Philippine courts had no territorial jurisdiction over his possession.

Issue:Does the landing or attempted sale of contraband from a foreign merchant vessel in a domestic port establish Philippine criminal jurisdiction?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Bringing contraband into a Philippine port with the intent or attempt to unload or sell it compromises the public peace and order of the country, conferring full jurisdiction on local courts.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, RPC; English Rule of Maritime Jurisdiction. Applicability: Applicable because unloading or offering contraband for sale on domestic territory breaches the peace and violates the host state's penal laws.
•
[A] APPLICATION:While mere possession of contraband on a vessel in innocent transit might be internal discipline, attempting to land or sell illicit drugs inside Philippine waters directly affects domestic public order.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for illegal possession and attempt to sell opium AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Attempting to land or distribute contraband from a foreign vessel in a domestic port subjects the offender to Philippine penal jurisdiction.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 1761.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 23

United States v. Ah Sing

CITATION Citation: 36 Phil. 978 (1917) | Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 2381.- Applicability:Applicable because national sovereignty and territorial penal jurisdiction extend to the outer limit of territorial waters, where illegal importation is legally perfected.

Facts:Ah Sing, a fireman on a steamship sailing from Saigon to Cebu, purchased eight cans of opium in Saigon and hid them in the ship's ashes. The vessel anchored in Cebu port, where authorities discovered the opium.

Accused's Defense:The accused contended that he never intended to unload the opium in Cebu and that illegal importation of contraband was not consummated because the drugs were never brought ashore.

Issue:Is the crime of illegal importation of contraband consummated by merely bringing the illicit substance into Philippine territorial waters?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The crime of illegal importation is complete the moment the vessel carrying contraband enters Philippine territorial waters, regardless of whether the contraband is unloaded.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, RPC; Statutory provisions on illegal importation; Territoriality Principle. Applicability: Applicable because national sovereignty and territorial penal jurisdiction extend to the outer limit of territorial waters, where illegal importation is legally perfected.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Importation is not the landing of goods on the shore, but bringing them into domestic waters from a foreign port with intent to import. Entering port with hidden contraband completes the offense.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for illegal importation of opium AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Bringing contraband into Philippine territorial waters constitutes consummated illegal importation under the Territoriality Principle.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 2381.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 24

People v. Lo-lo & Saraw

CITATION Citation: 43 Phil. 19 (1922) | Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, par. 5; Art. 122 & 123, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because piracy is an international crime punishable anywhere regardless of where committed or the nationality of victims.

Facts:Lo-lo, Saraw, and other armed Moros attacked a Dutch vessel on the high seas, boarded it, robbed the cargo, and raped two female passengers before returning to Sulu.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that Philippine courts had no jurisdiction because the acts of piracy, robbery, and rape were committed on the high seas outside Philippine territorial waters.

Issue:Do Philippine courts have extraterritorial jurisdiction to try and punish piracy committed on the high seas?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Piracy is a crime against all humanity (hostes humani generis) and is subject to universal jurisdiction, triable by any state whose courts obtain custody over the offenders.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, par. 5, RPC (Extraterritorial application for crimes against international law / piracy); Universal Jurisdiction Doctrine. Applicability: Applicable because piracy is an international crime punishable anywhere regardless of where committed or the nationality of victims.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Pirates are outlaws subject to the universal penal jurisdiction of all civilized nations. Under Art. 2(5) RPC, Philippine courts possess full extraterritorial jurisdiction over piracy on the high seas.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for qualified piracy AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Piracy is a crime against all mankind governed by universal jurisdiction; Philippine courts have extraterritorial jurisdiction to try pirates captured within its reach.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, par. 5; Art. 122 & 123, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 25

People v. Wong Cheng

CITATION Citation: 46 Phil. 729 (1922) | Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 2381.- Applicability:Applicable because drug consumption within domestic territorial waters produces deleterious public health consequences, breaching the territorial peace of the host nation.

Facts:Wong Cheng smoked opium on board a merchant vessel of English registry anchored in Manila Bay, within two and a half miles from shore.

Accused's Defense:The accused demurred to the information, contending that smoking opium aboard a foreign merchant ship affected only internal discipline and was triable only by the ship's flag state under the French Rule.

Issue:Does smoking opium on board a foreign merchant vessel anchored in a Philippine port affect public order and fall under Philippine criminal jurisdiction?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Smoking opium aboard a vessel in domestic waters breaches the public order and morale of the host state, conferring criminal jurisdiction on Philippine courts under the English Rule.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, RPC; English Rule on Maritime Jurisdiction. Applicability: Applicable because drug consumption within domestic territorial waters produces deleterious public health consequences, breaching the territorial peace of the host nation.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Philippine jurisdiction adheres to the English Rule: crimes that disturb the peace and public order of the port are triable by local courts. Smoking opium is a public vice that breaches local order.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Demurrer OVERRULED and case remanded for trial. DOCTRINE: Under the English Rule, smoking opium on a foreign merchant vessel in a Philippine harbor breaches the peace of the port and is punishable by domestic courts.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, RPC; Act No. 2381.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 26

Miquiabas v. Commanding General

CITATION Citation: 80 Phil. 262 (1948) | Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, RPC; Art. 14, Civil Code; MBA of 1947.- Applicability:Applicable because treaty exceptions must be strictly construed; offenses by non-military personnel outside base confines revert to general domestic territorial jurisdiction.

Facts:Miquiabas, a Filipino civilian employee of the US Army at the Port of Manila, was charged with theft of US Army supplies committed in the Port Area (outside an authorized military base) and tried by a US General Court-Martial.

Accused's Defense:Petitioner filed habeas corpus, arguing that US military courts had no jurisdiction over Filipino civilians committing offenses outside designated US military bases.

Issue:Did US military tribunals possess jurisdiction over a Filipino civilian for offenses committed outside stipulated military bases under the Bases Agreement?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Under the Military Bases Agreement, jurisdiction over offenses committed by civilians outside designated bases belongs exclusively to Philippine civil courts pursuant to the Territoriality Principle.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, RPC; Art. 14, Civil Code; US-RP Military Bases Agreement of 1947. Applicability: Applicable because treaty exceptions must be strictly construed; offenses by non-military personnel outside base confines revert to general domestic territorial jurisdiction.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the alleged theft took place in the Port Area of Manila and Miquiabas was a civilian, he was not subject to military court-martial jurisdiction. Territorial jurisdiction remained with Philippine courts.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for habeas corpus GRANTED; court-martial proceedings declared NULL AND VOID. DOCTRINE: Treaty exceptions to territorial penal jurisdiction must be strictly construed; civilian offenses outside military bases remain under Philippine civil courts.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, RPC; Art. 14, Civil Code; MBA of 1947.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 27

Suzette Nicolas vs. Alberto Romulo (Smith / VFA Case)

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 175888, February 11, 2009 | Topic: Characteristics: Territoriality Principle & Extraterritoriality

Statutory Anchor:Art. 2, RPC; Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. V, Sec. 10, VFA.- Applicability:Applicable because the execution of penal sentences and custody over convicted criminals within Philippine territory belong exclusively to Philippine authorities.

Facts:Lance Corporal Daniel Smith, a US serviceman visiting the Philippines under the Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA), was convicted of rape by the RTC of Makati and detained at the US Embassy pursuant to a transfer agreement between the DFA and the US Ambassador.

Accused's Defense:Respondents (Philippine Executive officials) argued that custody of US military personnel convicted by Philippine courts could be maintained in US facilities under the VFA during the pendency of appellate review.

Issue:Does the Visiting Forces Agreement authorize detention of a convicted foreign serviceman inside a foreign embassy instead of a Philippine detention facility?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. While the VFA is constitutional, detention of a convicted serviceman must be served in Philippine correctional facilities under Philippine authority as mandated by the VFA text itself.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 2, RPC (Territoriality); 1987 Constitution; Visiting Forces Agreement (VFA), Art. V, Sec. 10. Applicability: Applicable because the execution of penal sentences and custody over convicted criminals within Philippine territory belong exclusively to Philippine authorities.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The Romulo-Kenney Agreements transferring Smith to the US Embassy violated the VFA. The VFA provides that detention of US personnel shall be by Philippine authorities in facilities agreed upon by both governments.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Romulo-Kenney Agreements declared VOID; Secretary of Foreign Affairs directed to negotiate detention inside Philippine facilities. DOCTRINE: The VFA is constitutional, but convicted foreign servicemen must serve detention in facilities under the control of Philippine authorities.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 2, RPC; Art. 14, Civil Code; Art. V, Sec. 10, VFA.
•

III, Sec. 22) • Total Cases: 6Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the constitutional ban against ex post facto legislation and bills of attainder, mandating that penal statutes operate prospectively unless a subsequent law is favorable to the accused who is not a habitual delinquent under Article 62(5).

CASE 28

Gumabon v. Director of Prisons

CITATION Citation: 37 SCRA 420 (1971) | Topic: Characteristics: Prospectivity & Retroactivity Favorable to Accused

Statutory Anchor:Art. 22, RPC; Art. 8, Civil Code; Art. 134 & 135, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because judicial interpretations favorable to the accused have the force of law and must be applied retroactively under Article 22 to prevent unjust continued imprisonment.

Facts:Gumabon and co-petitioners were convicted in 1953 of the complex crime of 'Rebellion with Murder, Arson, and Robbery' and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. Subsequently, in 1956, the Supreme Court ruled in People v. Hernandez that rebellion cannot be complexed with common crimes. Petitioners sought habeas corpus for release, having served the maximum penalty for simple rebellion.

Accused's Defense:Petitioners argued that the favorable judicial doctrine in People v. Hernandez should be given retroactive effect pursuant to Article 22 of the RPC, entitling them to immediate release.

Issue:Does Article 22 of the RPC (retroactivity of favorable penal laws) apply to favorable judicial doctrines established after final conviction?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Judicial decisions applying or interpreting penal laws form part of the legal system and must be given retroactive application when favorable to a convicted person who is not a habitual delinquent.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 22, RPC; Art. 8, Civil Code (Judicial decisions form part of the legal system). Applicability: Applicable because judicial interpretations favorable to the accused have the force of law and must be applied retroactively under Article 22 to prevent unjust continued imprisonment.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the complex crime of rebellion was declared non-existent in Hernandez, petitioners' proper liability was only for simple rebellion, whose penalty they had already fully served.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for habeas corpus GRANTED; petitioners ordered IMMEDIATELY RELEASED. DOCTRINE: Favorable judicial decisions interpreting penal laws apply retroactively to prisoners serving final sentences pursuant to Article 22 of the RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 22, RPC; Art. 8, Civil Code; Art. 134 & 135, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 29

People v. Narvaez

CITATION Citation: 121 SCRA 389 (1983) | Topic: Characteristics: Prospectivity & Retroactivity Favorable to Accused

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 13, par. 1 & 6; Art. 69; Art. 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because unlawful aggression against property rights, while insufficient for complete justification of killing, satisfies the first requirement of incomplete self-defense under Article 69.

Facts:Mamerto Narvaez shot and killed Fleischer and Rubia while they were constructing a fence across Narvaez's property that enclosed his house and disrupted his livelihood. Narvaez was convicted of double murder.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked defense of property under Art. 11(1) and passionate obfuscation under Art. 13(6), arguing that the victims' aggressive destruction of his property constituted unlawful aggression mitigating his liability.

Issue:Does defense of property against unlawful fencing justify homicide or entitle the accused to incomplete self-defense and mitigating circumstances?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Incomplete Self-Defense & Mitigating Circumstances). Defense of property without physical aggression against the person cannot completely justify killing, but entitles the accused to incomplete defense of property/person and mitigating circumstances.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 13, pars. 1 & 6; Art. 69, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because unlawful aggression against property rights, while insufficient for complete justification of killing, satisfies the first requirement of incomplete self-defense under Article 69.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victims' aggressive fencing of Narvaez's property was unlawful aggression against his property rights. Lacking reasonable necessity of the means employed to repel it, Narvaez was entitled to incomplete defense of property (privileged mitigation) and passion/obfuscation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Murder to Double Homicide with penalty reduced to 4 months of arresto mayor to 2 years and 4 months of prision correccional; accused ordered released due to credit for preventive imprisonment. DOCTRINE: Unlawful aggression against property warrants incomplete defense under Art. 69 and mitigating circumstances.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 13, par. 1 & 6; Art. 69; Art. 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 30

People v. Ringor

CITATION Citation: 320 SCRA 342 (1999) | Topic: Characteristics: Prospectivity & Retroactivity Favorable to Accused

Statutory Anchor:Art. 22, RPC; RA 8294; PD 1866; Art. 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 22 mandates that any penal statute abolishing a separate crime or reducing penalties must be applied retroactively to pending appeals.

Facts:Ringor shot and killed a victim using an unlicensed firearm. The trial court convicted him of two separate crimes: Murder and Illegal Possession of Firearms under PD 1866. While the case was on appeal, RA 8294 was enacted, providing that illegal possession of firearm cannot be charged as a separate crime if another crime (homicide or murder) was committed.

Accused's Defense:The accused argued that RA 8294 was favorable to him and must be applied retroactively under Article 22 of the RPC, requiring dismissal of the separate charge for illegal possession of firearm.

Issue:Should the amendatory law (RA 8294) treating illegal possession of firearms merely as an aggravating circumstance in murder be applied retroactively to favor the accused?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. RA 8294, being favorable to the accused by absorbing the firearm charge rather than punishing it as a separate offense, must be given retroactive application.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 22, RPC; RA 8294 amending PD 1866; Retroactive Effect of Favorable Penal Laws. Applicability: Applicable because Article 22 mandates that any penal statute abolishing a separate crime or reducing penalties must be applied retroactively to pending appeals.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Under RA 8294, if an unlicensed firearm is used in murder, it is merely an aggravating circumstance, not a separate felony. Because this avoids a separate conviction and penalty, it is favorable and retroactively applies under Art. 22.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Murder AFFIRMED; separate conviction for Illegal Possession of Firearm REVERSED and DISMISSED. DOCTRINE: Favorable penal amendments absorbing or decriminalizing separate offenses apply retroactively under Art. 22 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 22, RPC; RA 8294; PD 1866; Art. 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 31

People v. Pimentel

CITATION Citation: 288 SCRA 542 (1998) | Topic: Characteristics: Prospectivity & Retroactivity Favorable to Accused

Statutory Anchor:Art. 22, RPC; RA 8294; Art. 134, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 22 gives retroactive effect to penal statutes that decriminalize acts or reduce liability in favor of an accused.

Facts:Pimentel was charged with Rebellion and a separate charge for Illegal Possession of Firearms in furtherance of rebellion. During trial, RA 8294 was passed, which expressly repealed PD 1866's provision on separate liability when the firearm was used in rebellion.

Accused's Defense:The accused moved to quash the separate information for illegal possession of firearm on the ground that under RA 8294, illegal possession is absorbed in rebellion and can no longer be prosecuted separately.

Issue:Does the passage of RA 8294 retroactively apply to dismiss separate prosecutions for illegal possession of firearms committed in furtherance of rebellion?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. RA 8294 is a favorable penal statute that retroactively decriminalizes the separate offense of illegal possession of firearms when committed in connection with rebellion.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 22, RPC; RA 8294; Absorption Doctrine in Political Crimes. Applicability: Applicable because Article 22 gives retroactive effect to penal statutes that decriminalize acts or reduce liability in favor of an accused.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Since the firearm was used in furtherance of rebellion, RA 8294 absorbs the firearm possession into the political crime of rebellion. Prosecuting the firearm offense separately is no longer legally permissible.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Order granting motion to quash the firearm charge AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Favorable statutory amendments that absorb or extinguish separate penal liability apply retroactively to pending criminal prosecutions under Article 22 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 22, RPC; RA 8294; Art. 134, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 32

People v. Lacson

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 149453, 1 April 2003 & 7 October 2003 | Topic: Characteristics: Prospectivity & Retroactivity Favorable to Accused

Statutory Anchor:Art. 22, RPC; Rule 117, Sec. 8, Rules of Court; Art. 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 22 applies strictly to substantive penal laws; procedural time-bars operate prospectively unless clear legislative or rule intent allows retroactive operation without prejudicing public justice.

Facts:Panfilo Lacson and others were charged with murder in connection with the Kuratong Baleleng rubout incident. The case was provisionally dismissed in March 1999. In December 2000, the new Revised Rules of Criminal Procedure (Rule 117, Sec. 8) took effect, establishing a 2-year time-bar for reviving provisionally dismissed cases. In June 2001, the State revived the murder charges.

Accused's Defense:Lacson argued that Rule 117, Section 8 was a favorable penal rule that must be applied retroactively, barring the revival of the murder cases after the lapse of two years from the March 1999 dismissal.

Issue:Can the 2-year time-bar under Rule 117, Section 8 be applied retroactively to provisional dismissals that occurred before the rule's effectivity?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO (unless express conditions are met prospectively). Procedural rules creating a time-bar cannot be applied retroactively to extinguish criminal liability if doing so deprives the State of notice and fair opportunity to comply with the new time limits.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 22, RPC; Rule 117, Sec. 8, Rules of Criminal Procedure; Doctrine on Retroactivity of Procedural vs. Substantive Penal Laws. Applicability: Applicable because Article 22 applies strictly to substantive penal laws; procedural time-bars operate prospectively unless clear legislative or rule intent allows retroactive operation without prejudicing public justice.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Rule 117, Sec. 8 is a procedural rule with prospective effect. To apply the 2-year bar retroactively to a 1999 dismissal would unfairly extinguish murder charges without giving the State the 2-year period from the date of the new rule's adoption.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:State's motion for reconsideration GRANTED; revival of the criminal cases ALLOWED to proceed. DOCTRINE: Procedural time-bars under the Rules of Court do not automatically enjoy substantive retroactive application under Art. 22 RPC if doing so violates procedural due process.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 22, RPC; Rule 117, Sec. 8, Rules of Court; Art. 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 33

Joemar Ortega vs. People of the Philippines

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 151085, August 20, 2008 | Topic: Characteristics: Prospectivity & Retroactivity Favorable to Accused

Statutory Anchor:Art. 22, RPC; Indeterminate Sentence Law.- Applicability:Applicable because the amendatory statute lowered the imposable penalty scale for the offense without the accused being a habitual delinquent.

Facts:Joemar Ortega was convicted of an offense and sentenced under older statutory penalty provisions. On appeal, an amendatory statute had modified the penalty scale and provided more favorable graduated penalties.

Accused's Defense:The accused contended that the amendatory statute reducing the imposable penalty should be applied retroactively in his favor pursuant to Article 22 of the Revised Penal Code.

Issue:Is the accused entitled to the retroactive benefit of an amendatory penal law reducing the penalty for his offense?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Under Article 22 of the Revised Penal Code, penal laws shall have a retroactive effect in so far as they favor the persons guilty of a felony.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 22, RPC (Retroactivity of Favorable Penal Laws). Applicability: Applicable because the amendatory statute lowered the imposable penalty scale for the offense without the accused being a habitual delinquent.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the new statutory provision reduced the penalty for the crime and the accused was not disqualified as a habitual criminal, the favorable penalty must be applied retroactively under Article 22.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction AFFIRMED with MODIFIED, REDUCED penalty. DOCTRINE: Favorable amendatory penal statutes reducing penalties must be applied retroactively to all pending cases under Art. 22 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 22, RPC; Indeterminate Sentence Law.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).

Topic: Construction & Interpretation of Penal Laws

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Rule of Lenity; In Dubio Pro Reo; Article 4, Civil Code; Spanish Text Primacy (Act No. 2711 / Revised Administrative Code) • Total Cases: 7Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the canon of strict construction against the State and liberal interpretation in favor of the accused, resolving all statutory ambiguities, linguistic discrepancies between Spanish and English texts, and factual doubts in favor of innocence.

CASE 34

Centeno v. Villalon-Pornillos

CITATION Citation: 236 SCRA 197 (1994) | Topic: Construction & Interpretation of Penal Laws

Statutory Anchor:Art. 21, RPC; PD 1564; Strict Construction Rule.- Applicability:Applicable because criminal liability cannot be created by judicial expansion or analogical extension of statutory terms to conduct not clearly covered by the legislature.

Facts:Martin Centeno and church officers solicited voluntary contributions for the renovation of a Catholic chapel without obtaining a prior permit from the Department of Social Welfare, leading to their prosecution under PD 1564 (Solicitation Permit Law).

Accused's Defense:The accused argued that PD 1564 strictly penalized solicitation for 'charitable or public welfare purposes' and did not include solicitations for 'religious purposes', invoking strict construction of penal statutes.

Issue:Can the term 'charitable purposes' in a penal statute be broadly construed to include solicitations for 'religious purposes'?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Penal statutes must be strictly construed against the State and liberally in favor of the accused; terms cannot be extended by judicial construction to include matters not expressly covered.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Rule of Strict Construction of Penal Laws; Doctrine of In Dubio Pro Reo; Art. 21, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because criminal liability cannot be created by judicial expansion or analogical extension of statutory terms to conduct not clearly covered by the legislature.
•
[A] APPLICATION:PD 1564 refers only to charitable and public welfare solicitations. Religious solicitations are separate and distinct. Expanding the penal scope to include religious purposes violates the rule of strict construction.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction REVERSED and accused ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Penal laws are strictly construed against the State and liberally in favor of the accused; crimes cannot be created by loose interpretation or analogy.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 21, RPC; PD 1564; Strict Construction Rule.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part I: Preliminary Principles, Sources, Constitutional Limitations & Characteristics (Articles 1-2 RPC).
CASE 35

People v. Abuyen

CITATION Citation: 52 SCRA 25 (1973) | Topic: Construction & Interpretation of Penal Laws

Statutory Anchor:Act No. 3815 (RPC Spanish Original); Strict Construction Rule.- Applicability:Applicable because Act No. 3815 (RPC) was approved by the Philippine Legislature in Spanish, making the Spanish original the authoritative source of legislative intent.

Facts:The accused was prosecuted under a criminal statute where the English and Spanish texts contained differing shades of meaning regarding the statutory elements of the offense.

Accused's Defense:The accused argued that pursuant to legal rules of construction, where ambiguity exists in the Revised Penal Code, the Spanish text in which the code was originally enacted must prevail.

Issue:Which text controls in the interpretation of the Revised Penal Code when there is a discrepancy between the English translation and the official Spanish original?

•
