[A] APPLICATION:Without conspiracy, the act of one is not the act of all. Because the State failed to prove which officer's bullet hit the victim, proximate cause was not established as to the petitioner.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Homicide REVERSED and accused ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Without conspiracy, criminal liability for homicide under Art. 4(1) RPC requires direct proof linking the specific accused's bullet to the fatal injury.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 72

People v. Adriano

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 205228, 15 July 2015 | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because when an attack is treacherous from its inception, the qualifying circumstance applies to all victims killed by the assault under Article 4(1).

Facts:Adriano and armed companions opened fire on their intended target, Danilo Cabanas, inside a vehicle. Stray bullets missed Cabanas and struck an innocent bystander, 7-year-old girl Ofelia, instantly killing her.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed lack of intent to shoot or kill the young girl, asserting that she was hit purely by accident (aberratio ictus) and treachery could not apply to the unintended victim.

Issue:Under Article 4(1) RPC (aberratio ictus), is the killing of an unintended third party by stray gunfire murder or homicide, and does treachery qualify the killing?

•
[A] ANSWER:MURDER. Under Article 4(1), an assailant is liable for the death of an unintended third party (aberratio ictus); treachery qualifying the attack against the intended target transfers to the unintended victim.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 1, RPC (Aberratio Ictus / Mistake in Blow); Art. 248, RPC (Treachery). Applicability: Applicable because when an attack is treacherous from its inception, the qualifying circumstance applies to all victims killed by the assault under Article 4(1).
•
[A] APPLICATION:The gunmen ambushed Cabanas with sudden, overwhelming gunfire (treachery). Under aberratio ictus, the felonious intent and treachery transferred to the fatal shooting of the young girl.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: In aberratio ictus (mistake in the blow) under Art. 4(1) RPC, treachery present in the primary assault transfers to and qualifies the killing of the unintended bystander.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 73

People v. Bendecio

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 138981, 16 October 2000 | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because throwing a lethal stone during a brawl is an unlawful act; the accidental hitting of an unintended victim is a direct consequence punishable under Article 4(1).

Facts:Bendecio threw a heavy stone at his intended rival during a brawl. The stone missed the rival and struck an innocent bystander in the head, causing severe skull fracture and death.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that he had no intention to injure the bystander and that missing his target was an accident that should excuse or reduce his liability.

Issue:Is the accused criminally liable for homicide when his felonious missile misses the intended target and kills an innocent bystander (aberratio ictus)?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Homicide under Art. 4[1] RPC). Under aberratio ictus, throwing a lethal projectile unlawfully transfers criminal liability for homicide to the unintended fatality.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 1, RPC (Aberratio Ictus); Art. 249, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because throwing a lethal stone during a brawl is an unlawful act; the accidental hitting of an unintended victim is a direct consequence punishable under Article 4(1).
•
[A] APPLICATION:The act of hurling a large stone was felonious. Under Art. 4(1), the accused is criminally responsible for the death resulting from his unlawful missile, even though the person killed was different from the one intended.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: In aberratio ictus, an offender throwing a dangerous projectile is fully liable for homicide under Art. 4(1) RPC if it strikes and kills an unintended bystander.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 74

People v. Gemoya

CITATION Citation: 342 SCRA 63 (2000) | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 49, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because shooting an intended human target under a mistake of identity does not negate criminal intent; the offender is fully liable for the homicide or murder committed.

Facts:Gemoya and companions stalked and shot a man whom they mistakenly believed to be their mortal enemy, 'Wilfredo'. The victim was actually an innocent man named Rosendo who bore a strong physical resemblance to Wilfredo.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that because they intended to shoot Wilfredo and not Rosendo, they were acting under an error in personae and could not be convicted of intentional murder of Rosendo.

Issue:How does mistake in identity (error in personae) affect criminal liability for murder under Article 4(1) and Article 49 of the RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:LIABLE FOR MURDER (under Art. 4[1] and Art. 49). In error in personae, the accused is criminally liable for the felony committed; the penalty rule in Art. 49 applies if the intended crime carries a different penalty.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 1; Art. 49; Art. 248, RPC (Error in Personae). Applicability: Applicable because shooting an intended human target under a mistake of identity does not negate criminal intent; the offender is fully liable for the homicide or murder committed.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The killers intended to kill a human being with treachery and executed their plan. Mistaking Rosendo for Wilfredo was error in personae, which does not diminish criminal liability for murder under Art. 4(1).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: In error in personae (mistake in identity), criminal liability for murder is not extinguished under Art. 4(1) RPC, as the felonious intent to kill was present.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 49, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 75

People v. Guillen

CITATION Citation: 85 Phil. 307 (1950) | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 48, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because a single felonious explosion producing multiple crimes creates a compound complex crime under Article 48, where the lack of specific intent toward bystanders is overridden by Article 4(1).

Facts:Julio Guillen hurled a hand grenade at President Manuel Roxas during a public political rally at Plaza Miranda. The grenade bounced off the grandstand and exploded in the crowd, killing Simeon Varela and seriously wounding several others, while President Roxas escaped unharmed.

Accused's Defense:Guillen admitted throwing the grenade to assassinate President Roxas, but claimed he had no personal grudge or intent to kill Simeon Varela or injure the bystanders (praeter intentionem).

Issue:Does the throwing of a grenade to assassinate a public figure which kills an unintended bystander constitute the complex crime of Murder with Attempted Murder under Article 48 and Article 4(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. By performing a single act (throwing a grenade) that produced murder and multiple attempted murders, the accused is guilty of a complex crime under Article 48, punishable by the maximum penalty for the gravest offense.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 1; Art. 48; Art. 248, RPC (Complex Crime / Aberratio Ictus). Applicability: Applicable because a single felonious explosion producing multiple crimes creates a compound complex crime under Article 48, where the lack of specific intent toward bystanders is overridden by Article 4(1).
•
[A] APPLICATION:Guillen acted with direct intent to kill using explosives (murder). Under Art. 4(1) and Art. 48, his single act produced Murder of Varela and Multiple Attempted Murders of other attendees, requiring the death penalty.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Guillen CONVICTED of the Complex Crime of Murder with Multiple Attempted Murders and sentenced to DEATH. DOCTRINE: Throwing a grenade that kills unintended bystanders while targeting another creates a complex crime under Art. 48 and Art. 4(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 48, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 76

People v. Sabalones

CITATION Citation: 294 SCRA 751 (1998) | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 49, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the unlawful act of ambushing a vehicle with automatic weapons was deliberate and felonious; mistaking the identity of the passengers does not negate culpability.

Facts:Sabalones and his armed gang ambushed and riddled a vehicle with high-powered gunfire, believing it carried their rival Beronga and his men. The vehicle actually carried innocent civilians, killing two passengers and severely wounding others.

Accused's Defense:Accused contended that they were acting under mistake in identity (error in personae) and aberratio ictus, arguing that the absence of intent to kill these specific innocent victims precluded murder.

Issue:Does mistake in identity (error in personae) or aberratio ictus exempt ambushing gunmen from murder liability under Article 4(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Under Article 4(1) RPC, an assailant who commits a treacherous ambush is fully liable for murder even if the persons killed were not the intended enemies.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 1; Art. 248; Art. 49, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the unlawful act of ambushing a vehicle with automatic weapons was deliberate and felonious; mistaking the identity of the passengers does not negate culpability.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The execution of the ambush was planned and treacherous. Whether treated as error in personae or aberratio ictus, the perpetrators are fully responsible for the resulting deaths and injuries under Art. 4(1).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Convictions for Two Counts of Murder and Multiple Frustrated Murders AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Mistake of identity (error in personae) does not mitigate or excuse liability for murder under Art. 4(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 49, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 77

People v. Hilario

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 128732, 2 March 1999 | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because shooting at a human being with intent to kill is an intentional felony; the stray bullet hitting another does not convert the intentional crime into mere negligence.

Facts:Hilario aimed and fired his gun at his adversary during an argument. The bullet missed the adversary and struck an innocent companion walking beside him, causing instant death.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked aberratio ictus and lack of motive against the companion, claiming that the death was accidental and should be punished as simple reckless imprudence.

Issue:Is the killing of an innocent companion through aberratio ictus punishable as an intentional felony (homicide/murder) under Article 4(1) RPC or simple negligence?

•
[A] ANSWER:INTENTIONAL FELONY (Homicide under Art. 4[1] RPC). In aberratio ictus, the felonious intent to kill directed at one person is transferred by law to the unintended victim who is killed.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 1; Art. 249, RPC (Aberratio Ictus Doctrine). Applicability: Applicable because shooting at a human being with intent to kill is an intentional felony; the stray bullet hitting another does not convert the intentional crime into mere negligence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Hilario intentionally fired a deadly weapon with homicidal intent. Under Art. 4(1), he is liable for the intentional killing of the companion despite the error in the direction of the blow.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: In aberratio ictus, homicidal intent directed at one person transfers to the unintended victim, resulting in liability for an intentional felony under Art. 4(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 78

People v. Balmores

CITATION Citation: 85 Phil. 493 (1950) | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(2), 48, 166, 315, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 4(2) applies only when the act performed does not constitute any other punishable felony under the Revised Penal Code.

Facts:Balmores altered a losing Philippine Charity Sweepstakes ticket by pasting digits to match the first-prize winning ticket and presented it for payment at the PCSO teller window, where the teller immediately detected the forgery.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that the forgery was so clumsy and obvious that it was an impossible crime under Article 4(2) RPC rather than consummated falsification and attempted estafa.

Issue:Does the clumsy alteration of a lottery ticket presented for encashment constitute an impossible crime under Article 4(2) or the complex crime of Attempted Estafa through Falsification of an Obligation/Document under Articles 166 and 48 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:COMPLEX CRIME OF ATTEMPTED ESTAFA THROUGH FALSIFICATION. An impossible crime occurs only when the act is inherently impossible of consummation and does not constitute any other felony; altering the ticket constituted consummated falsification.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 2; Art. 48; Art. 166, RPC (Falsification & Impossible Crime Doctrine). Applicability: Applicable because Article 4(2) applies only when the act performed does not constitute any other punishable felony under the Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Balmores completed the alteration of the ticket (falsification). Because his act constituted the felony of falsification, it could not be relegated to an impossible crime under Article 4(2).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ATTEMPTED ESTAFA THROUGH FALSIFICATION OF GOVERNMENT OBLIGATION AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: If the acts performed already constitute an independent felony (e.g. falsification), Art. 4(2) on impossible crime cannot apply.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(2), 48, 166, 315, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 79

Intod v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: 215 SCRA 52 (1992) | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(2), 59, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the offenders performed all acts with intent to kill, but the execution was inherently impossible due to the total physical absence of the target victim.

Facts:Sulpicio Intod and three armed companions went to the house of Bernardina Palangpangan with intent to kill her. They fired multiple rifle shots directly into her bedroom. Unknown to them, Palangpangan was sleeping elsewhere that night, and the room was empty.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that because the intended victim was not in the room, it was physically impossible to kill her, rendering their liability an impossible crime under Article 4(2) RPC rather than attempted murder.

Issue:Does firing into an empty bedroom where the intended victim is absent constitute Attempted Murder under Art. 6 or an Impossible Crime under Art. 4(2) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:IMPOSSIBLE CRIME (Article 4, Paragraph 2 RPC). The crime was an impossible crime due to physical impossibility; the evil intent could not produce a crime against persons because the intended victim was not present.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 2; Art. 59, RPC (Impossible Crimes due to Physical or Legal Impossibility). Applicability: Applicable because the offenders performed all acts with intent to kill, but the execution was inherently impossible due to the total physical absence of the target victim.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Under Art. 4(2), criminal liability is incurred for an act which would be an offense against persons were it not for the inherent physical impossibility of its accomplishment. Firing at an empty bed is the classic example of physical impossibility.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Attempted Murder to IMPOSSIBLE CRIME under Art. 4(2) RPC (penalty of arresto mayor imposed under Art. 59). DOCTRINE: Firing at an empty room where the target is absent constitutes an impossible crime under Art. 4(2) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(2), 59, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).
CASE 80

Jacinto v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 162540, 13 July 2009 | Topic: Criminal Liability: Praeter Intentionem, Aberratio Ictus, Error in Personae, Impossible Crimes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(2), 59, 310, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the offender had the evil intent to commit qualified theft, but the crime against property was impossible of accomplishment due to the inherent worthless nature of the check.

Facts:Gemma Jacinto, a collector for Mega Foam, received a postdated check of P10,000 from a customer. Instead of remitting it to the company, she conspired to deposit it into her husband's bank account. Unknown to her, the check was completely unfunded and bounced upon presentment.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that because the check bounced and had no monetary value, no actual theft or gain occurred, claiming she could not be convicted of qualified theft.

Issue:Is the unlawful taking and deposit of a postdated check that bounces an impossible crime under Article 4(2) RPC or Qualified Theft under Article 310?

•
[A] ANSWER:IMPOSSIBLE CRIME. The unlawful taking of a worthless bouncing check constitutes an impossible crime of qualified theft due to factual/legal impossibility of gaining monetary value from a worthless check.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 2; Art. 59; Art. 308 & 310, RPC (Impossible Crime of Theft). Applicability: Applicable because the offender had the evil intent to commit qualified theft, but the crime against property was impossible of accomplishment due to the inherent worthless nature of the check.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the check was unfunded and dishonored, Mega Foam suffered no pecuniary loss and the accused derived no gain. The acts satisfied all elements of an impossible crime under Article 4(2).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Qualified Theft to IMPOSSIBLE CRIME under Art. 4(2) and Art. 59 RPC (sentenced to 6 months of arresto mayor and fine). DOCTRINE: Stealing a worthless bouncing check constitutes an impossible crime under Art. 4(2) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(2), 59, 310, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part II: Felonies, Dolo/Culpa, Mistake of Fact, Proximate Cause & Impossible Crimes (Articles 3-5 RPC).

Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 6, Revised Penal Code; Subjective and Objective Phases of Felonies • Total Cases: 23Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the progressive development of felonies from external overt inception without all acts of execution (attempted), through performance of all acts of execution that fail to produce the felony due to independent causes (frustrated), to complete realization of all statutory elements (consummated).

CASE 81

United States v. Eduave

CITATION Citation: 36 Phil. 209 (1917) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the wound was mortal and all executive acts were completed; survival resulted purely from independent medical intervention, fulfilling the statutory definition of a frustrated felony.

Facts:Eduave stabbed a young girl in the back with a dagger, inflicting a deep penetrating wound that would have caused fatal hemorrhage had it not been for immediate, skillful surgical and medical intervention.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that because the victim survived and recovered, he should only be held liable for attempted homicide, claiming he did not perform all acts of execution.

Issue:Is the crime Frustrated Murder or Attempted Murder when the assailant inflicts a mortal wound performing all acts of execution, but the victim survives due to independent medical assistance?

•
[A] ANSWER:FRUSTRATED MURDER. The crime is frustrated when the offender performs all the acts of execution which should produce the felony as a consequence, but which, nevertheless, do not produce it by reason of causes independent of the will of the perpetrator.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 2, RPC (Frustrated Felony); Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the wound was mortal and all executive acts were completed; survival resulted purely from independent medical intervention, fulfilling the statutory definition of a frustrated felony.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Eduave inflicted a mortal stab wound, completing the subjective phase of execution. The non-fatal result was due entirely to external medical treatment, constituting frustrated murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for FRUSTRATED MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Inflicting a mortal wound where the victim survives solely through timely medical assistance constitutes a frustrated felony under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 82

People v. Enriquez

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 158797, 29 July 2005 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because when the injury is superficial and non-fatal, the subjective phase is incomplete with respect to causing death, legally precluding the frustrated stage.

Facts:Enriquez struck the victim with a bolo during an altercation, causing a superficial slash wound on the victim's shoulder that required only minor outpatient medical attention.

Accused's Defense:Accused contended that the minor, non-mortal nature of the wound showed absence of intent to kill and that he should only be convicted of slight physical injuries or attempted homicide.

Issue:Is an assailant guilty of Frustrated Homicide or Attempted Homicide when the wound inflicted is non-mortal and does not endanger the victim's life?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE. Where the wound inflicted is non-mortal, the offender has not performed all acts of execution necessary to produce death, reducing the crime to the attempted stage.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3, RPC (Attempted Felony); Art. 249, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because when the injury is superficial and non-fatal, the subjective phase is incomplete with respect to causing death, legally precluding the frustrated stage.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the bolo wound did not touch vital organs and was non-fatal, the acts of execution were not fully performed to cause death. With intent to kill present, the offense is attempted homicide.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Frustrated Homicide to ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE. DOCTRINE: If the wound inflicted is non-mortal, the crime is only Attempted Homicide under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 83

People v. Listerio

CITATION Citation: 335 SCRA 40 (2000) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the frustrated stage requires proof that the injuries would have caused death without medical intervention; non-mortal wounds limit liability to the attempted stage.

Facts:Listerio and companions assaulted Marlon and Jeonito Araque with bladed weapons. Marlon died from multiple stab wounds, while Jeonito sustained non-fatal stab wounds requiring ten days of medical treatment.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that as to the surviving victim Jeonito, the offense was only slight physical injuries rather than frustrated murder, because the injuries were superficial.

Issue:Does inflicting non-mortal stab wounds with intent to kill constitute Attempted Murder or Frustrated Murder?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED MURDER. When the wounds inflicted are non-mortal and the victim was not in imminent danger of death, the crime is Attempted Murder.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the frustrated stage requires proof that the injuries would have caused death without medical intervention; non-mortal wounds limit liability to the attempted stage.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Medical evidence confirmed that Jeonito's wounds were superficial and not fatal. While intent to kill was present, the failure to inflict mortal wounds reduced the crime as to Jeonito to attempted murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED to Murder (as to Marlon) and ATTEMPTED MURDER (as to Jeonito). DOCTRINE: Assault with intent to kill resulting in non-mortal wounds constitutes Attempted, not Frustrated, Murder.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 84

People v. Erinia

CITATION Citation: 84 Phil. 589 (1949) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 249, 254, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because intent to kill (animus interficiendi) elevates the act of firing a gun from mere illegal discharge under Article 254 to attempted homicide under Article 6.

Facts:Erinia discharged his firearm at a person during a heated dispute. The shot missed the intended victim and hit nobody. The prosecution charged him with Attempted Homicide.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that merely firing a shot without hitting anyone constituted the lesser offense of Illegal Discharge of Firearm under Article 254 RPC rather than attempted homicide.

Issue:Does discharging a firearm directly at a person with intent to kill constitute Attempted Homicide under Art. 6 or Illegal Discharge of Firearm under Art. 254 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE. Firing a firearm directly at a person with intent to kill is an overt executive act of homicide, constituting Attempted Homicide; illegal discharge applies only when intent to kill is absent.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 249 & 254, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because intent to kill (animus interficiendi) elevates the act of firing a gun from mere illegal discharge under Article 254 to attempted homicide under Article 6.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Erinia aimed directly at the victim with clear intent to kill. The missing of the shot was a cause independent of his will, completing the elements of attempted homicide.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Firing a firearm directly at an individual with intent to kill constitutes Attempted Homicide under Art. 6 RPC, absorbing illegal discharge.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 249, 254, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 85

People v. Hernandez

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 141221, 7 March 2002 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 266-A, 336, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because commencement of the crime by overt acts directed toward carnal knowledge, interrupted by external arrival of the mother, fulfills the attempted stage.

Facts:Hernandez forced a 12-year-old girl into a secluded area, stripped her clothes, and lay on top of her with an erect penis. Before any penile contact or penetration could occur, the victim's mother shouted and arrived, causing Hernandez to flee.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that without any physical penetration or touching of the sexual organ, he committed only acts of lasciviousness, not attempted rape.

Issue:Does mounting a naked victim with an erect penis with intent to have carnal knowledge constitute Attempted Rape or Acts of Lasciviousness?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED RAPE. Laying on top of a naked victim with an erect organ ready to penetrate constitutes the commencement of rape by overt acts directly pointing to carnal knowledge.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 266-A, RPC (Attempted Rape). Applicability: Applicable because commencement of the crime by overt acts directed toward carnal knowledge, interrupted by external arrival of the mother, fulfills the attempted stage.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Hernandez performed overt acts demonstrating unambiguous intent to have sexual intercourse. The intervention of the mother prevented consummation, making the offense attempted rape.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ATTEMPTED RAPE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Overt acts directly commencing carnal knowledge, interrupted by an external cause prior to penetration, constitute Attempted Rape under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 266-A, 336, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 86

People v. Orita

CITATION Citation: 184 SCRA 105 (1990) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 266-A, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because under established criminal law doctrine, rape requires no full penetration or hymenal rupture; the slightest labial entry completes all statutory elements.

Facts:Orita dragged the victim into a grassy area, undressed her, and pressed his male organ against her labia majora, producing slight labial lacerations, but did not achieve full penile insertion into the vaginal canal.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that without full vaginal penetration or rupture of the hymen, he could only be convicted of frustrated rape or attempted rape.

Issue:Is there a crime of 'Frustrated Rape' under Philippine criminal law, and does mere entry of the labia consummate rape?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO FRUSTRATED RAPE / CONSUMMATED RAPE. There is no frustrated rape in Philippine jurisprudence; the slightest touching or penetration of the labia majora/pudenda by the male organ consummates the crime of rape.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6 & Art. 335 / 266-A, RPC (Consummation of Rape). Applicability: Applicable because under established criminal law doctrine, rape requires no full penetration or hymenal rupture; the slightest labial entry completes all statutory elements.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Medical findings showed contusions on the labia majora. Because the male organ made entry into the labia, all elements of rape were executed, consummating the felony.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for CONSUMMATED RAPE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: In rape, the slightest penetration of the labia consummates the felony; there is no intermediate stage of 'frustrated rape' under Philippine law.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 266-A, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 87

People v. Campuhan

CITATION Citation: 329 SCRA 270 (2000) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 266-A, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because entry into the pudenda/labia is the defining boundary between attempted and consummated rape.

Facts:Campuhan placed his penis on top of the mons pubis and between the thighs of a 4-year-old girl. Medical examination showed completely intact hymen, no vaginal laceration, and no semen inside the vaginal orifice.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that without proof of penetration of the labia majora, he could not be convicted of consummated rape.

Issue:Is touching the external thighs or mons pubis without penetration of the labia majora Consummated Rape or Attempted Rape?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED RAPE. Consummation of rape requires at least the slightest penetration of the labia; rubbing the organ on the thighs or mons pubis without entering the labia constitutes Attempted Rape.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 266-A, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because entry into the pudenda/labia is the defining boundary between attempted and consummated rape.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The medical findings conclusively proved that the male organ never entered the labia majora. Because penetration was not commenced beyond the external skin, the offense remained attempted rape.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Consummated Rape to ATTEMPTED RAPE. DOCTRINE: To consummate rape, there must be proof of entry into the labia majora; external contact without labial entry is Attempted Rape.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 266-A, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 88

People vs. Agao

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 222971, 7 January 2019 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 266-A, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the prosecution bears the burden of proving labial entry beyond reasonable doubt to sustain consummated rape; failure of proof reduces the offense to attempted rape.

Facts:Agao was prosecuted for statutory rape of an 8-year-old child. The victim testified that the accused touched her private parts with his penis, but medical evidence revealed no hymenal lacerations and no labial trauma.

Accused's Defense:Accused denied penetration, asserting that the evidence failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that the penis penetrated the labia majora.

Issue:Does the evidence establish consummated rape or attempted rape where medical findings show no penetration of the labia?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED RAPE. When penetration of the labia is doubtful or unproven by medical and testimonial evidence, the accused can only be convicted of Attempted Rape.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 266-A, RPC; In Dubio Pro Reo. Applicability: Applicable because the prosecution bears the burden of proving labial entry beyond reasonable doubt to sustain consummated rape; failure of proof reduces the offense to attempted rape.
•
[A] APPLICATION:While the overt acts demonstrated intent to rape, the prosecution failed to prove labial entry. Resolving doubt in favor of the accused, the crime was attempted rape.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED to ATTEMPTED RAPE. DOCTRINE: Failure to prove labial penetration beyond reasonable doubt reduces the conviction from Consummated to Attempted Rape under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 266-A, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 89

Cruz v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 166441, 30 November 2006 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 294, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because an overt act directly commencing execution through intimidation was performed, which was interrupted by an external cause (police arrival).

Facts:Cruz approached a parked delivery truck, drew a knife, and demanded the driver hand over the cash collection. Before the driver could give the money, a passing police patrol car arrived, prompting Cruz to run away empty-handed.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that because no money was taken and no violence was inflicted, he performed only preparatory acts not amounting to attempted robbery.

Issue:Does demanding money at knife-point without securing the money constitute Attempted Robbery under Article 6 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The drawing of a weapon and demand for money constitute overt executive acts commencing robbery directly by intimidation; the failure to obtain cash due to police arrival constitutes Attempted Robbery.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 294, RPC (Attempted Robbery). Applicability: Applicable because an overt act directly commencing execution through intimidation was performed, which was interrupted by an external cause (police arrival).
•
[A] APPLICATION:Cruz passed beyond mere preparation into execution by using a deadly weapon to intimidate the victim. The sudden arrival of police was an external cause preventing consummation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ATTEMPTED ROBBERY AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Threatening a victim with a weapon while demanding money constitutes an overt act of Attempted Robbery under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 294, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 90

Lutap v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 177579, 13 August 2008 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 280, 299, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because unlawful entry through an unusual opening with intent to steal constitutes an executive overt act of robbery, not mere trespass.

Facts:Lutap cut the wire screen of a residential house at night, climbed through the window, and entered the bedroom. As he was searching drawers, the homeowner awoke, screamed, and apprehended him before he could carry anything away.

Accused's Defense:Accused contended that he was guilty only of trespass to dwelling, not attempted robbery, because no property was touched or taken.

Issue:Is entering a dwelling through an unusual opening at night to steal Attempted Robbery under Art. 299/6 RPC or Simple Trespass to Dwelling under Art. 280?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED ROBBERY. Entering a dwelling through an opening not intended for ingress (scaling/cutting) with intent to gain constitutes an overt commencement of Robbery in an Inhabited House.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 299, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because unlawful entry through an unusual opening with intent to steal constitutes an executive overt act of robbery, not mere trespass.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Cutting the screen and searching drawers established animus lucrandi. The homeowner's awakening was an independent external cause preventing actual taking, making the crime attempted robbery.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ATTEMPTED ROBBERY IN AN INHABITED HOUSE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Unlawful entry into a dwelling by cutting a screen with intent to steal constitutes Attempted Robbery under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 280, 299, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 91

United States v. Adiao

CITATION Citation: 38 Phil. 754 (1918) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 308, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the taking was complete once the inspector exerted control over the belt and hid it in his desk, satisfying all elements of consummated theft.

Facts:Adiao, a customs inspector, abstracted a leather belt from baggage under customs inspection and concealed it in his desk drawer inside the customs building, where it was discovered by supervisors shortly thereafter.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that because the belt was never removed from the customs building, the crime was only frustrated or attempted theft.

Issue:Is the crime of theft consummated the moment the offender obtains complete physical custody of the item with intent to gain, even if it is not removed from the premises?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Consummated Theft). Theft is consummated upon the complete taking (apoderamiento) of personal property with intent to gain; removal from the building or premises is not required.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6 & Art. 308, RPC (Elements of Consummated Theft). Applicability: Applicable because the taking was complete once the inspector exerted control over the belt and hid it in his desk, satisfying all elements of consummated theft.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The act of removing the belt from the baggage and placing it in his private desk constituted complete possession. The theft was fully consummated.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for CONSUMMATED THEFT AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Theft is consummated the moment complete unlawful custody is gained, regardless of whether the property was taken out of the building.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 308, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 92

People v. Dino

CITATION Citation: 45 O.G. 3446 (1948) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 308, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable to illustrate the jurisprudential evolution rejecting the 'frustrated theft' theory in Philippine criminal law.

Facts:Dino, a driver of an army truck inside a military depot, loaded boxes of military supplies with intent to steal them. As his truck approached the exit gate, military sentries inspected the cargo, discovered the stolen goods, and arrested him before the truck could leave the depot.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that because the supplies were intercepted at the gate and never left the military depot premises, the crime was only frustrated theft.

Issue:Under early Court of Appeals doctrine, was theft intercepted at the gate considered frustrated theft? (Reconciled by Valenzuela v. People)

•
[A] ANSWER:HISTORICAL FRUSTRATED THEFT DOCTRINE (Overruled by Valenzuela v. People). While Dino was held guilty of frustrated theft under earlier jurisprudence, the Supreme Court in Valenzuela definitively ruled that theft has no frustrated stage and is consummated upon taking.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6 & Art. 308, RPC; Overruling Doctrine of Valenzuela v. People (2007). Applicability: Applicable to illustrate the jurisprudential evolution rejecting the 'frustrated theft' theory in Philippine criminal law.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Earlier cases required the ability to freely dispose of property. In 2007, the Supreme Court abandoned Dino and ruled that unlawful taking itself consummates theft.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Historic ruling OVERRULED by Valenzuela v. People. DOCTRINE: The doctrine in People v. Dino recognizing frustrated theft is abandoned; under modern RPC jurisprudence, theft is consummated upon taking.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 308, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 93

Aristotel Valenzuela v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 160188, 21 June 2007 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 308, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 308 defines theft solely by taking (apoderamiento) with intent to gain; freedom of disposition is not a statutory element.

Facts:Valenzuela loaded stolen supermarket items into a cart, loaded them into a taxi, and was intercepted at the parking lot exit by security guards before driving away.

Accused's Defense:Accused contended that because he was caught before leaving the mall premises, he never had full unhampered disposition of the goods and could only be guilty of frustrated theft.

Issue:Can an accused be convicted of frustrated theft under the Revised Penal Code?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Theft has only two stages: Attempted and Consummated. The moment the offender takes physical possession of the personal property of another with intent to gain, the felony is consummated.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6 & Art. 308, RPC; Definitive Jurisprudential Abolition of Frustrated Theft. Applicability: Applicable because Article 308 defines theft solely by taking (apoderamiento) with intent to gain; freedom of disposition is not a statutory element.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Unlawful taking was complete the moment the detergent was loaded into the cart and taxi. The theft was fully consummated; the concept of frustrated theft does not exist under Philippine law.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for CONSUMMATED THEFT AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Under the Revised Penal Code, there is no crime of frustrated theft; theft is either attempted or consummated.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 308, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 94

People v. Lamahang

CITATION Citation: 61 Phil. 703 (1935) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 280, 299, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because attempted robbery requires overt acts showing unequivocal intention to steal, whereas making a hole could equally indicate trespass, arson, or mischief.

Facts:Aurelio Lamahang was caught at early dawn making an opening in the wall of a store using an iron bar. Before he could enter or take any property, a policeman caught him.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that making a hole in a wall was an equivocal act that did not unequivocally point to robbery, and that he could only be convicted of attempted trespass to dwelling or malicious mischief.

Issue:Does making an opening in a wall without entering or taking property constitute Attempted Robbery or Attempted Trespass to Dwelling?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED TRESPASS TO DWELLING. An attempted felony requires overt acts directly and unequivocally leading to the commission of the specific offense; where the act is equivocal, it cannot be deemed attempted robbery.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 280, 299, RPC; Equivocal Acts Doctrine. Applicability: Applicable because attempted robbery requires overt acts showing unequivocal intention to steal, whereas making a hole could equally indicate trespass, arson, or mischief.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Lamahang's act of breaking the wall showed an intent to enter, but did not directly prove intent to rob. The crime was therefore Attempted Trespass to Dwelling.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Attempted Robbery to ATTEMPTED TRESPASS TO DWELLING. DOCTRINE: An overt act must directly and unequivocally point to the specific felony intended; equivocal acts cannot sustain a conviction for attempted robbery.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 280, 299, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 95

People v. Salvilla

CITATION Citation: 184 SCRA 671 (1990) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 294, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the taking and control of the victim's money and jewelry inside the premises fully satisfied the element of unlawful taking.

Facts:Salvilla and armed robbers entered a store, seized money and jewelry, and held the owners hostage inside the building when police surrounded the premises. During negotiations inside, they retained custody of the loot in their bags before surrendering.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that because they were trapped inside the building and could not carry the loot away into the streets, the robbery was only attempted or frustrated.

Issue:Is robbery consummated the moment the culprits take possession of the loot inside the building, even if they are trapped by police and unable to carry it away?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Consummated Robbery). Robbery is consummated upon the taking of personal property by violence or intimidation; it is not necessary that the robbers leave the premises or achieve safe escape.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6 & Art. 294, RPC (Consummation of Robbery). Applicability: Applicable because the taking and control of the victim's money and jewelry inside the premises fully satisfied the element of unlawful taking.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The culprits exerted complete dominion over the money and jewelry by placing them in bags while holding the victims hostage. The robbery was fully consummated.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for CONSUMMATED ROBBERY WITH SERIOUS PHYSICAL INJURIES AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Robbery is consummated upon taking possession of property through violence/intimidation, even if the robbers are trapped inside the premises.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 294, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 96

People v. Bulalayao

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 103494, 18 August 1994 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 294(2), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because whenever a rape is committed on the occasion of a robbery, the law merges them into a single indivisible special complex crime.

Facts:Accused broke into a house, stole jewelry, and raped the female occupant before fleeing.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that robbery and rape were separate offenses and that the taking was not accompanied by violence against property.

Issue:Does the commission of rape on the occasion of robbery constitute the special complex crime of Robbery with Rape under Article 294(2) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. When rape is committed on the occasion or by reason of a robbery, all participants in the robbery are guilty of the special complex crime of Robbery with Rape.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 294, par. 2, RPC (Special Complex Crime of Robbery with Rape). Applicability: Applicable because whenever a rape is committed on the occasion of a robbery, the law merges them into a single indivisible special complex crime.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The robbery was consummated and the rape was perpetrated during the same incident. Under Art. 294(2), the offense is the single indivisible special complex crime of Robbery with Rape.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH RAPE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Rape committed on the occasion of robbery creates the special complex crime of Robbery with Rape under Art. 294(2) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 294(2), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 97

People v. Borinaga

CITATION Citation: 55 Phil. 433 (1930) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the assailant completed the full subjective phase of striking the fatal blow with treachery; non-death resulted from an external physical obstruction.

Facts:Borinaga struck a deadly knife blow from behind aiming at the victim's back. The knife pierced through the back of the heavy wooden chair the victim was sitting on and glanced off the victim's jacket, inflicting only a slight superficial scratch on his back.

Accused's Defense:Accused contended that because the injury was a mere scratch, he could only be convicted of attempted murder or slight physical injuries, not frustrated murder.

Issue:Is an assailant who strikes a lethal blow with intent to kill guilty of Frustrated Murder when the deadly blow is deflected by an external object (chair) without his knowledge?

•
[A] ANSWER:FRUSTRATED MURDER. The accused performed all the acts of execution which should have produced the murder; the failure of the fatal result was due to an external impediment (the chair) independent of the will of the perpetrator.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 2; Art. 248, RPC (Frustrated Murder). Applicability: Applicable because the assailant completed the full subjective phase of striking the fatal blow with treachery; non-death resulted from an external physical obstruction.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Borinaga delivered a knife thrust with all his force into what he believed was the victim's vital organs. Having executed every act required on his part to kill, the offense was frustrated murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for FRUSTRATED MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Delivering a fatal blow that is deflected by an external obstacle after completing all acts of execution constitutes Frustrated Murder under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 98

People v. Sy Pio

CITATION Citation: 94 Phil. 885 (1954) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because where the wound is non-mortal and does not produce death by external medical intervention, all acts of execution have not been performed.

Facts:Sy Pio entered an office and shot Tan Siong Kiap, killing him. He then fired a shot at Ong Hua, striking him in the shoulder. Ong Hua ran into a back room and locked the door. Sy Pio did not pursue him and left the building.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that as to Ong Hua, the wound was non-fatal and he did not perform all acts of execution, making his liability attempted murder rather than frustrated murder.

Issue:Is the shooting of a victim in a non-vital organ who escapes and locks a door Attempted Murder or Frustrated Murder?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED MURDER. Because the gunshot wound in the shoulder was non-mortal, the accused did not perform all acts of execution necessary to produce death, limiting liability to the attempted stage.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because where the wound is non-mortal and does not produce death by external medical intervention, all acts of execution have not been performed.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The shoulder wound did not place Ong Hua's life in jeopardy. Because Sy Pio did not perform all acts necessary to produce death, the crime was attempted murder as to Ong Hua.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Frustrated Murder to ATTEMPTED MURDER (as to Ong Hua). DOCTRINE: Shooting a victim inflicting a non-mortal wound is Attempted Murder under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 99

People v. Trinidad

CITATION Citation: 162 SCRA 714 (1988) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the wound was superficial and could not have caused death; the execution was incomplete.

Facts:Trinidad shot the victim during a sudden attack. The bullet grazed the victim's forearm, causing a minor flesh wound that healed in seven days.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that the minor wound showed absence of intent to kill, or at most attempted homicide rather than frustrated murder.

Issue:Does a non-mortal grazing gunshot wound inflicted with treachery constitute Attempted Murder or Frustrated Murder?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED MURDER. When the assailant fails to inflict a mortal wound, the crime has not reached the frustrated stage and is Attempted Murder.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the wound was superficial and could not have caused death; the execution was incomplete.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the gunshot grazed only the arm and was not mortal, all acts of execution were not performed. With treachery present, the offense was attempted murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED to ATTEMPTED MURDER. DOCTRINE: Gunshot wounds that are non-mortal limit criminal liability to Attempted Murder under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 100

People v. Ravelo

CITATION Citation: G.R. Nos. 78781-82, 15 October 1991 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the absence of a mortal wound precludes the legal finding that all acts of execution were performed.

Facts:Ravelo and co-assailants ambushed two brothers. One brother was shot and killed instantly; the other brother was shot in the thigh, fell to the ground, and survived after the gunmen fled believing both were dead.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that as to the surviving brother, the leg wound was non-mortal, requiring conviction for attempted murder rather than frustrated murder.

Issue:Is the shooting of a victim in the leg Frustrated Murder or Attempted Murder where the wound is non-mortal?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED MURDER. Where the medical testimony proves that the wound was non-fatal and would not cause death, the crime is Attempted Murder.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the absence of a mortal wound precludes the legal finding that all acts of execution were performed.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The thigh wound did not sever major arteries and was not fatal. Under Art. 6, the crime was attempted murder as to the surviving brother.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED to Murder (for deceased) and ATTEMPTED MURDER (for surviving victim). DOCTRINE: Inflicting a non-fatal bullet wound constitutes Attempted Murder under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 101

People v. Kalalo

CITATION Citation: 59 Phil. 715 (1934) | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 249, 254, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because firing at enemies during a deadly dispute demonstrates intent to kill, establishing attempted homicide.

Facts:During a land boundary dispute, Kalalo and his co-accused shot and killed two opponents. When the other opponents fled, Kalalo fired several shots at the fleeing men without hitting any of them.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that firing at fleeing opponents without hitting anyone was merely illegal discharge of firearm under Article 254, not attempted homicide.

Issue:Does firing multiple shots at fleeing adversaries with intent to kill constitute Attempted Homicide or Illegal Discharge of Firearm?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE. Discharging a firearm at fleeing adversaries with homicidal intent constitutes Attempted Homicide; illegal discharge applies only when intent to kill is absent.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 249 & 254, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because firing at enemies during a deadly dispute demonstrates intent to kill, establishing attempted homicide.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The intent to kill was evidenced by the preceding fatal shooting of two companions. Firing at the fleeing victims directly commenced homicide by overt acts.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Convictions for Murder and ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Discharging a firearm at fleeing victims with intent to kill constitutes Attempted Homicide under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 249, 254, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 102

Guzman, Jr. v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 178512, 26 November 2014 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 249, 265, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because intent to kill is the essential element distinguishing attempted homicide from physical injuries.

Facts:Guzman struck the victim with a bolo on the left arm during a heated boundary dispute. The wound required medical treatment for only seven days.

Accused's Defense:Accused contended that there was no intent to kill and the minor injury constituted only slight physical injuries.

Issue:Does striking a person with a bolo on the arm during an argument constitute Attempted Homicide or Less Serious/Slight Physical Injuries?

•
[A] ANSWER:LESS SERIOUS PHYSICAL INJURIES (Absence of Intent to Kill). When the wound is superficial, located in a non-vital part, and there is no clear evidence of intent to kill, the offense is physical injuries, not attempted homicide.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 265 & 266, RPC (Physical Injuries); Art. 6 & 249, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because intent to kill is the essential element distinguishing attempted homicide from physical injuries.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The blow was directed at the arm and was not followed up with further attacks. The absence of animus interficiendi reduced the crime to physical injuries.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Attempted Homicide to LESS SERIOUS PHYSICAL INJURIES. DOCTRINE: Without clear proof of intent to kill, a non-mortal wound on a non-vital body part constitutes physical injuries, not attempted homicide.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 249, 265, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 103

Etino v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 206518, 17 August 2016 | Topic: Stages of Execution (Attempted, Frustrated, Consummated)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 6, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the distinguishing factor between frustrated and attempted homicide is the mortal nature of the wound.

Facts:Etino hacked his nephew with a bolo, inflicting a wound on the back of the neck and shoulder. The doctor testified that the wound was about 4 inches long, but could not categorically state that it was mortal or life-threatening.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that without medical testimony proving the wound was mortal, he could not be convicted of frustrated homicide.

Issue:Is an assailant guilty of Frustrated Homicide or Attempted Homicide when the doctor cannot establish that the wound inflicted was mortal?

•
[A] ANSWER:ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE. To sustain a conviction for Frustrated Homicide, the prosecution must prove beyond reasonable doubt that the wound was mortal; if not mortal, the offense is Attempted Homicide.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 6, par. 3; Art. 249, RPC; Burden of Proving Mortal Wound. Applicability: Applicable because the distinguishing factor between frustrated and attempted homicide is the mortal nature of the wound.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the attending physician failed to declare that the neck/shoulder wound would have caused death without medical intervention, the crime remained at the attempted stage.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED from Frustrated Homicide to ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE. DOCTRINE: In homicide cases, failure to prove that the wound was mortal reduces liability to Attempted Homicide under Art. 6 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 6, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).

Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 8, Revised Penal Code; Collective Criminal Responsibility (The Act of One is the Act of All) • Total Cases: 12Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the rules on collective liability when two or more persons agree concerning the commission of a felony and decide to commit it, rendering each conspirator equally liable as a co-principal for all crimes committed in pursuance of the common unlawful design.

CASE 104

People v. Peralta

CITATION Citation: 25 SCRA 759 (1968) | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because when offenders unite in a common criminal design, individual acts merge into collective liability.

Facts:Inmates belonging to the 'OXO' gang inside New Bilibid Prison organized a coordinated, simultaneous assault on members of the rival 'Sigue-Sigue' gang, murdering multiple rival inmates during a prison riot.

Accused's Defense:Individual gang members argued that they did not personally strike the fatal blows and should not be held liable for murder in the absence of proof of individual fatal participation.

Issue:Does proof of membership and active participation in an organized gang conspiracy make each participant liable as a principal for all resulting murders?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. When conspiracy is established, the act of one is the act of all, and all conspirators are equally liable as principals regardless of the extent of their individual physical blows.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8 & Art. 17, RPC (Conspiracy and Collective Liability). Applicability: Applicable because when offenders unite in a common criminal design, individual acts merge into collective liability.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The evidence proved a pre-arranged plan among OXO gang members to exterminate rivals. Each participating inmate was liable as a principal for all murders committed.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Convictions for Multiple Murders AFFIRMED with collective death sentences. DOCTRINE: In conspiracy under Art. 8 RPC, the act of one is the act of all; all conspirators bear equal liability as principals.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 105

United States v. Bautista

CITATION Citation: 6 Phil. 581 (1906) | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 136, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 8 establishes the exception where conspiracy is explicitly punished as an independent crime by statute.

Facts:Bautista and companions formed a secret society, took oaths of allegiance, and agreed to take up arms to overthrow the United States Government in the Philippines. They were arrested before launching any military rebellion.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that merely agreeing to form an army without executing overt acts of armed rebellion was not punishable under criminal law.

Issue:Is conspiracy to commit treason or rebellion punishable as a separate crime under Philippine penal law?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. While conspiracy to commit a crime is generally not punishable, conspiracy is directly punishable by express statutory provision in crimes against national security and public order (Treason, Rebellion, Sedition).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8, par. 1; Art. 136, RPC; Act No. 292 (Crimes against Sovereign Authority). Applicability: Applicable because Article 8 establishes the exception where conspiracy is explicitly punished as an independent crime by statute.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Under Article 8 RPC, conspiracy alone is punishable when specifically provided by law, as in conspiracy to commit rebellion under Article 136. The agreement and plan completed the offense.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Conspiracy to Overthrow the Government AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Conspiracy is punishable as a separate felony when expressly provided by law under Art. 8 RPC (e.g. Treason, Rebellion, Sedition).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 136, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 106

Quidet v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 170289, 8 April 2008 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 14, 1987 Constitution.- Applicability:Applicable because conspiracy requires proof of intentional agreement and common design, which cannot be deduced from mere presence.

Facts:Jimmy Quidet was present when his companion suddenly assaulted and killed the victim with a knife. Quidet merely stood near the path and did not assist, hold the victim, or strike any blow.

Accused's Defense:Quidet argued that mere passive companionship and presence without proof of prior agreement or overt participation does not establish conspiracy.

Issue:Does companionship or presence at the scene of the crime establish conspiracy to commit murder?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Conspiracy must be proved beyond reasonable doubt by positive and convincing evidence; mere companionship, presence, or relationship does not prove conspiracy.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8, RPC; Presumption of Innocence (1987 Const. Art. III, Sec. 14). Applicability: Applicable because conspiracy requires proof of intentional agreement and common design, which cannot be deduced from mere presence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The prosecution presented no proof of prior agreement between Quidet and the assailant. Because Quidet performed no overt act, conspiracy was not established.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction REVERSED and Jimmy Quidet ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Conspiracy must be proved with the same quantum of evidence as the crime itself; mere presence does not establish conspiracy under Art. 8 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, RPC; Art. III, Sec. 14, 1987 Constitution.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 107

People v. Belmonte

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 224588, 10 July 2019 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because simultaneous, coordinated assault restraining the victim while delivering lethal stabs proves community of criminal design.

Facts:Belmonte and three co-accused surrounded the victim. One held the victim's arms while Belmonte stabbed him in the chest, and the others struck him with wooden clubs, ensuring his death.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that there was no prior meeting or plan, asserting that each acted independently in a spontaneous fight.

Issue:Can implied conspiracy be inferred from synchronized, simultaneous overt acts showing a unity of criminal purpose?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Direct proof of prior agreement is not required; conspiracy may be inferred from the concerted, synchronized actions of the accused showing a common criminal design.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8 & Art. 17, RPC (Implied Conspiracy). Applicability: Applicable because simultaneous, coordinated assault restraining the victim while delivering lethal stabs proves community of criminal design.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The acts of holding the victim's arms and clubbing him while Belmonte stabbed his chest demonstrate synchronized cooperation and shared intent to kill.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Convictions for MURDER AFFIRMED against all accused as co-conspirators. DOCTRINE: Implied conspiracy arises when the concerted, simultaneous acts of the perpetrators demonstrate a unity of purpose.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 108

People v. Lago

CITATION Citation: 358 SCRA 609 (2001) | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 17, 294(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because conspirators in robbery are collectively liable for any homicide committed on the occasion thereof as part of the common criminal plan.

Facts:Lago drove a getaway motorcycle and served as lookout while his armed companion entered a gasoline station, robbed the cashier, and shot the security guard dead.

Accused's Defense:Lago argued that he had no intent to kill the security guard and was liable only as an accomplice to simple robbery.

Issue:Is a getaway driver and lookout equally liable as a principal for the special complex crime of Robbery with Homicide under the doctrine of conspiracy?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. In a conspiracy to commit robbery, all conspirators are liable as principals for Robbery with Homicide, even if they acted only as lookouts or drivers, unless they actively tried to prevent the killing.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8; Art. 17; Art. 294(1), RPC. Applicability: Applicable because conspirators in robbery are collectively liable for any homicide committed on the occasion thereof as part of the common criminal plan.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Lago facilitated the escape and secured the perimeter. Having conspired to commit robbery, he is fully liable as a principal for the resulting robbery with homicide.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE as Principal AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: A lookout or getaway driver in a robbery conspiracy is liable as a principal for Robbery with Homicide under Art. 8 and 294(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 17, 294(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 109

People v. Real

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 101857, 11 August 1993 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because blocking escape during a lethal assault constitutes overt cooperation showing adoption of the common homicidal intent.

Facts:Accused-appellants joined in chasing and cornering a victim after a fistfight, and when the main assailant pulled a knife and stabbed the victim, the companions kicked and blocked the victim from escaping.

Accused's Defense:Appellants claimed they had no prior plan with the stabber and only engaged in a fistfight, negating conspiracy to commit murder.

Issue:Does joining in cornering a victim and preventing his escape during a fatal stabbing establish conspiracy to commit murder?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Actively trapping and blocking the victim while a co-assailant delivers fatal stabs demonstrates concurrence of will and common design, establishing conspiracy.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8 & Art. 17, RPC (Conspiracy). Applicability: Applicable because blocking escape during a lethal assault constitutes overt cooperation showing adoption of the common homicidal intent.
•
[A] APPLICATION:By preventing the victim's escape, the appellants actively facilitated the killing. Their concerted actions proved implied conspiracy.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Convictions for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Preventing the victim from escaping while a companion delivers fatal blows proves conspiracy under Art. 8 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 110

People v. Ibasco

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 138676, 27 May 2004 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 249, 266, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because spontaneous fights lack the pre-arranged consensus required for conspiracy under Article 8.

Facts:During a spontaneous drunken brawl at a dance hall, Ibasco and another man simultaneously attacked the victim. One inflicted a minor fist blow while the other suddenly drew a knife and stabbed the victim to death.

Accused's Defense:Ibasco argued that in a spontaneous brawl without prior plan, each person is liable only for his own independent acts, negating conspiracy for the unexpected stabbing.

Issue:Does a sudden, spontaneous brawl without evidence of prior agreement or coordinated lethal intent establish conspiracy for a fatal stabbing committed by one participant?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. In spontaneous brawls, conspiracy cannot be presumed; each participant is liable only for his own individual acts in the absence of clear proof of common homicidal design.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8, RPC; Individual Liability in Spontaneous Brawls. Applicability: Applicable because spontaneous fights lack the pre-arranged consensus required for conspiracy under Article 8.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Ibasco engaged only in fist blows and did not know his companion carried a knife. Because there was no common design to kill, Ibasco was liable only for physical injuries.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction of Ibasco MODIFIED to SLIGHT PHYSICAL INJURIES; companion convicted of Homicide. DOCTRINE: In spontaneous brawls, conspiracy is not presumed; participants are liable only for their individual acts.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 249, 266, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 111

People v. Cajara

CITATION Citation: 341 SCRA 192 (2000) | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because pre-arranged ambush and simultaneous hacking establish beyond doubt the existence of a prior conspiracy.

Facts:Cajara and companions lay in wait along a dark trail armed with bolos. When the victim passed, they simultaneously sprang from the bushes and hacked the victim to death.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed alibi and denied having any prior agreement with the other assailants.

Issue:Does lying in wait and executing a coordinated ambush prove conspiracy and treachery?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Lying in wait and launching a coordinated surprise attack proves both conspiracy under Art. 8 and treachery qualifying the crime to murder under Art. 248.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8 & Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because pre-arranged ambush and simultaneous hacking establish beyond doubt the existence of a prior conspiracy.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The synchronized ambush and shared weapons demonstrated a unified plan to kill with treachery. All participants are liable as co-principals.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Convictions for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Executing a coordinated ambush establishes conspiracy and treachery under Art. 8 and 248 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 112

People v. Masonson

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 138676, 21 September 2001 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders
