Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because conspiracy requires agreement to commit the felony prior to or during its execution.

Facts:Masonson arrived at the scene of an assault after the victim had already been fatally wounded by others. He shouted insults at the dying victim but did not touch him.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that shouting insults after the fatal assault does not constitute conspiracy or participation as a principal or accomplice.

Issue:Does verbal abuse uttered after the infliction of fatal wounds make a person a co-conspirator in murder?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Conspiracy must precede or accompany the commission of the crime; post-assault insults without prior agreement or contribution do not establish conspiracy.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8, RPC; Requirement of Concurrence of Will. Applicability: Applicable because conspiracy requires agreement to commit the felony prior to or during its execution.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Masonson played no part in planning or executing the attack. Uttering words after the fatal assault does not constitute conspiracy to commit murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction REVERSED and Masonson ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Words uttered after the completion of a fatal assault do not constitute conspiracy under Art. 8 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 113

People v. Tolentino

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 139173, 15 May 2002 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 17, 294(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because in robbery conspiracies, homicide committed on the occasion of the robbery is imputed to all co-conspirators.

Facts:Tolentino and companions boarded a passenger jeepney, drew knives, announced a hold-up, and divested passengers of their belongings while one stabbed a resisting passenger.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that he only took bags and did not intend the stabbing of the passenger, claiming liability only for simple robbery.

Issue:Are all participants in a jeepney robbery conspiracy liable for Robbery with Homicide when one conspirator stabs a resisting victim?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. When conspiracy to commit robbery is proven, all conspirators are liable for the resulting homicide committed by any of them, unless they actively endeavored to prevent the killing.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8; Art. 294(1), RPC. Applicability: Applicable because in robbery conspiracies, homicide committed on the occasion of the robbery is imputed to all co-conspirators.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Tolentino participated in the robbery hold-up. Because he did not try to stop the stabbing, he is equally liable as a principal for Robbery with Homicide.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: In a robbery conspiracy, all participants are liable as principals for Robbery with Homicide under Art. 8 and 294(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 17, 294(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 114

People v. Layson

CITATION Citation: 30 SCRA 92 (1969) | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 14, 160, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because manufacturing prison knives and planning an execution prove direct conspiracy and evident premeditation.

Facts:Inmates Layson, Ragman, Cecilio, and Garces conspired in their prison cell to kill a fellow inmate who was an informer. They made makeshift knives, cornered the victim in the toilet, and stabbed him 42 times.

Accused's Defense:Accused pleaded guilty but argued that they acted under passion and obfuscation caused by the victim's alleged abusive reporting to prison guards.

Issue:Does a premeditated prison assassination by multiple inmates establish conspiracy, evident premeditation, and treachery?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Making weapons and planning the murder in advance proves conspiracy and evident premeditation; cornering the unarmed victim establishes treachery.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8; Art. 14, pars. 13 & 16; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because manufacturing prison knives and planning an execution prove direct conspiracy and evident premeditation.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The inmates planned the assassination days before and executed it with overwhelming treachery. All four are co-principals in Murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Convictions for MURDER AFFIRMED with DEATH PENALTY (quasi-recidivism under Art. 160). DOCTRINE: Pre-arranged assassination by prison inmates establishes conspiracy, evident premeditation, and treachery.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 14, 160, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).
CASE 115

People v. Peralta

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 133267, 8 August 2002 | Topic: Conspiracy, Proposal, and Multiple Offenders

Statutory Anchor:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because physically restraining the victim ensures the execution of the killing without risk, proving conspiracy and treachery.

Facts:Peralta and companions surrounded a victim during an altercation. Peralta held the victim while his co-accused stabbed him repeatedly.

Accused's Defense:Peralta argued that he merely held the victim to pacify him and did not intend for his companion to stab the victim.

Issue:Does restraining the victim's arms while a companion delivers fatal stabs establish conspiracy to commit murder?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Restraining the victim to render him helpless while a companion stabs him proves conspiracy and treachery.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 8 & Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because physically restraining the victim ensures the execution of the killing without risk, proving conspiracy and treachery.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Peralta's act of holding the victim's arms deprived the victim of all defense and enabled the fatal stabbing, establishing conspiracy.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER as Co-Principal AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Restraining the victim while a companion inflicts fatal stabs establishes conspiracy and treachery under Art. 8 and 248 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 8, 17, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part III: Stages of Execution, Light Felonies, Conspiracy & Plurality (Articles 6-10 RPC).

PART: III. CIRCUMSTANCES AFFECTING CRIMINAL LIABILITY

Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 11, Paragraphs 1 through 6, Revised Penal Code • Total Cases: 17Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors situations where the act of the person is strictly lawful and in accordance with law, completely extinguishing both criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto, requiring unlawful aggression as the indispensable condition for defense.

CASE 116

People v. Genosa

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 135981, 15 January 2004 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 13(6), 13(9), 246, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because unlawful aggression is the indispensable condition sine qua non of self-defense under Article 11(1).

Facts:Marivic Genosa shot her husband Ben while he was sleeping in their bedroom after a violent altercation where Ben had severely beaten her earlier that evening.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked self-defense based on Battered Woman Syndrome (BWS), asserting that she acted under continuous fear of death.

Issue:Can complete self-defense be sustained when the accused shoots her abusive husband while he is asleep?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO (Complete Self-Defense Fails; Mitigating Circumstances Recognized). Complete self-defense requires unlawful aggression at the time of the fatal act; because the husband was asleep, aggression had ceased, but BWS was recognized as mitigating circumstances under Art. 13(9) & (6).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 13, pars. 6 & 9, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because unlawful aggression is the indispensable condition sine qua non of self-defense under Article 11(1).
•
[A] APPLICATION:When the fatal shot was fired, Ben was asleep and unarmed. The absence of actual, present unlawful aggression precluded complete self-defense, but cumulative abuse warranted mitigation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Parricide MODIFIED with penalty reduced; accused ordered released due to credit for time served. DOCTRINE: Unlawful aggression is indispensable for self-defense; killing a sleeping abuser does not qualify for complete self-defense under Art. 11(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 13(6), 13(9), 246, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 117

People v. Dulin

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 171284, 29 June 2015 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because self-defense requires present or imminent aggression; once the aggressor flees or is disarmed, unlawful aggression ceases and self-defense cannot be invoked.

Facts:Alfredo Dulin and Batulan engaged in a mutual fight. Batulan initially brandished a bolo, but was disarmed and ran away. Dulin pursued the fleeing Batulan and stabbed him multiple times in the back, killing him.

Accused's Defense:Dulin claimed self-defense, arguing that Batulan started the fight and was the initial aggressor.

Issue:Is self-defense available when the accused pursues and kills an opponent after the latter has been disarmed and is fleeing?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. When the initial unlawful aggression has ceased, the person defending himself no longer has any right to pursue, assault, or kill the adversary; doing so constitutes retaliation, not self-defense.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1, RPC (Self-Defense / Ceased Unlawful Aggression). Applicability: Applicable because self-defense requires present or imminent aggression; once the aggressor flees or is disarmed, unlawful aggression ceases and self-defense cannot be invoked.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Once Batulan was disarmed and ran away, there was no longer any danger to Dulin's life. Pursuing and stabbing him in the back was an act of vengeance and retaliation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: When unlawful aggression ceases, self-defense is unavailable; pursuing and killing a fleeing adversary constitutes retaliation under Art. 11(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 118

People v. Olarbe

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 227421, 23 July 2018 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 11(2), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because midnight home invasion by an armed felon shooting at the occupants represents acute, continuous unlawful aggression justifying lethal defense.

Facts:An armed intruder (Arca), a known violent criminal carrying a gun and bolo, forced his way into Rodolfo Olarbe's home at midnight, pointed a gun at Olarbe and his wife, and fired. Olarbe grappled with Arca, seized the bolo, and hacked Arca to death to protect his wife and himself.

Accused's Defense:Olarbe invoked complete self-defense and defense of his wife (relative) under Article 11(1) and 11(2) RPC.

Issue:Is an accused completely justified in killing an armed midnight home invader who fired a gun at him and his wife?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Complete Self-Defense and Defense of Relative). All three elements of self-defense and defense of relative were present: continuous mortal aggression by an armed intruder, reasonable necessity of the means employed in the dark, and total lack of provocation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, pars. 1 & 2, RPC (Self-Defense & Defense of Relatives). Applicability: Applicable because midnight home invasion by an armed felon shooting at the occupants represents acute, continuous unlawful aggression justifying lethal defense.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Olarbe was in mortal danger inside his own home at midnight. Reasonable necessity of means does not require mathematical equality; grappling for weapons to neutralize a lethal intruder is fully justified.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment REVERSED; Rodolfo Olarbe FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Killing an armed midnight home intruder who fired at the occupants is completely justified under Art. 11(1) & (2) RPC; reasonable necessity does not demand mathematical parity.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 11(2), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 119

Nacnac v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 191913, 21 March 2012 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the intoxicated officer's act of drawing his gun created real, imminent peril to the commander's life, satisfying all elements of self-defense.

Facts:PO2 Rolando Nacnac was on duty as officer-in-charge at a police outpost. A drunken, belligerent subordinate officer (Tugaoen) cursed him, refused to follow orders, drew his service firearm from its holster, and advanced threateningly. Nacnac drew his service weapon and fired a single shot, killing Tugaoen.

Accused's Defense:Nacnac invoked complete self-defense and lawful performance of police duty under Article 11(1) and 11(5) RPC.

Issue:Is a police commander justified under self-defense in shooting an insubordinate, intoxicated officer who draws his firearm during a confrontation?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Complete Self-Defense). Drawing a firearm and advancing aggressively constitutes imminent, mortal unlawful aggression; firing a single defensive shot is reasonably necessary.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1, RPC (Self-Defense). Applicability: Applicable because the intoxicated officer's act of drawing his gun created real, imminent peril to the commander's life, satisfying all elements of self-defense.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Nacnac was confronted by an armed, drunken subordinate drawing a lethal weapon. He was not required to wait until the gun was fired before defending himself. His single defensive shot was reasonably necessary.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Homicide REVERSED and PO2 Nacnac FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Drawing a gun during a hostile confrontation constitutes unlawful aggression justifying immediate lethal self-defense under Art. 11(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 120

People v. Eduarte

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 88232, 26 February 1990 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because unlawful aggression had completely ceased when the parties separated; returning with a weapon is an act of aggression, not self-defense.

Facts:Eduarte and the victim had a fistfight. After being separated, Eduarte went home, got a hunting knife, returned to where the victim was sitting, and stabbed him to death.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed self-defense, arguing that the victim started the earlier altercation and punched him first.

Issue:Can self-defense be invoked when an accused leaves the scene of a fistfight and returns later armed to kill his opponent?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Self-defense requires present, actual unlawful aggression. When the fight has ended, leaving and returning with a deadly weapon constitutes revenge and premeditated retaliation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1, RPC (Unlawful Aggression / Retaliation). Applicability: Applicable because unlawful aggression had completely ceased when the parties separated; returning with a weapon is an act of aggression, not self-defense.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The prior altercation was over. When Eduarte returned armed, he became the primary unlawful aggressor. Self-defense cannot be founded on past, completed aggression.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Leaving the scene after an altercation and returning armed constitutes retaliation and revenge, barring self-defense under Art. 11(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 121

People v. Apolinar

CITATION Citation: CA-G.R. No. 4909, 38 O.G. 2870 (1940) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because human life is superior to property rights; lethal force in defense of property is justifiable only when accompanied by serious danger to the defender's person.

Facts:Apolinar was guarding his palay plantation at night. He saw a man carrying a bundle of stolen palay walking away. Apolinar shouted at him to stop, but the thief kept walking. Apolinar fired his shotgun, shooting the thief in the back and killing him.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked defense of property under Article 11(1) RPC, claiming he had the right to defend his agricultural produce against theft.

Issue:Does defense of property justify shooting and killing a fleeing thief who poses no physical danger to the defender's life?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Defense of property justifies killing only when coupled with an unlawful physical attack against the person of the defender; shooting a fleeing thief without danger to life is not justifiable.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1, RPC (Defense of Property vs. Defense of Person). Applicability: Applicable because human life is superior to property rights; lethal force in defense of property is justifiable only when accompanied by serious danger to the defender's person.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The thief was unarmed and walking away with palay. There was no physical aggression against Apolinar's person. Using deadly force to protect palay exceeded reasonable necessity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with mitigating circumstances. DOCTRINE: Defense of property alone does not justify the taking of human life; there must be concurrent unlawful aggression endangering the person under Art. 11(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 122

United States v. Bumanglag

CITATION Citation: 14 Phil. 644 (1909) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(2), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the life of the brother was in mortal peril from a violent beating, justifying the use of a weapon to repel the attack.

Facts:Bumanglag came upon an armed man violently choking and beating his brother with a heavy wooden cudgel, threatening to kill him. Bumanglag picked up a bolo and struck the assailant, killing him.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked defense of relative under Article 11(2) RPC to protect his brother's life.

Issue:Is an accused justified in killing an assailant who is actively assaulting and choking his brother with a deadly weapon?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Complete Defense of Relative). All elements of defense of relative were met: unlawful aggression against the brother, reasonable necessity of the means used to stop the mortal beating, and lack of provocation by the defender.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 2, RPC (Defense of Relatives). Applicability: Applicable because the life of the brother was in mortal peril from a violent beating, justifying the use of a weapon to repel the attack.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The violent choking and clubbing constituted mortal unlawful aggression against the brother. Bumanglag acted promptly to save his brother's life without excessive force.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Accused FULLY ACQUITTED under Art. 11(2) RPC. DOCTRINE: Killing an assailant to protect a relative whose life is in imminent peril from a violent armed assault is fully justified under Art. 11(2) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(2), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 123

People v. Narvaez

CITATION Citation: 121 SCRA 389 (1983) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because unlawful aggression against property is recognized, but lacks reasonable necessity when met with fatal shotgun blasts.

Facts:Narvaez was resting in his house when Fleischer and Rubia aggressively erected a fence across his yard, cutting off his house and destroying his banana plants despite his repeated pleas to stop.

Accused's Defense:Narvaez took his shotgun and shot both men, claiming defense of property under Art. 11(1) and passion/obfuscation under Art. 13(6).

Issue:Does aggressive unlawful fencing of property satisfy the requirement of unlawful aggression to grant incomplete defense of property under Articles 11(1) and 69 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Incomplete Defense of Property). The aggressive destruction of property rights constituted unlawful aggression, but shooting with a shotgun lacked reasonable necessity of the means employed, entitling the accused to privileged incomplete defense under Art. 69.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 13, pars. 1 & 6; Art. 69, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because unlawful aggression against property is recognized, but lacks reasonable necessity when met with fatal shotgun blasts.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Unlawful aggression against property was present, fulfilling the condition sine qua non. The lack of reasonable necessity reduced the defense to incomplete justification under Art. 69.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED to Double Homicide with penalty reduced to arresto mayor and prision correccional; accused released due to credit for preventive detention. DOCTRINE: Unlawful aggression against property entitles the accused to incomplete defense under Art. 69 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 124

United States v. Esmedia

CITATION Citation: 17 Phil. 260 (1910) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(2), 13(6), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because defense of relative cannot protect a corpse; however, seeing a father killed generates legitimate passion and obfuscation mitigating liability under Article 13(6).

Facts:The Esmedia brothers saw their elderly father lying dead on the ground, having been killed in an earlier altercation by the victims. Upon seeing their father's corpse, the sons attacked and hacked the perpetrators to death while the latter were resting.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked defense of relative under Article 11(2) and passion/obfuscation under Article 13(6) RPC.

Issue:Can defense of relative be invoked when the relative is already dead and the attack against the perpetrators is committed in retaliation?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO (Defense of Relative Fails; Passion/Obfuscation Mitigates). Defense of relative requires present or imminent unlawful aggression; once the relative is dead, the aggression has ceased and killing the killers is revenge, not defense.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 2; Art. 13, par. 6, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because defense of relative cannot protect a corpse; however, seeing a father killed generates legitimate passion and obfuscation mitigating liability under Article 13(6).
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the father was already dead, there was no danger to defend against. The killings were retaliatory, but the sight of their slain father entitled the sons to mitigating passion/obfuscation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Passion and Obfuscation. DOCTRINE: Defense of relative cannot be invoked after the relative has already died; retaliation is not defense under Art. 11(2) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(2), 13(6), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 125

People v. Toring

CITATION Citation: 191 SCRA 38 (1990) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(3), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 11(3) justifies acts performed to defend any third person from unlawful aggression provided the defender is not motivated by personal resentment.

Facts:Toring saw an armed man (victim) holding a knife against a stranger's throat during a brawl. Toring picked up a knife, rushed forward, and stabbed the aggressor in the back, killing him to save the stranger's life.

Accused's Defense:Toring invoked defense of stranger under Article 11(3) RPC, claiming he acted solely to protect the stranger from being slaughtered.

Issue:Is an accused justified in killing an armed assailant under Defense of Stranger when acting to save a stranger whose life is under imminent knife attack?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Complete Defense of Stranger). All elements of defense of stranger were satisfied: unlawful aggression against the stranger, reasonable necessity of the means employed to stop the knife assault, and the defender was not induced by revenge or resentment.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 3, RPC (Defense of Stranger). Applicability: Applicable because Article 11(3) justifies acts performed to defend any third person from unlawful aggression provided the defender is not motivated by personal resentment.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The stranger was under imminent mortal threat from a knife pressed to his throat. Toring intervened without any personal motive or prior grudge. His action was completely justified.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Accused FULLY ACQUITTED under Art. 11(3) RPC. DOCTRINE: Killing an armed assailant to save a stranger from imminent deadly assault is completely justified under Defense of Stranger (Art. 11[3] RPC).
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(3), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 126

Masipequiña v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: 176 SCRA 499 (1989) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 11(3), 11(5), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because lawful fulfillment of duty justifies using necessary force to neutralize an armed, violent lunatic threatening the lives of law enforcers.

Facts:Patrolman Masipequiña and a barangay captain were sent to apprehend a violent, deranged lunatic (Leopoldo) armed with a bolo. Leopoldo charged at them swinging the bolo. Masipequiña fired a warning shot, but Leopoldo kept charging and hacked the barangay captain. Masipequiña fired at Leopoldo, killing him.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked complete self-defense, defense of stranger, and lawful fulfillment of duty under Article 11(1), 11(3), and 11(5) RPC.

Issue:Is a police officer justified in shooting an armed, violent lunatic who attacks officers with a bolo during a lawful arrest?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Complete Justification). The officer acted in lawful fulfillment of duty and self-defense/defense of stranger; the violent charge of a bolo-wielding lunatic created mortal danger requiring lethal force.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, pars. 1, 3, & 5, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because lawful fulfillment of duty justifies using necessary force to neutralize an armed, violent lunatic threatening the lives of law enforcers.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Masipequiña was executing a lawful order to secure a dangerous lunatic. Warning shots failed, and the lunatic actively hacked an officer. Firing at the attacker was reasonably necessary.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Homicide REVERSED; Patrolman Masipequiña FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: A police officer is completely justified under Art. 11(5) & (1) RPC in shooting an armed violent attacker to preserve life during lawful arrest.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 11(3), 11(5), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 127

People v. Retubado

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 148560, 20 February 2004 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because self-defense requires real, imminent danger to life or limb; a slight push does not justify deadly gunfire.

Facts:Retubado had an argument with the victim Emmanuel. Emmanuel pushed Retubado on the shoulder and uttered insults. Retubado drew a .45 caliber pistol and shot Emmanuel four times in the chest, killing him instantly.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed self-defense, arguing that Emmanuel was taller and stronger and initiated unlawful aggression by pushing his shoulder.

Issue:Does a light push on the shoulder constitute unlawful aggression justifying shooting the unarmed victim four times?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. A mere push or verbal insult is not unlawful aggression endangering life; shooting an unarmed victim four times is disproportionate retaliation, not self-defense.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 1, RPC (Unlawful Aggression & Reasonable Necessity). Applicability: Applicable because self-defense requires real, imminent danger to life or limb; a slight push does not justify deadly gunfire.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victim was unarmed. A slight push did not threaten Retubado's life. Drawing a .45 caliber pistol and pumping four bullets into the victim was gross overreaction and intentional killing.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: A slight push or verbal insult does not constitute unlawful aggression; firing multiple shots at an unarmed person negates self-defense under Art. 11(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 128

Tan v. Standard Vacuum Oil Co.

CITATION Citation: 91 Phil. 672 (1952) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(4), 101, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because sacrificing property to prevent a catastrophic explosion is justified, but the benefited community/owner bears subsidiary civil compensation under Article 101.

Facts:A gasoline tanker truck caught fire while discharging fuel at a service station in a densely populated commercial area. To prevent a catastrophic explosion that would incinerate the entire neighborhood, the driver drove the burning truck away, steering it into a vacant lot where it destroyed plaintiff's nearby house and property.

Accused's Defense:Defendants invoked State of Necessity under Article 11(4) RPC, asserting that sacrificing plaintiff's house was necessary to prevent a far greater catastrophic disaster to the city.

Issue:Does State of Necessity under Article 11(4) justify damaging property to avert a greater evil, and what is the civil liability under Article 101 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:JUSTIFIED (Criminal Liability Extinguished; Civil Liability Borne by Benefited Parties). The driver was criminally justified under State of Necessity; under Article 101, those benefited by averting the greater evil must pay civil indemnity to the owner of the destroyed property.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 4; Art. 101, RPC (State of Necessity / Civil Liability). Applicability: Applicable because sacrificing property to prevent a catastrophic explosion is justified, but the benefited community/owner bears subsidiary civil compensation under Article 101.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The threat of widespread explosion was imminent and real. Driving the burning truck away was the only viable means to save hundreds of lives. The act was justified, with civil indemnity assessed under Art. 101.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Driver JUSTIFIED from criminal liability; civil indemnity ORDERED paid under Art. 101 RPC. DOCTRINE: State of Necessity under Art. 11(4) extinguishes criminal liability, but civil indemnity is assessed under Art. 101 against those benefited.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(4), 101, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 129

People v. Delima

CITATION Citation: 46 Phil. 738 (1922) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(5), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because arresting an escaped armed felon who violently attacks the arresting officer satisfies all requirements of fulfillment of duty and self-defense.

Facts:Felipe Delima, a policeman, was pursuing an escaped notorious convict (Napisa) armed with a pointed bamboo lance. When Delima cornered him and ordered him to surrender, Napisa charged at Delima with the lance. Delima fired his service revolver, killing Napisa.

Accused's Defense:Delima invoked lawful fulfillment of duty and complete self-defense under Article 11(5) and 11(1) RPC.

Issue:Is a police officer justified in killing a dangerous escaped convict who refuses to surrender and attacks the arresting officer with a deadly weapon?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Complete Justification under Art. 11[5] RPC). The killing was committed in the lawful fulfillment of a duty as an arresting officer when resisting lethal force from an escaped felon.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 5; Art. 11, par. 1, RPC (Fulfillment of Duty). Applicability: Applicable because arresting an escaped armed felon who violently attacks the arresting officer satisfies all requirements of fulfillment of duty and self-defense.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Delima was under legal obligation to recapture the escaped convict. When Napisa attacked with a deadly lance, Delima was justified in using lethal force to effect the arrest and protect his life.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment of conviction REVERSED; Policeman Delima FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: A peace officer who kills an escaped armed convict charging with a lethal weapon acts in lawful fulfillment of duty under Art. 11(5) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(5), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 130

People v. Belbes

CITATION Citation: 334 SCRA 610 (2000) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(5), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because police officers may only use reasonable force; using excessive, lethal rifle fire against an unarmed person negates complete justification but warrants incomplete defense under Article 69.

Facts:Patrolman Belbes responded to a disturbance at a school dance. A student (Bataller) was drunk and disorderly. When Bataller turned around with his hands in his pockets, Belbes immediately fired several bursts from his M16 armalite rifle, shooting Bataller dead.

Accused's Defense:Belbes claimed fulfillment of duty under Article 11(5) and self-defense, asserting he suspected the student was drawing a concealed firearm.

Issue:Can a police officer invoke fulfillment of duty when he sprays an unarmed, unruly student with M16 rifle fire without verified threat or resistance?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO (Incomplete Fulfillment of Duty / Privileged Mitigation). Fulfillment of duty requires that the injury or homicide be the necessary consequence of the lawful performance of duty; spraying an unarmed student with an M16 is excessive and unlawful.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 5; Art. 13, par. 1; Art. 69, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because police officers may only use reasonable force; using excessive, lethal rifle fire against an unarmed person negates complete justification but warrants incomplete defense under Article 69.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Belbes responded in his official capacity, but firing an assault rifle at an unarmed drunk student exceeded the necessity of the performance of duty. He was entitled only to incomplete fulfillment of duty.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with privileged mitigating circumstance of Incomplete Fulfillment of Duty (Art. 69 RPC). DOCTRINE: Firing an M16 assault rifle at an unarmed unruly citizen exceeds reasonable necessity under Art. 11(5) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(5), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 131

Cabanlig v. Sandiganbayan

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 148431, 28 July 2005 | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(5), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the officer acted in the actual performance of his duty to secure a dangerous criminal who wrestled for a weapon and attempted violent escape.

Facts:Police officers, including Cabanlig, were escorting an arrested armed robbery-holdup leader (Valderama) in a police vehicle. While in transit, Valderama suddenly grabbed a police rifle, attempted to overpower his escort, and jumped out of the moving vehicle to escape. After warning shouts were ignored, Cabanlig fired and killed the escaping felon.

Accused's Defense:Cabanlig invoked lawful performance of duty under Article 11(5) RPC to prevent the escape of a dangerous, violent robber who had grabbed a weapon.

Issue:Is a police officer justified under Article 11(5) in shooting an escaping armed robbery suspect who wrestled for a service rifle and jumped from a police vehicle?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Complete Fulfillment of Duty). The police officer acted in the lawful exercise of duty to prevent the escape of a dangerous felon who demonstrated violent resistance.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 5, RPC (Fulfillment of Duty / Lawful Exercise of Right). Applicability: Applicable because the officer acted in the actual performance of his duty to secure a dangerous criminal who wrestled for a weapon and attempted violent escape.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Valderama was a notorious armed robber who attempted to seize a police rifle and escape. Warning shots were unheeded. Under the circumstances, firing to disable the fleeing robber was a necessary consequence of duty.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Sandiganbayan judgment REVERSED; Police Officer Cabanlig FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: A police officer is justified under Art. 11(5) RPC in shooting an escaping violent felon who fought for a weapon and ignored commands to halt.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(5), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 132

Tabuena v. Sandiganbayan

CITATION Citation: 268 SCRA 332 (1997) | Topic: Justifying Circumstances: Self-Defense, Defense of Relatives & Strangers, State of Necessity, Fulfillment of Duty

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(6), 217, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because subordinate officials are bound to obey presidential orders valid on their face, negating the fraudulent intent (animus lucrandi) required for malversation.

Facts:Luis Tabuena, General Manager of the Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA), and his finance officer disbursed P55 Million in MIAA funds in cash directly to the private secretary of President Ferdinand Marcos pursuant to a direct, urgent written presidential memorandum instructing payment for government intelligence operations.

Accused's Defense:Tabuena invoked obedience to an order issued by a superior for a lawful purpose under Article 11(6) RPC and good faith performance of presidential directives, negating malversation.

Issue:Is a subordinate public official exempt from malversation under Article 11(6) RPC when disbursing funds in good faith obedience to a direct written presidential directive appearing lawful on its face?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Justified / Negation of Dolo). Subordinate officials acting in good faith pursuant to a presidential directive that carries the presumption of regularity are justified under Article 11(6) and lack criminal intent for malversation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 11, par. 6, RPC (Obedience to Lawful Order of Superior); Presumption of Regularity; Good Faith Negating Malice. Applicability: Applicable because subordinate officials are bound to obey presidential orders valid on their face, negating the fraudulent intent (animus lucrandi) required for malversation.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The presidential order came from the highest executive authority and appeared lawful on its face. Tabuena derived no personal gain and acted in good faith obedience, negating criminal intent.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Sandiganbayan conviction REVERSED; Tabuena and co-accused FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Good faith obedience to a superior order issued with apparent lawful authority under Art. 11(6) RPC negates criminal intent in malversation.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(6), 217, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).

Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 12, Paragraphs 1 through 7, Revised Penal Code; R.A. 9344 / R.A. 10630 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act) • Total Cases: 30Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors conditions where the act remains wrongful but the actor is exempted from criminal liability due to the complete absence of intelligence (insanity, imbecility, infancy/lack of discernment) or freedom of action (irresistible force, uncontrollable fear, unavoidable accident, insuperable cause), while civil liability generally survives under Article 101.

CASE 133

People v. Bonoan

CITATION Citation: 64 Phil. 87 (1937) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 12(1) requires total deprivation of reason and discernment, which dementia praecox medically establishes.

Facts:Celestino Bonoan stabbed and killed a stranger on the street without any motive or provocation. Bonoan had a documented medical history of dementia praecox (schizophrenia) and had been confined in mental institutions multiple times before and after the homicide.

Accused's Defense:Bonoan invoked insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, claiming he was completely deprived of reason and intelligence at the time of the stabbing due to dementia praecox.

Issue:Is an accused diagnosed with dementia praecox (schizophrenia) exempt from criminal liability for murder under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt by Reason of Insanity). When medical and behavioral evidence proves the accused was completely deprived of intelligence and reason at the time of the offense due to mental disease, he is exempt from criminal liability under Art. 12(1).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC (Insanity or Imbecility as Exempting Circumstance). Applicability: Applicable because Article 12(1) requires total deprivation of reason and discernment, which dementia praecox medically establishes.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Medical testimony from government alienists proved Bonoan suffered from acute dementia praecox before, during, and after the stabbing. He was completely deprived of free will and reason.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction REVERSED; Bonoan ACQUITTED on ground of INSANITY and ordered confined in the National Psychopathic Hospital. DOCTRINE: Dementia praecox resulting in total deprivation of intelligence exempts the accused under Art. 12(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 134

People v. Ambal

CITATION Citation: 100 SCRA 325 (1980) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 246, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the law distinguishes medical eccentricities and character disorders from legal insanity which totally extinguishes discernment.

Facts:Ambal struck his wife with a bolo, killing her, because she refused to cook lunch. Ambal was diagnosed as having a 'psychopathic personality' with low intelligence and explosive temper.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, claiming his psychopathic personality and uncontrollable rage deprived him of reason.

Issue:Does a psychopathic personality, explosive temper, or low intelligence constitute legal insanity under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Legal insanity requires total deprivation of reason, intelligence, and free will; psychopathic personality, emotional instability, or depravity of character does not exempt the accused.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC; M'Naghten Standard / Complete Deprivation of Reason Test. Applicability: Applicable because the law distinguishes medical eccentricities and character disorders from legal insanity which totally extinguishes discernment.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Ambal understood the nature and wrongfulness of his acts. His psychopathic personality showed moral weakness and explosive anger, not total extinction of intelligence.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for PARRICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Psychopathic personality, emotional outbursts, or depravity do not constitute legal insanity under Art. 12(1) RPC; there must be complete deprivation of reason.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 246, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 135

People v. Puno

CITATION Citation: 106 SCRA 375 (1981) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the presumption of sanity prevails unless the defense proves total insanity existing at the precise time of the felonious act.

Facts:Puno killed his victim with a bolo. He had experienced sporadic psychotic episodes in the past, but the evidence showed he carried out the attack during a lucid interval, hiding the weapon and escaping systematically.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, presenting evidence of prior mental treatment.

Issue:Is an accused exempt from criminal liability for murder if the crime was committed during a lucid interval between psychotic episodes?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. An offense committed during a lucid interval is punishable; the defense must prove that the accused was totally insane at the exact moment of the commission of the crime.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC; Lucid Interval Doctrine. Applicability: Applicable because the presumption of sanity prevails unless the defense proves total insanity existing at the precise time of the felonious act.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Puno planned the attack, concealed the weapon, and fled intelligently. These cognitive actions proved he was in a lucid interval at the time of the killing.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Crimes committed during lucid intervals are fully punishable; insanity must exist at the precise moment of execution under Art. 12(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 136

People v. Dungo

CITATION Citation: 199 SCRA 860 (1991) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the burden of proving insanity rests strictly on the defense by clear and convincing medical evidence.

Facts:Dungo stabbed a lady teacher to death inside her clinic. He claimed that he had a sudden blackout and epileptic seizure during which he killed the teacher without awareness.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, claiming an epileptic seizure and acute mental illness produced total blackout and loss of consciousness.

Issue:Does a claim of temporary blackout or epilepsy sustain the defense of insanity under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. In the absence of medical proof of total loss of reason and consciousness at the time of the killing, mere claims of blackout or epilepsy do not rebut the presumption of sanity.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC; Presumption of Sanity. Applicability: Applicable because the burden of proving insanity rests strictly on the defense by clear and convincing medical evidence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Dungo remembered closing the clinic door, drawing the knife, and washing his bloody hands before fleeing. These conscious acts disproved total unconsciousness or insanity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Claims of blackout or epileptic seizures do not prove insanity under Art. 12(1) RPC when contradicted by conscious, purposeful conduct before and after the crime.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 137

People v. Yam-id

CITATION Citation: 308 SCRA 659 (1999) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because legal insanity requires proof that the offender was completely incapable of distinguishing right from wrong.

Facts:Yam-id hacked two victims to death with a bolo. At trial, he presented witnesses who testified that he acted strangely, muttered to himself, and stared blankly prior to the incident.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked insanity under Article 12(1) RPC based on strange, eccentric behavior observed by relatives.

Issue:Does strange, eccentric behavior or moodiness establish legal insanity under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Eccentricity, moodiness, or peculiar demeanor does not equal legal insanity; there must be clear proof of total breakdown of the mental faculty depriving the accused of all reason.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC; Quantum of Proof for Insanity. Applicability: Applicable because legal insanity requires proof that the offender was completely incapable of distinguishing right from wrong.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Strange behavior and muttering do not prove complete loss of reason. In the absence of expert psychiatric evidence establishing psychosis, the presumption of sanity controls.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Double Murder AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Eccentricity and peculiar behavior do not constitute legal insanity under Art. 12(1) RPC; total deprivation of reason must be clearly established.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 138

People v. Valledor

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 129291, 3 July 2002 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because somnambulism is valid only when the act is performed in an involuntary state of sleep, which is negated by daytime conscious conduct.

Facts:Valledor entered a house in broad daylight and stabbed three people, killing one and wounding two. He claimed that he had a dream that someone was trying to kill him and woke up in a haze.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked somnambulism and insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, asserting he was in a somnambulistic dream state.

Issue:Can an accused invoke somnambulism (sleepwalking) for violent stabbing attacks committed in broad daylight while awake and walking around?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Somnambulism requires proof of a spontaneous sleepwalking state at night; a daytime attack requiring deliberate entry into another's house and multi-person stabbings disproves sleepwalking.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC (Somnambulism as Insanity/Lack of Volition). Applicability: Applicable because somnambulism is valid only when the act is performed in an involuntary state of sleep, which is negated by daytime conscious conduct.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Valledor walked into the victims' house in the afternoon, selected targets, and attacked them deliberately. These acts demonstrated waking consciousness, completely refuting somnambulism.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Murder and Frustrated Murders AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Somnambulism does not apply to daytime attacks requiring conscious, deliberate movements and purposeful targeting.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 139

People v. Belonio

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 148695, 27 May 2004 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 13(9), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 12(1) demands total loss of intelligence; partial mental deficiency is treated as a mitigating circumstance under Article 13(9).

Facts:Belonio entered a classroom and stabbed a public school teacher to death with a hunting knife. He had mild mental deficiency and a history of substance abuse.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, asserting he suffered from acute psychosis that completely extinguished his criminal responsibility.

Issue:Does mild mental deficiency combined with drug abuse constitute exempting insanity under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO (Mitigating, not Exempting). Mental retardation or drug-induced impairment that does not amount to total deprivation of intelligence does not exempt the accused, though it may mitigate penalty under Art. 13(9).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1; Art. 13, par. 9, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because Article 12(1) demands total loss of intelligence; partial mental deficiency is treated as a mitigating circumstance under Article 13(9).
•
[A] APPLICATION:Psychiatric reports showed Belonio knew right from wrong despite diminished intellect. Because reason was not totally extinguished, he was entitled only to mitigating illness diminishing willpower.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 13(9) RPC. DOCTRINE: Partial mental deficiency is not exempting insanity under Art. 12(1), but constitutes a mitigating circumstance under Art. 13(9) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 13(9), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 140

People v. Pantoja

CITATION Citation: 25 SCRA 468 (1968) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because emotional rage arising from wounded pride or anger is not a mental disease exempting from criminal culpability.

Facts:Pantoja, a soldier, went on a shooting rampage inside an army camp, killing two fellow soldiers and wounding others following a heated disciplinary reprimand from his commander.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed temporary insanity and emotional outburst under Article 12(1) RPC.

Issue:Does temporary explosive emotional fury triggered by disciplinary reprimand constitute exempting insanity under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Emotional outbursts, uncontrollable rage, or anger do not constitute legal insanity; an accused must be completely deprived of reason by a diseased mind.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC (Insanity Standard). Applicability: Applicable because emotional rage arising from wounded pride or anger is not a mental disease exempting from criminal culpability.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Pantoja's shooting was motivated by anger and revenge. Emotional rage without underlying psychosis is not insanity under Article 12(1).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Double Murder AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Uncontrollable anger or emotional outbursts do not constitute legal insanity under Art. 12(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 141

People v. Roa

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 128659, 21 June 2000 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the critical inquiry under Article 12(1) is the mental state of the accused at the very moment the felonious act was committed.

Facts:Roa struck his neighbor with an iron pipe, killing him. The defense presented psychiatric testimony that Roa suffered from paranoid schizophrenia months after the incident.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, relying on post-incident psychiatric diagnosis.

Issue:Does a psychiatric examination conducted months after the crime establish legal insanity at the time of the commission of the felony?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Insanity must be proven to exist at the exact time of the commission of the crime; medical condition months later does not establish retrospective insanity.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the critical inquiry under Article 12(1) is the mental state of the accused at the very moment the felonious act was committed.
•
[A] APPLICATION:No witness testified that Roa was insane on the day of the killing. Post-incident psychiatric evaluation months later failed to prove insanity at the precise moment of the attack.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Insanity must be proven to exist at the precise time of the crime; subsequent psychiatric diagnosis does not establish retrospective insanity under Art. 12(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 142

People v. Buenaflor

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 176251, 19 June 2007 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because clear and convincing evidence is required to overcome the statutory presumption of sanity.

Facts:Buenaflor hacked his neighbor to death while the victim was working on his farm. The defense presented testimonies from neighbors that the accused was quiet and occasionally laughed to himself.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed insanity under Article 12(1) RPC based on strange behavior and mood swings.

Issue:Is the testimony of non-expert witnesses on strange demeanor sufficient to prove legal insanity under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The defense failed to present expert medical proof or conclusive evidence of total deprivation of reason at the time of the killing.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC; Presumption of Sanity. Applicability: Applicable because clear and convincing evidence is required to overcome the statutory presumption of sanity.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Buenaflor selected his victim, carried a weapon to the farm, and fled after the attack. These acts proved cognitive awareness, refuting the claim of insanity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Lay testimony on odd behavior without expert medical evidence cannot overcome the presumption of sanity under Art. 12(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 143

People v. Nuñez

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 112092, 1 March 2001 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(1), 15, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because voluntary substance intoxication is governed by Article 15 (which may even be aggravating if habitual), not Article 12(1) insanity.

Facts:Nuñez entered the victim's house at night and stabbed him to death. Nuñez was an active shabu (methamphetamine) user and claimed that drug-induced hallucinations compelled him to kill.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked insanity under Article 12(1) RPC, claiming drug-induced psychosis.

Issue:Does temporary psychosis or hallucination induced by voluntary drug consumption constitute exempting insanity under Article 12(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Voluntary drug consumption or temporary intoxication is not legal insanity; unless drug use has produced permanent, chronic organic mental disease, it does not exempt.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1; Art. 15, RPC (Alternative Circumstance of Intoxication). Applicability: Applicable because voluntary substance intoxication is governed by Article 15 (which may even be aggravating if habitual), not Article 12(1) insanity.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Nuñez's hallucinations were the direct result of voluntary shabu intake. Because there was no permanent mental disease, the condition was voluntary intoxication, not exempting insanity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Voluntary drug-induced psychosis is not exempting insanity under Art. 12(1) RPC; it is governed by the rules on intoxication under Art. 15 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(1), 15, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 144

People v. Taneo

CITATION Citation: 58 Phil. 255 (1933) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 3, 12(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because a felony requires voluntary human action; an act done during an unconscious dream state has no voluntariness or dolo.

Facts:Potenciano Taneo was sleeping with his pregnant wife. In the middle of the night, while in a deep sleep, Taneo dreamed that his house was under attack by armed men and that he had to defend his wife. Still asleep, he grabbed a bolo, swung it wildly in his dream state, and slashed his wife and father, killing his wife and injuring his father before waking up and crying in horror.

Accused's Defense:Taneo invoked somnambulism (sleepwalking / lack of consciousness and free will) under Article 12(1) RPC.

Issue:Is an act committed while in a bona fide somnambulistic dream state exempt from criminal liability due to complete absence of volition and intelligence?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt on Ground of Somnambulism / Lack of Volition). An act committed during a true sleepwalking dream state lacks free will, consciousness, and criminal intent, completely exempting the actor from penal liability.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 1, RPC (Somnambulism / Total Deprivation of Will and Intelligence); Art. 3, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because a felony requires voluntary human action; an act done during an unconscious dream state has no voluntariness or dolo.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The evidence conclusively proved Taneo was deeply asleep in a dream state. He loved his wife and had no motive to harm her. The physical acts were purely automatic and unconscious.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment of conviction REVERSED; Potenciano Taneo FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Acts committed in a bona fide somnambulistic (sleepwalking) dream state lack voluntariness and exempt the actor under Art. 12(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 3, 12(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 145

Guevarra v. Hon. Ignacio Almodovar

CITATION Citation: 169 SCRA 476 (1989) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(3), 365, RPC; RA 9344.- Applicability:Applicable because discernment (understanding the moral difference between right and wrong) is an indispensable prerequisite to prosecute a child in conflict with the law.

Facts:An 11-year-old boy was shooting target birds with an air rifle. A pellet struck and killed his playmate. The boy was prosecuted for Homicide through Reckless Imprudence under Article 365 RPC.

Accused's Defense:The minor argued that under Article 12(3) RPC, a minor over 9 and under 15 is exempt from criminal liability unless proven to have acted with discernment, and discernment cannot exist in quasi-offenses of negligence.

Issue:Can a minor between 9 and 15 years old be convicted of a crime committed through reckless imprudence (culpa) without proof of discernment?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. In both intentional felonies and crimes committed through reckless imprudence, a minor between 9 and 15 years old is exempt unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that the child acted with discernment.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 3; Art. 365, RPC; Discernment Requirement (superseded by RA 9344). Applicability: Applicable because discernment (understanding the moral difference between right and wrong) is an indispensable prerequisite to prosecute a child in conflict with the law.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Discernment applies equally to intentional felonies and culpable felonies. The prosecution failed to prove that the 11-year-old child possessed full discernment regarding firearms danger.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Criminal proceedings against the minor DISMISSED. DOCTRINE: Under Art. 12(3) RPC and juvenile justice principles, a child cannot be held liable for intentional or culpable felonies without proof of discernment.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(3), 365, RPC; RA 9344.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 146

People v. Doqueña

CITATION Citation: 68 Phil. 580 (1939) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(3), 68, 249, RPC; RA 9344.- Applicability:Applicable to demonstrate how discernment is deduced from the conscious, evasive, and purposeful overt acts of a minor.

Facts:A 13-year-old boy challenged a playmate during a game of volleyball, drew a knife, chased the victim, and stabbed him to death. He then hid the knife and fled to another town.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked minority under Article 12(3) RPC, claiming he was exempt as a minor acting without discernment.

Issue:How is discernment proved in a minor over 9 and under 15 under Article 12(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:DISCERNMENT PROVED BY CONDUCT. Discernment may be established by the totality of the child's conduct, including the selection of the weapon, concealment, flight, and behavior before and after the crime.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 3, RPC (Minority with Discernment). Applicability: Applicable to demonstrate how discernment is deduced from the conscious, evasive, and purposeful overt acts of a minor.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Chasing the victim with a knife, hiding the weapon, and fleeing to another town proved that the 13-year-old child fully understood the moral and legal consequences of his wrongful act.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment finding minor acted WITH DISCERNMENT AFFIRMED (with privileged mitigation and sentence suspension). DOCTRINE: Discernment under Art. 12(3) RPC is demonstrated by the minor's conscious actions, concealment of weapons, and flight.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(3), 68, 249, RPC; RA 9344.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 147

People v. Navarro

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 173794, 27 August 2008 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12, 22, RPC; RA 9344.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 22 commands that favorable laws modifying criminal responsibility and penalties apply retroactively to pending cases.

Facts:Navarro, who was 16 years old at the time of the crime, was convicted of Murder. While his appeal was pending, Republic Act No. 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act of 2006) took effect.

Accused's Defense:Navarro argued that RA 9344, which raised the age of absolute exemption to 15 and established diversion and sentence suspension for minors between 15 and 18 acting without discernment, applied retroactively in his favor.

Issue:Does RA 9344 apply retroactively to favor a child in conflict with the law whose case is pending on appeal?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. RA 9344 is a favorable penal and welfare statute that applies retroactively under Article 22 RPC to all minors who committed offenses prior to its enactment.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:RA 9344 (Juvenile Justice and Welfare Act); Art. 22, RPC; Art. 12, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because Article 22 commands that favorable laws modifying criminal responsibility and penalties apply retroactively to pending cases.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Under RA 9344, Navarro is entitled to the privileged mitigating circumstance of minority and sentence suspension, requiring remand for juvenile rehabilitation and disposition.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction MODIFIED; case REMANDED to Family Court for disposition and rehabilitation under RA 9344. DOCTRINE: RA 9344 applies retroactively under Art. 22 RPC to all pending cases involving children in conflict with the law.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12, 22, RPC; RA 9344.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 148

Jose v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 148371, 12 August 2004 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(2), 68, 308, RPC; RA 9344.- Applicability:Applicable because minority lowers the imposable penalty by one or two degrees as a matter of substantive right under Article 68.

Facts:Jose was convicted of theft. On appeal, he claimed he was under 18 years old at the time of the commission of the offense and presented a delayed registered birth certificate and testimony of his mother.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked privileged mitigating circumstance of minority under Article 13(2) and Article 68 RPC.

Issue:What evidence is required to prove minority to entitle an accused to the privileged mitigating circumstance of minority under Article 68 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:CERTIFICATE OF LIVE BIRTH OR COMPETENT SECONDARY EVIDENCE. A birth certificate, baptismal certificate, school records, or credible parental testimony establish minority in the absence of contrary proof.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 2; Art. 68, RPC (Privileged Mitigation of Minority); Rules on Proof of Age. Applicability: Applicable because minority lowers the imposable penalty by one or two degrees as a matter of substantive right under Article 68.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The birth certificate and mother's testimony proved Jose was 17 years old when the theft was committed. He was entitled to the privileged reduction of penalty under Art. 68.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction AFFIRMED with PRIVILEGED MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Minority (penalty lowered by one degree under Art. 68 RPC). DOCTRINE: Credible proof of minority entitles the accused to a mandatory reduction of penalty by degrees under Art. 68 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(2), 68, 308, RPC; RA 9344.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 149

People v. Jacinto

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 182239, 16 March 2011 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12, RPC; Sec. 6, RA 9344.- Applicability:Applicable because RA 9344 places the burden on the State to allege and prove discernment for all minors between 15 and 18 years of age.

Facts:Jacinto was convicted of robbery with homicide committed when he was 17 years old. The prosecution failed to present independent evidence proving that Jacinto acted with discernment.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked RA 9344, arguing that as a 17-year-old child, the burden was on the prosecution to prove discernment beyond reasonable doubt.

Issue:Under RA 9344, is a child between 15 and 18 years old exempt from criminal liability if the prosecution fails to allege and prove discernment?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Under RA 9344, a minor over 15 but under 18 is exempt from criminal liability unless the prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that he acted with discernment.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:RA 9344, Sec. 6; Art. 12, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because RA 9344 places the burden on the State to allege and prove discernment for all minors between 15 and 18 years of age.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the prosecution failed to prove discernment, Jacinto was exempt from criminal liability and subject only to civil liability and juvenile intervention programs.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Criminal conviction SET ASIDE; accused DISCHARGED from penal liability and committed to juvenile welfare authorities under RA 9344. DOCTRINE: Minors over 15 but under 18 are exempt from criminal liability under RA 9344 unless the State proves discernment.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12, RPC; Sec. 6, RA 9344.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 150

People v. Arpon

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 183563, 14 December 2011 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 68, 266-A, RPC; RA 9344.- Applicability:Applicable because discernment is demonstrated when a minor understands the immorality and criminal consequences of his sexual assault.

Facts:Arpon, 17 years old, was charged with statutory rape. The prosecution established that Arpon lured the child, threatened her with violence, and warned her not to tell her parents.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked minority and claimed exemption under RA 9344 for lack of proof of discernment.

Issue:Does luring a victim and threatening her into silence demonstrate discernment in a 17-year-old minor under RA 9344?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Discernment Established). The minor's calculated overt acts, threats, and attempts to conceal the crime proved beyond reasonable doubt that he acted with full discernment.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:RA 9344, Sec. 6; Art. 68, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because discernment is demonstrated when a minor understands the immorality and criminal consequences of his sexual assault.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Arpon's deliberate acts of luring and intimidation showed full moral comprehension of wrongfulness. He was convicted with privileged mitigation of minority.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for RAPE AFFIRMED with PRIVILEGED MITIGATION of Minority under Art. 68 RPC and RA 9344. DOCTRINE: Threatening a victim and concealing a crime prove discernment in minors between 15 and 18 under RA 9344.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 68, 266-A, RPC; RA 9344.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 151

Sierra v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 182941, 3 July 2009 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 68, RPC; RA 9344.- Applicability:Applicable because sentence suspension is an administrative/rehabilitative measure applicable to children, which lapses upon reaching adulthood, though penalty reduction under Art. 68 remains permanent.

Facts:Sierra was convicted of a crime committed when he was a minor. On appeal, he reached the age of majority (over 21 years old) and sought sentence suspension under RA 9344.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that sentence suspension should still apply even if he reached the age of majority during appeal.

Issue:Can sentence suspension under RA 9344 still be granted to an offender who reached the age of majority during the pendency of the case?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO (Suspension Inapplicable; Privileged Mitigation Retained). Sentence suspension applies only while the offender is still a minor; once the offender reaches majority, sentence suspension lapses, but privileged mitigation of minority remains.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:RA 9344; Art. 68, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because sentence suspension is an administrative/rehabilitative measure applicable to children, which lapses upon reaching adulthood, though penalty reduction under Art. 68 remains permanent.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because Sierra reached 21 years old, sentence suspension was no longer available. However, his sentence was reduced by one degree under Article 68 RPC.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction AFFIRMED with MODIFIED penalty reflecting privileged mitigation of minority under Art. 68 RPC. DOCTRINE: Reaching majority during appeal terminates sentence suspension under RA 9344, but retains privileged mitigation under Art. 68 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 68, RPC; RA 9344.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 152

People v. Bindoy

CITATION Citation: 56 Phil. 15 (1931) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(4), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Bindoy was attempting to regain his knife from an unlawful grabber; the backward motion that struck an unseen bystander was pure accident without negligence.

Facts:Donato Bindoy was struggling with Pacas for the possession of a tuba knife. As Bindoy forcefully wrenched the knife back from Pacas, the blade flew backward and accidentally struck Emigdio Faustino, an innocent bystander standing behind him whom Bindoy did not see, inflicting a fatal chest wound.
