Accused's Defense:Bindoy invoked exempting circumstance of Accident under Article 12(4) RPC, claiming he was performing a lawful act of retaining his property with due care, completely lacking intent to harm the bystander.

Issue:Is an accused exempt from criminal liability for homicide under Article 12(4) RPC when a weapon strikes a bystander purely by accident during a struggle for possession?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt by Reason of Accident). All four elements of accident under Art. 12(4) were present: performing a lawful act with due care, injury caused by mere accident, without fault, and without intention of causing it.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 4, RPC (Exemption by Reason of Accident / Caso Fortuito). Applicability: Applicable because Bindoy was attempting to regain his knife from an unlawful grabber; the backward motion that struck an unseen bystander was pure accident without negligence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Bindoy did not know the victim was standing behind him. Struggling to pull back his knife was not unlawful. The tragic fatal blow was a pure casualty occurring without fault or malice.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment of conviction REVERSED; Donato Bindoy FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: An injury caused purely by accident in the performance of an act with due care without fault or malice exempts under Art. 12(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(4), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 153

U.S. v. Tanedo

CITATION Citation: 15 Phil. 196 (1910) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(4), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because lawful hunting carried out with reasonable care in a wooded area fulfills all criteria of accident under Article 12(4).

Facts:Tanedo went wild chicken hunting in the forest with a shotgun. He saw chickens in the bushes, aimed, and fired. Unknown to him, a man was walking hidden behind the dense thicket. A stray pellet ricocheted off a tree trunk and struck the hidden man in the head, killing him.

Accused's Defense:Tanedo invoked Accident under Article 12(4) RPC, asserting he was engaged in lawful hunting with due care and could not see the victim behind the dense brush.

Issue:Is a hunter exempt under Article 12(4) RPC when a ricocheting shotgun pellet strikes and kills a person hidden in dense brush?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt on Ground of Accident). Hunting wild game in the forest is lawful; firing at game with due care where a ricochet strikes an unseen person is a pure accident without criminal liability.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 4, RPC (Accident). Applicability: Applicable because lawful hunting carried out with reasonable care in a wooded area fulfills all criteria of accident under Article 12(4).
•
[A] APPLICATION:Tanedo had no reason to suspect a human being was hidden behind the foliage. Firing at game in the wilderness was lawful. The ricocheting pellet was a pure fortuity.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Homicide REVERSED; Tanedo FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: A ricocheting bullet striking an unseen person during lawful hunting without negligence is an exempting accident under Art. 12(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(4), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 154

Pomoy v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 150647, 29 September 2004 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(4), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because grappling to retain a service weapon from an aggressive arrestee is a lawful act with due care; accidental discharge during the struggle is exempt.

Facts:Police Officer Pomoy was investigating an unruly arrestee inside the police station. The arrestee suddenly lunged forward, grappled with Pomoy, and grabbed Pomoy's service revolver. During the violent physical struggle for the weapon, the gun accidentally fired twice, killing the arrestee.

Accused's Defense:Pomoy invoked Accident under Article 12(4) RPC and lawful performance of duty, asserting the weapon discharged accidentally during the scuffle initiated by the arrestee.

Issue:Is a police officer exempt under Article 12(4) RPC when his service gun discharges during a sudden grapple initiated by a detainee?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt by Reason of Accident). The gun discharge occurred during a violent grapple initiated by the detainee to grab the weapon; the officer was performing lawful duty and acted without fault or criminal intent.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 4, RPC (Accident); Art. 11, par. 5, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because grappling to retain a service weapon from an aggressive arrestee is a lawful act with due care; accidental discharge during the struggle is exempt.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Physical evidence and powder burns confirmed a point-blank grapple. Pomoy did not intentionally aim or pull the trigger. The firing was an accidental casualty during a lawful struggle.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Homicide REVERSED; Police Officer Pomoy FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Accidental discharge of a service firearm during a sudden physical grapple initiated by an arrestee is an exempting accident under Art. 12(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(4), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 155

People v. Macal

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 211062, 13 January 2016 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(4), 246, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the defense of accident requires total absence of fault, malice, and intent to kill; multiple stab wounds physically contradict accidental injury.

Facts:Arnel Macal stabbed his wife multiple times in the neck and chest during a heated quarrel inside their bedroom, killing her.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed Accident under Article 12(4) RPC, arguing that his wife attacked him with a knife and she was accidentally stabbed when they grappled and fell to the floor.

Issue:Can an accused invoke accident under Article 12(4) RPC when the victim sustains multiple deep penetrating stab wounds in vital organs?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Multiple deep stab wounds in vital areas (neck and chest) conclusively negate accident and demonstrate deliberate intent to kill (dolo).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 4; Art. 246, RPC (Parricide). Applicability: Applicable because the defense of accident requires total absence of fault, malice, and intent to kill; multiple stab wounds physically contradict accidental injury.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victim suffered multiple fatal stab wounds in the neck and chest. The severity and location of the wounds are physical evidence of intentional parricide, completely refuting the defense of accident.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for PARRICIDE AFFIRMED with Reclusion Perpetua. DOCTRINE: Multiple deep stab wounds in vital organs completely negate the defense of accident under Art. 12(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(4), 246, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 156

People v. Delector

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 128214, 21 September 2000 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(4), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because accident requires the exercise of due care; shooting blindly without verification constitutes actionable negligence.

Facts:Delector heard noises outside his house at night. Without verifying what was outside or turning on lights, he fired his shotgun through the wooden window into the dark yard, killing his brother-in-law who was visiting.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed Accident under Article 12(4) RPC and mistake of fact, claiming he believed an armed robber was outside.

Issue:Does firing a shotgun into the dark without verifying who is outside constitute exempting accident or reckless imprudence/homicide?

•
[A] ANSWER:HOMICIDE / RECKLESSNESS (Accident Negated). Firing blindly into the dark is gross negligence and a reckless unlawful act, completely negating the element of 'performing a lawful act with due care' required for accident.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 4; Art. 249, 365, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because accident requires the exercise of due care; shooting blindly without verification constitutes actionable negligence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Delector acted with reckless disregard for life by firing into the dark without visual verification. Failing to exercise due care bars the exempting circumstance of accident.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Firing blindly into the dark without verification is gross negligence that negates the defense of accident under Art. 12(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(4), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 157

United States v. Caballeros

CITATION Citation: 4 Phil. 350 (1905) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(5), 12(6), 19, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because being forced at gunpoint to assist murderers under threat of death completely extinguishes criminal culpability.

Facts:Caballeros and Baculi were captured by an armed band of murderous bandits who had just killed two American teachers. At gunpoint and under immediate threat of death, the bandits forced Baculi to dig a grave and bury the corpses.

Accused's Defense:Baculi invoked exempting circumstance of Uncontrollable Fear and Irresistible Force under Article 12(5) & 12(6) RPC, asserting he buried the bodies only to save his life.

Issue:Is a person who buries murder victims under immediate threat of death from armed bandits exempt as an accessory under Article 12(5) and 12(6) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt by Reason of Irresistible Force and Uncontrollable Fear). Baculi acted under irresistible physical compulsion and uncontrollable fear of an equal or greater evil (immediate death).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, pars. 5 & 6, RPC (Irresistible Force and Uncontrollable Fear). Applicability: Applicable because being forced at gunpoint to assist murderers under threat of death completely extinguishes criminal culpability.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Baculi had no connection with the bandits and was their captive. Under immediate threat of death, he buried the corpses. His acts were entirely compelled by uncontrollable fear.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction of Baculi as Accessory REVERSED and Baculi FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Performing acts under immediate, mortal threat from armed criminals is completely exempt under Art. 12(5) & (6) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(5), 12(6), 19, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 158

United States v. Exaltacion

CITATION Citation: 3 Phil. 339 (1904) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(6), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the threat to life was real, imminent, and continuous, leaving no reasonable alternative to preserve life.

Facts:Exaltacion and companions were captured by an armed insurgent commander in the mountains. Surrounded by armed rebels, they were forced at gunpoint to sign an oath of allegiance to the revolutionary government.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked uncontrollable fear of death under Article 12(6) RPC, arguing that refusing to sign meant instant execution.

Issue:Is signing an oath of allegiance to rebels under gunpoint and threat of death exempt from treason or rebellion under Article 12(6) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Signing documents under the immediate fear of death by armed captors is compelled by uncontrollable fear of an equal or greater injury, exempting the actors.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 6, RPC (Uncontrollable Fear of an Equal or Greater Injury). Applicability: Applicable because the threat to life was real, imminent, and continuous, leaving no reasonable alternative to preserve life.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The accused were captives in the wilderness surrounded by armed rebels. Signing the oath was the only means to avert immediate execution. They were exempt under Art. 12(6).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment of conviction REVERSED and accused FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Oaths signed under immediate, mortal duress by armed rebels are exempt under Art. 12(6) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(6), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 159

People v. Anod

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 186420, 25 August 2009 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(5), 12(6), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the defense of duress requires clear proof that the evil threatened was greater than or at least equal to the crime committed, and that the actor had no means of avoidance.

Facts:Anod participated in stabbing a victim. He claimed that an armed NPA commander ordered him to stab the victim, threatening to shoot Anod if he refused.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked uncontrollable fear and irresistible force under Article 12(5) & 12(6) RPC.

Issue:Can an accused invoke uncontrollable fear when he actively participated in a murder without showing that the threat was immediate and continuous leaving no opportunity for escape?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Duress and uncontrollable fear require proof that the threat was real, imminent, and continuous, leaving no possibility of escape or self-defense; speculative or remote fear does not exempt.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, pars. 5 & 6, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the defense of duress requires clear proof that the evil threatened was greater than or at least equal to the crime committed, and that the actor had no means of avoidance.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Anod joined the armed group voluntarily and took part in the stabbing without attempting to escape when opportunities were present. The threat was not of such nature as to extinguish free will.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Uncontrollable fear under Art. 12(6) RPC requires real, imminent, and inescapable mortal threat; speculative fear does not exempt from murder liability.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(5), 12(6), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 160

People v. Dansal

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 105002, 17 July 1997 | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(6), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because holding a flashlight under the guns of armed killers is compelled by imminent fear of death, negating criminal participation.

Facts:Dansal was forced by armed communist rebels to accompany them to a secluded area. While present, the rebels executed a civilian. Dansal held a flashlight as ordered, but did not strike the victim or carry a weapon.

Accused's Defense:Dansal invoked uncontrollable fear under Article 12(6) RPC, arguing he was held captive and feared execution if he disobeyed the armed commanders.

Issue:Is an unarmed civilian forced by armed rebels to accompany them and hold a flashlight exempt from murder under Article 12(6) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt by Reason of Uncontrollable Fear). Dansal acted under the immediate, imminent compulsion of armed rebels who held him captive, establishing uncontrollable fear under Art. 12(6).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 6, RPC (Uncontrollable Fear of Equal or Greater Evil). Applicability: Applicable because holding a flashlight under the guns of armed killers is compelled by imminent fear of death, negating criminal participation.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Dansal had no prior agreement with the rebels and was forced under armed escort. His passive holding of the light under gunpoint was product of uncontrollable fear.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment of conviction REVERSED; Dansal FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Passive assistance compelled at gunpoint by armed insurgents is completely exempt under Art. 12(6) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(6), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 161

U.S. v. Vicentillo

CITATION Citation: 19 Phil. 118 (1911) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(7), 125, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 12(7) exempts any person who fails to perform an act required by law when prevented by an insurmountable, lawful or physical impediment.

Facts:A municipal president (mayor) arrested an individual for a felony on a remote island. The statute required delivery of the detainee to the judicial authorities within statutory time limits. Due to severe oceanic storms and impassable waters, the vessel could not sail, delaying the transfer for three days.

Accused's Defense:The mayor invoked Insuperable Cause under Article 12(7) RPC, asserting that violent maritime storms rendered compliance with the statutory deadline physically impossible.

Issue:Does severe, impassable weather preventing the delivery of a prisoner constitute an exempting insuperable cause under Article 12(7) RPC for delay in delivery of detainees?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt by Insuperable Cause). An insuperable obstacle or physical impossibility preventing the performance of a statutory duty completely exempts the public officer from criminal liability under Art. 12(7).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 7, RPC (Insuperable Cause); Art. 125, RPC (Delay in Delivery of Detained Persons). Applicability: Applicable because Article 12(7) exempts any person who fails to perform an act required by law when prevented by an insurmountable, lawful or physical impediment.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The stormy seas made navigation impossible without risking the lives of all on board. This physical impossibility was a classic insuperable cause exempting the mayor from criminal liability for delay.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Arbitrary Detention REVERSED; Mayor Vicentillo FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Physical impossibility of compliance due to natural impediments (e.g. storms) is an exempting Insuperable Cause under Art. 12(7) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(7), 125, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).
CASE 162

People v. Bandian

CITATION Citation: 52 Phil. 200 (1928) | Topic: Exempting Circumstances: Insanity, Minority, Accident, Force, Fear, Insuperable Cause

Statutory Anchor:Art. 12(7), 255, 276, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because penal liability for omission requires the physical capability to perform the duty; total medical incapacitation is an insurmountable physical obstacle.

Facts:Valentina Bandian, an unwed mother, gave birth alone in a thicket. Immediately after delivery, she suffered severe, catastrophic postpartum uterine hemorrhage, lost consciousness, and lay comatose. The newborn infant died of exposure before she regained consciousness hours later.

Accused's Defense:Bandian invoked Insuperable Cause under Article 12(7) RPC, claiming she was physically incapacitated by comatose postpartum hemorrhage from caring for the child.

Issue:Is a mother who fails to care for her newborn infant due to postpartum hemorrhage and unconsciousness exempt from infanticide/abandonment under Article 12(7) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Exempt by Reason of Insuperable Cause). The severe medical hemorrhage and comatose state rendered it physically impossible for the mother to perform her parental duty, completely exempting her under Art. 12(7).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 12, par. 7, RPC (Insuperable Cause); Art. 3, RPC (Omission). Applicability: Applicable because penal liability for omission requires the physical capability to perform the duty; total medical incapacitation is an insurmountable physical obstacle.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Bandian was comatose and bleeding heavily. Her inability to care for the infant was not willful neglect, but the result of an insuperable medical catastrophe.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Infanticide REVERSED; Valentina Bandian FULLY ACQUITTED. DOCTRINE: Total physical incapacitation (e.g. comatose hemorrhage) preventing performance of duty is an exempting Insuperable Cause under Art. 12(7) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 12(7), 255, 276, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part IV: Justifying & Exempting Circumstances (Articles 11-12 RPC).

Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 13, Paragraphs 1 through 10, Revised Penal Code; Article 64 & Article 68, RPC • Total Cases: 19Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors circumstances that do not free the actor from criminal responsibility but reduce the penalty due to diminished voluntariness, lesser perversity, incomplete justification/exemption, immediate provocation/vindication, voluntary surrender, or analogous grounds.

CASE 163

People v. Ural

CITATION Citation: 56 SCRA 138 (1974) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(3), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because praeter intentionem applies only when the means employed could not reasonably be expected to cause death; burning a person with gasoline is naturally fatal.

Facts:Policeman Ural, inside the municipal jail, poured kerosene on a drunken detainee (Napola) and set him on fire with a match, causing fatal burns. Ural claimed he did not intend to kill the detainee and was only trying to quiet him down.

Accused's Defense:Ural claimed mitigating circumstance of lack of intent to commit so grave a wrong (praeter intentionem) under Article 13(3) RPC.

Issue:Can an accused who pours kerosene on a human being and lights a match claim the mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem under Article 13(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Setting a human being on fire is inherently lethal and cruel; the notable disparity between means and outcome required for praeter intentionem is completely absent.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 3; Art. 248, RPC (Murder with Treachery / Cruelty). Applicability: Applicable because praeter intentionem applies only when the means employed could not reasonably be expected to cause death; burning a person with gasoline is naturally fatal.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Pouring flammable fuel on a locked-up detainee and igniting it demonstrates clear homicidal cruelty. The fatal outcome was natural and expected, barring mitigation under Art. 13(3).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Setting a person on fire is inherently deadly; the mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem under Art. 13(3) RPC cannot be appreciated.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(3), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 164

People v. Reyes

CITATION Citation: 61 Phil. 341 (1935) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 13(3), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 13(3) mitigates penalty where the offender used moderate physical force without lethal weapons, yet death unexpectedly resulted.

Facts:Reyes struck the victim with his fist on the jaw during an argument. The victim stumbled, fell backward, hit his head on the concrete pavement, suffered skull fracture, and died.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked praeter intentionem under Article 13(3) RPC, arguing he only intended to deliver a fist blow and never intended to cause death.

Issue:Does delivering an ordinary fist blow that causes a fatal fall on concrete entitle the assailant to the mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem under Article 13(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. A simple fist blow is not normally a deadly weapon; the disparity between a fist blow and death entitles the offender to mitigating praeter intentionem.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 3; Art. 4, par. 1; Art. 249, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because Article 13(3) mitigates penalty where the offender used moderate physical force without lethal weapons, yet death unexpectedly resulted.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Reyes used only his bare fist and did not follow up when the victim fell. Because the fatal result was far beyond the natural force of a fist punch, praeter intentionem was present.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Praeter Intentionem (penalty reduced). DOCTRINE: A fist blow causing death through a fall on pavement warrants the mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem under Art. 13(3) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 13(3), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 165

People v. Leonor

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 125053, 25 March 1999 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the presence of unlawful aggression without the concurrence of reasonable necessity reduces liability by one or two degrees under Article 69.

Facts:Leonor was attacked by the victim with a stone during an altercation. Leonor wrestled the stone away, but instead of retreating, took out a hunting knife and stabbed the unarmed victim seven times.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed incomplete self-defense under Article 13(1) in relation to Article 11(1) RPC.

Issue:Is the accused entitled to incomplete self-defense when unlawful aggression was present initially but the means used to repel it was grossly disproportionate?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Incomplete Self-Defense / Privileged Mitigation). Unlawful aggression was present (stone attack), satisfying the indispensable requirement; the lack of reasonable necessity in stabbing seven times resulted in Incomplete Self-Defense under Art. 13(1) and Art. 69.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 1; Art. 11, par. 1; Art. 69, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the presence of unlawful aggression without the concurrence of reasonable necessity reduces liability by one or two degrees under Article 69.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The initial stone attack by the victim established unlawful aggression. Leonor's excessive use of a knife after disarming the victim negated complete defense, but qualified for privileged incomplete defense.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with PRIVILEGED MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Incomplete Self-Defense under Art. 69 RPC. DOCTRINE: Unlawful aggression coupled with disproportionate defensive means entitles the accused to privileged incomplete self-defense under Art. 13(1) & 69 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 166

Miranda v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 176298, 25 January 2012 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 11(1), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 69 mandates a penalty reduction of one or two degrees when the majority of conditions for self-defense are met, with unlawful aggression present.

Facts:Miranda was assaulted by the victim who struck him with a piece of wood. Miranda drew a knife and stabbed the victim in the abdomen. The victim survived after hospital surgery.

Accused's Defense:Miranda invoked incomplete self-defense under Article 13(1) RPC.

Issue:Does the presence of unlawful aggression with excessive defensive force constitute incomplete self-defense reducing the penalty by degrees?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The presence of initial unlawful aggression by the victim entitles the accused to the privileged mitigating circumstance of Incomplete Self-Defense under Art. 13(1) and 69 RPC.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 1; Art. 69, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because Article 69 mandates a penalty reduction of one or two degrees when the majority of conditions for self-defense are met, with unlawful aggression present.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victim initiated the physical assault with wood (unlawful aggression). Miranda's knife stabbing exceeded reasonable necessity, entitling him to privileged mitigation under Art. 69.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ATTEMPTED HOMICIDE MODIFIED with penalty reduced by one degree under Art. 69 RPC. DOCTRINE: Incomplete self-defense requires unlawful aggression and warrants privileged penalty reduction under Art. 13(1) & 69 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 11(1), 13(1), 69, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 167

Urbano v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 182750, 20 January 2009 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 4(1), 13(3), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 4(1) establishes proximate causation for infection resulting from wounds, while Article 13(3) mitigates liability where the fatal result was far beyond the force applied.

Facts:Urbano punched the victim Brigido on the cheek during a sudden fistfight. Brigido suffered a superficial cut. Brigido neglected the wound, developed tetanus infection days later, and died.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked praeter intentionem under Article 13(3) and lack of proximate cause, claiming a single punch was never intended to cause fatal tetanus.

Issue:Is an assailant who inflicts a superficial fist cut liable for homicide when the victim dies of tetanus, and is he entitled to mitigating praeter intentionem under Art. 13(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:LIABLE FOR HOMICIDE WITH PRAETER INTENTIONEM. The punch was the proximate cause introducing infection, but Urbano is entitled to the mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem due to the vast disparity between a fist blow and tetanus death.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 4, par. 1; Art. 13, par. 3; Art. 249, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because Article 4(1) establishes proximate causation for infection resulting from wounds, while Article 13(3) mitigates liability where the fatal result was far beyond the force applied.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The punch broke the skin through which tetanus entered. Urbano could not foresee fatal tetanus from a fist blow, entitling him to mitigating praeter intentionem under Art. 13(3).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Praeter Intentionem under Art. 13(3) RPC. DOCTRINE: Delivering a fist blow that leads to fatal tetanus infection is Homicide with mitigating praeter intentionem under Art. 13(3) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 4(1), 13(3), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 168

Oriente v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 155095, 30 January 2007 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(3), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because praeter intentionem is unavailable when the weapon used and the vital body part targeted inherently cause death.

Facts:Oriente struck the victim on the head with a hollow block during a sudden street brawl. The blow caused skull fracture and fatal hemorrhage.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem under Article 13(3) RPC, arguing he only threw the hollow block to defend himself in a rumble.

Issue:Does hitting a person on the head with a heavy hollow block entitle the accused to mitigating praeter intentionem under Article 13(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. A concrete hollow block is a heavy, dangerous weapon; striking a person on the head with it naturally and logically produces fatal brain trauma, negating praeter intentionem.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 3; Art. 249, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because praeter intentionem is unavailable when the weapon used and the vital body part targeted inherently cause death.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Hurlng a heavy concrete block directly at the victim's head demonstrates lethal force. The fatal result was directly commensurate with the dangerous means employed.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED without mitigation. DOCTRINE: Striking a victim on the head with a heavy concrete block is inherently lethal, barring the mitigating circumstance of praeter intentionem under Art. 13(3) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(3), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 169

People v. Racal

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 224886, 4 September 2017 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(4), 13(7), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because provocation that is grave, immediate, and originating from the offended party diminishes the offender's culpability.

Facts:The victim challenged Racal to a fight, insulted his family, and slapped him in public. Immediately provoked, Racal drew a knife and stabbed the victim to death.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked sufficient provocation under Article 13(4) and voluntary surrender under Article 13(7) RPC.

Issue:Does immediate violent reaction to public physical slapping and insults constitute mitigating sufficient provocation under Article 13(4) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The physical slap and verbal insults in public were sufficient, immediate, and originated entirely from the victim, satisfying all elements of mitigating provocation under Art. 13(4).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 4 & par. 7, RPC (Sufficient Provocation and Voluntary Surrender). Applicability: Applicable because provocation that is grave, immediate, and originating from the offended party diminishes the offender's culpability.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victim's public slapping of Racal was unjust and sufficient to trigger an immediate reaction. The presence of provocation and voluntary surrender reduced the penalty.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with TWO MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCES (penalty reduced by one degree). DOCTRINE: Public physical slap immediately preceding retaliation constitutes mitigating sufficient provocation under Art. 13(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(4), 13(7), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 170

United States v. Ampar

CITATION Citation: 37 Phil. 201 (1917) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(4), 265, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the gravity of provocation is measured relative to the social standing, age, and circumstances of the person provoked.

Facts:A 70-year-old man (Ampar) was eating in a public market when the victim approached him, loudly called him a shameless thief and swindler in front of a large crowd, and made mocking gestures. Highly humiliated, Ampar struck the victim with a piece of wood, causing injury.

Accused's Defense:Ampar invoked mitigating circumstance of sufficient provocation under Article 13(4) RPC.

Issue:Does publicly humiliating an elderly man by calling him a thief constitute mitigating sufficient provocation under Article 13(4) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. For a 70-year-old man to be publicly branded a thief in a crowded market is grave and sufficient provocation that immediately incites retaliation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 4, RPC (Sufficient Provocation). Applicability: Applicable because the gravity of provocation is measured relative to the social standing, age, and circumstances of the person provoked.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Publicly degrading an elderly person's honor with false accusations of theft is adequate provocation justifying the application of Article 13(4).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Physical Injuries AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Sufficient Provocation. DOCTRINE: Severe public verbal insult degrading an elderly person's honor constitutes sufficient provocation under Art. 13(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(4), 265, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 171

People v. Pajares

CITATION Citation: 210 SCRA 237 (1992) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(4), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because being struck by a stone is an unjust physical assault that produces natural provocation immediately prior to the crime.

Facts:The victim threw a stone that hit Pajares on the chest. Enraged, Pajares drew a weapon, chased the victim, and killed him.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed self-defense and mitigating circumstance of sufficient provocation under Article 13(4) RPC.

Issue:Does being hit by a thrown stone entitle the assailant to the mitigating circumstance of sufficient provocation under Article 13(4) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Sufficient Provocation Mitigates; Self-Defense Fails). While self-defense fails because unlawful aggression ceased upon the victim running away, the stone attack constitutes mitigating sufficient provocation under Art. 13(4).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 4, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because being struck by a stone is an unjust physical assault that produces natural provocation immediately prior to the crime.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The stone thrown by the victim was an unjustified physical attack that immediately provoked Pajares. He is entitled to mitigating provocation under Art. 13(4).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Sufficient Provocation under Art. 13(4) RPC. DOCTRINE: An assault with a stone immediately preceding retaliation constitutes mitigating sufficient provocation under Art. 13(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(4), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 172

Napone, Jr. v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 193085, 29 November 2017 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(5), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 13(5) expressly includes grave offenses committed against brothers/relatives, and allows a proximate interval of time for vindication.

Facts:Napone learned that the victim had severely beaten his younger brother, causing serious injuries. Hours later, Napone confronted the victim and fatally shot him to avenge his brother.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked immediate vindication of a grave offense under Article 13(5) RPC.

Issue:Does killing an assailant hours after he severely assaulted the accused's brother qualify for the mitigating circumstance of vindication of a grave offense under Article 13(5) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Vindication of a grave offense does not require instantaneous retaliation; it allows a reasonable lapse of time for the grave emotional distress and sense of outrage to persist.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 5, RPC (Immediate Vindication of a Grave Offense to Relatives). Applicability: Applicable because Article 13(5) expressly includes grave offenses committed against brothers/relatives, and allows a proximate interval of time for vindication.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Severe physical assault on a younger brother is a grave offense. The lapse of hours between learning of the assault and the confrontation was within the reasonable proximate period allowed for vindication under Art. 13(5).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Vindication of Grave Offense under Art. 13(5) RPC (penalty reduced). DOCTRINE: Vindication of a grave offense under Art. 13(5) RPC allows a proximate time interval between the offense against a relative and the retaliatory act.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(5), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 173

David v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: 290 SCRA 727 (1998) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(5), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because an attack on the chastity of one's wife is a grave moral injury to the family recognized as a grave offense under Article 13(5).

Facts:David shot the victim after the victim made defamatory statements and spread malicious rumors attacking the honor and chastity of David's wife.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed vindication of a grave offense under Article 13(5) RPC.

Issue:Do grave defamatory statements attacking the chastity of an accused's wife constitute a grave offense justifying mitigation under Article 13(5) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Attacks against the honor and chastity of a spouse constitute a grave offense warranting the mitigating circumstance of vindication under Art. 13(5).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 5, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because an attack on the chastity of one's wife is a grave moral injury to the family recognized as a grave offense under Article 13(5).
•
[A] APPLICATION:The malicious slanders against David's wife inflicted profound emotional distress. Confronting and shooting the defamer warranted mitigating vindication of a grave offense.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 13(5) RPC. DOCTRINE: Grave defamation against the honor and chastity of a spouse constitutes a grave offense under Art. 13(5) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(5), 249, RPC.
•
