CASE 174

United States v. Hicks

CITATION Citation: 14 Phil. 217 (1909) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(6), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 13(6) requires that the impulse generating passion must stem from legitimate feelings; emotions rooted in illicit relationships do not qualify.

Facts:Hicks lived illicitly with a woman (Agustina). After several years, she left him and cohabited with another man. Hicks went to her house armed with a revolver, pleaded with her to return, and when she refused, shot her dead in cold blood.

Accused's Defense:Accused invoked passion and obfuscation under Article 13(6) RPC, arguing that his jealousy and deep heartbreak clouded his reason.

Issue:Can an accused invoke passion and obfuscation arising from the refusal of a former concubine or illicit lover to return to an adulterous/illicit relationship?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Passion and obfuscation must arise from lawful, legitimate sentiments; jealousy arising from illicit or immoral relationships cannot be recognized as a mitigating circumstance.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 6, RPC (Passion and Obfuscation). Applicability: Applicable because Article 13(6) requires that the impulse generating passion must stem from legitimate feelings; emotions rooted in illicit relationships do not qualify.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Hicks had no lawful marital right over the victim. His resentment stemmed from the termination of an illicit cohabitation. Selfish jealousy is not a legitimate passion under Art. 13(6).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with DEATH PENALTY. DOCTRINE: Passion and obfuscation under Art. 13(6) RPC must arise from lawful, legitimate sentiments; jealousy from illicit relationships does not mitigate.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(6), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 175

United States v. De la Cruz

CITATION Citation: 9 Phil. 276 (1907) | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(6), 247, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because witnessing sexual infidelity in the home produces natural, overwhelming obfuscation of reason, fulfilling Article 13(6).

Facts:De la Cruz arrived at his home and discovered his common-law wife in flagrante in the bedroom engaged in sexual intercourse with another man. Overcome with overwhelming emotional fury and blinding passion, De la Cruz drew a knife and killed his common-law wife.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed passion and obfuscation under Article 13(6) RPC and death under exceptional circumstances under Article 247 RPC.

Issue:Does catching a common-law wife in flagrante delicto in the act of sexual infidelity entitle the accused to the mitigating circumstance of passion and obfuscation under Article 13(6) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Passion & Obfuscation Mitigates; Art. 247 Inapplicable). While Article 247 applies only to legally married spouses, catching a live-in partner in flagrante produces overwhelming blinding passion that mitigates liability under Art. 13(6).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 6; Art. 247, 249, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because witnessing sexual infidelity in the home produces natural, overwhelming obfuscation of reason, fulfilling Article 13(6).
•
[A] APPLICATION:Witnessing flagrant sexual infidelity in one's home produces spontaneous emotional devastation. The sudden shock and moral rage established mitigating passion/obfuscation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Passion and Obfuscation (penalty reduced). DOCTRINE: Catching a live-in partner in flagrante sexual infidelity constitutes mitigating passion and obfuscation under Art. 13(6) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(6), 247, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 176

People v. Placer

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 128456, 17 June 1999 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(7), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 13(7) rewards an offender who saves the State the expense and trouble of manhunt by spontaneously submitting to justice.

Facts:Placer committed homicide. Before an arrest warrant was issued, he walked to the municipal police station, introduced himself to the desk officer, and voluntarily yielded himself and his weapon to the custody of the authorities.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed the mitigating circumstance of Voluntary Surrender under Article 13(7) RPC.

Issue:What are the requisites for the mitigating circumstance of Voluntary Surrender under Article 13(7) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:REQUISITES SATISFIED. Voluntary surrender requires: (1) the offender has not been actually arrested; (2) he surrendered himself to a person in authority or an agent; and (3) the surrender was voluntary, spontaneous, and unconditional.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 7, RPC (Voluntary Surrender). Applicability: Applicable because Article 13(7) rewards an offender who saves the State the expense and trouble of manhunt by spontaneously submitting to justice.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Placer presented himself at the police station unconditionally before any warrant was executed. The surrender was spontaneous and voluntary, satisfying all statutory requirements.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Voluntary Surrender under Art. 13(7) RPC. DOCTRINE: Spontaneous and unconditional surrender to police before arrest entitles the offender to mitigation under Art. 13(7) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(7), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 177

De Vera v. De Vera

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 172832, 7 April 2009 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(7), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because voluntary surrender must be spontaneous and unconditional, indicating acknowledgment of guilt and saving the state from tracking the offender.

Facts:De Vera went into hiding for two years following a killing. When a police SWAT team cornered him in an apartment with arrest warrants, he raised his hands and surrendered without armed resistance.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed voluntary surrender under Article 13(7) RPC, asserting he did not fire at the arresting officers.

Issue:Does submitting to arresting officers after a prolonged flight when cornered by police constitute voluntary surrender under Article 13(7) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Surrendering only after being cornered and tracked down by police with arrest warrants is mere submission to arrest, not spontaneous voluntary surrender.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 7, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because voluntary surrender must be spontaneous and unconditional, indicating acknowledgment of guilt and saving the state from tracking the offender.
•
[A] APPLICATION:De Vera hid for two years and yielded only because escape was physically impossible. Submission when cornered does not merit mitigation under Art. 13(7).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED without mitigation of voluntary surrender. DOCTRINE: Yielding to police when cornered with an arrest warrant is mere submission, not voluntary surrender under Art. 13(7) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(7), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 178

People v. Quijano

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 102450, 17 May 1993 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(7), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 13(7) requires a plea of guilty prior to trial evidence presentation to demonstrate genuine repentance and save state trial resources.

Facts:Quijano initially pleaded not guilty to murder. After the prosecution presented several witnesses establishing his guilt, Quijano moved to withdraw his plea of not guilty and entered a plea of guilty.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed the mitigating circumstance of Voluntary Confession of Guilt under Article 13(7) RPC.

Issue:Can a plea of guilty entered after the prosecution has already commenced the presentation of evidence be appreciated as a mitigating circumstance under Article 13(7) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. To be mitigating under Article 13(7), the voluntary plea of guilty must be made in open court prior to the presentation of evidence by the prosecution.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 7, RPC (Plea of Guilty Requirement). Applicability: Applicable because Article 13(7) requires a plea of guilty prior to trial evidence presentation to demonstrate genuine repentance and save state trial resources.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because Quijano changed his plea only after the prosecution's evidence had exposed his guilt, the plea was an act of tactical surrender, not spontaneous confession.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED without mitigation of plea of guilty. DOCTRINE: A plea of guilty must be entered before the prosecution begins presenting evidence to be mitigating under Art. 13(7) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(7), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 179

People v. Javier

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 130489, 19 February 2002 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(9), 246, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because chronic physiological/psychological distress that impairs self-control without totally extinguishing discernment warrants mitigation under Article 13(9).

Facts:Javier killed his wife with a bolo. He claimed that he had been suffering from insomnia, severe headaches, and deep mental depression for months prior to the incident, which diminished his self-control.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed mitigating circumstance of illness diminishing willpower under Article 13(9) RPC.

Issue:Does chronic mental depression and severe headache diminishing willpower without depriving reason qualify as a mitigating circumstance under Article 13(9) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Illness of the offender that diminishes willpower without depriving him of consciousness of his acts is a mitigating circumstance under Article 13(9).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 9, RPC (Illness Diminishing Willpower). Applicability: Applicable because chronic physiological/psychological distress that impairs self-control without totally extinguishing discernment warrants mitigation under Article 13(9).
•
[A] APPLICATION:Medical testimony and family witnesses corroborated that Javier suffered from chronic insomnia and severe depression. His mental illness diminished his willpower, entitling him to mitigation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for PARRICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 13(9) RPC (penalty reduced). DOCTRINE: Chronic mental or physical illness diminishing willpower without total loss of reason mitigates under Art. 13(9) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(9), 246, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 180

Canta v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 140937, 28 February 2001 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(10), 308, RPC; PD 533.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 13(10) authorizes courts to recognize any other circumstance of similar nature and analogous effect to the enumerated mitigating factors.

Facts:Narciso Canta took a cow belonging to the complainant under an honest belief that it was his father's lost animal. Upon being informed of the true ownership, he immediately returned the cow and assisted in returning it to the owner.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed analogous mitigating circumstance under Article 13(10) RPC, having voluntarily restored the property upon discovering his error.

Issue:Does spontaneous, voluntary return of property upon discovering a mistake constitute an analogous mitigating circumstance under Article 13(10) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Voluntary restitution of property analogous to voluntary surrender or spontaneous repentance qualifies as an analogous mitigating circumstance under Article 13(10).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 13, par. 10, RPC (Analogous Mitigating Circumstances). Applicability: Applicable because Article 13(10) authorizes courts to recognize any other circumstance of similar nature and analogous effect to the enumerated mitigating factors.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Canta acted under an honest mistake and immediately surrendered the animal upon notification. His conduct was analogous to voluntary surrender and repentance under Art. 13(10).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Accused ACQUITTED of Cattle Rustling (lack of dolo / honest mistake); analogous mitigating principles recognized. DOCTRINE: Spontaneous restitution and surrender of property is an analogous mitigating circumstance under Art. 13(10) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(10), 308, RPC; PD 533.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 181

Eduarte v. People

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 176566, 16 April 2009 | Topic: Mitigating Circumstances (Incomplete Defenses, Age, Provocation, Vindication, Passion, Surrender, Illness)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 13(7), 15, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the alternative circumstance of intoxication requires affirmative proof by the defense that the drunkenness was neither habitual nor intentional.

Facts:The accused was convicted of homicide. He claimed mitigating circumstances of non-habitual intoxication and voluntary surrender.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that his drunkenness clouded his judgment and he presented himself to the barangay captain.

Issue:Must the defense prove that intoxication was non-habitual and not subsequent to the plan to commit the crime to merit mitigation?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Intoxication is mitigating only when proven to be non-habitual and not intentionally incurred to bolster courage; failing proof, it cannot be appreciated.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 15 & Art. 13, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the alternative circumstance of intoxication requires affirmative proof by the defense that the drunkenness was neither habitual nor intentional.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The defense presented no evidence regarding drinking habits. However, voluntary surrender to the barangay captain was established and appreciated as mitigating.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with MITIGATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Voluntary Surrender. DOCTRINE: Intoxication requires affirmative proof of non-habituality; voluntary surrender to barangay authorities is mitigating under Art. 13(7) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 13(7), 15, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).

Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 14, Paragraphs 1 through 21, Revised Penal Code; Rule 110, Section 8 & 9, Rules of Criminal Procedure • Total Cases: 35Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors conditions that increase the penalty to its maximum period or qualify an offense into a higher distinct crime due to greater perversity, abuse of public position, treachery (alevosia), evident premeditation, nighttime, superior strength, or craft, requiring specific allegation in the Information.

CASE 182

People v. Ordiales

CITATION Citation: 42 SCRA 238 (1971) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(1), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the officer used his service gun and police uniform to intimidate the victim and commit the murder.

Facts:Ordiales, a municipal policeman in uniform and armed with a service firearm, shot an unarmed civilian inside a restaurant following a minor disagreement over a table.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed self-defense, arguing that the victim reached for his waistline.

Issue:Does a police officer who uses his official service weapon and authority to commit an unjustified shooting incur the aggravating circumstance of Taking Advantage of Official Position under Article 14(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. When a public officer uses the influence, prestige, and service weapon entrusted to him by the government to facilitate a crime, Article 14(1) applies as an aggravating circumstance.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 1, RPC (Taking Advantage of Public Position). Applicability: Applicable because the officer used his service gun and police uniform to intimidate the victim and commit the murder.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Ordiales abused his official status as a law enforcer to shoot an unarmed citizen with his government-issued weapon. This constitutes aggravating abuse of public position.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Taking Advantage of Public Position under Art. 14(1) RPC. DOCTRINE: A police officer using his service gun and authority to commit murder incurs aggravating circumstance under Art. 14(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(1), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 183

People v. Torrida

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 84154, 21 June 1991 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(2), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the crime was perpetrated in the direct presence of a public authority performing public duties, defying the authority of the State.

Facts:Torrida and companions attacked and killed the victim in the direct presence and hearing of the municipal mayor, who was trying to mediate a community dispute.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed alibi and denied knowing the mayor was present.

Issue:Does committing a murder in the presence of a municipal mayor acting in an official capacity constitute the aggravating circumstance of In Contempt of or with Insult to Public Authorities under Article 14(2) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Committing a felony in the presence of a person in authority engaged in the exercise of public functions without the authority being the victim constitutes the aggravating circumstance under Art. 14(2).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 2, RPC (In Contempt of or with Insult to Public Authorities). Applicability: Applicable because the crime was perpetrated in the direct presence of a public authority performing public duties, defying the authority of the State.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The mayor was present in his official capacity to maintain peace. Murdering the victim in front of the mayor displayed brazen contempt for public authority under Art. 14(2).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 14(2) RPC. DOCTRINE: Committing a murder in the direct presence of a public officer exercising official functions is aggravating under Art. 14(2) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(2), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 184

People v. Rodil

CITATION Citation: 109 SCRA 308 (1981) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(3), 48, 148, 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because an assault on an officer in uniform constitutes direct assault under Article 148, which complexes with murder under Article 48.

Facts:Rodil was caught carrying an unlicensed firearm by PC Lieutenant Masana in uniform. As Lt. Masana was disarming him, Rodil suddenly pulled a concealed dagger and stabbed Lt. Masana to death.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed self-defense and argued that the victim was not in uniform.

Issue:Does killing a military/police officer in uniform while performing official duty constitute Murder with the Direct Assault and the Aggravating Circumstance of Disrespect of Rank under Article 14(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:COMPLEX CRIME OF DIRECT ASSAULT WITH MURDER. Killing an agent of authority in uniform while performing duty constitutes direct assault complexed with murder, absorbing disrespect of rank.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 3; Art. 48; Art. 148 & 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because an assault on an officer in uniform constitutes direct assault under Article 148, which complexes with murder under Article 48.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Lt. Masana was in full uniform performing law enforcement duty. Stabbing him with treachery constituted the complex crime of Direct Assault upon a Person in Authority with Murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for COMPLEX CRIME OF DIRECT ASSAULT WITH MURDER AFFIRMED with Death Penalty. DOCTRINE: Stabbing an officer in uniform performing duty constitutes Direct Assault with Murder under Art. 48, 148, & 248 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(3), 48, 148, 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 185

United States v. Manuel Rodriguez

CITATION Citation: 19 Phil. 150 (1911) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(4), 294(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 14(4) requires a special relationship of confidence and trust between victim and offender that was intentionally exploited to commit the crime.

Facts:Rodriguez was welcomed into the home of a close friend as an overnight houseguest. While the family slept, Rodriguez took the host's jewelry and cash, killed the host when he woke up, and escaped.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed alibi and denied having abused any special relationship.

Issue:Does a houseguest who robs and kills his host while enjoying hospitality incur the aggravating circumstance of Abuse of Confidence and Ungratefulness under Article 14(4) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The accused abused the immediate trust and hospitality extended by the host to enter the home and commit robbery and murder, satisfying Article 14(4).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 4; Art. 294(1), RPC. Applicability: Applicable because Article 14(4) requires a special relationship of confidence and trust between victim and offender that was intentionally exploited to commit the crime.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The host opened his home and gave shelter to Rodriguez based on trust. Exploiting that hospitality to steal and kill constitutes grave abuse of confidence and ungratefulness.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Abuse of Confidence under Art. 14(4) RPC. DOCTRINE: Exploiting domestic hospitality as a houseguest to rob and kill constitutes aggravating abuse of confidence under Art. 14(4) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(4), 294(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 186

United States v. Licarte

CITATION Citation: 23 Phil. 10 (1912) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(5), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because public buildings dedicated to the administration of justice demand special sanctity and respect under the law.

Facts:Licarte engaged in a violent physical altercation and stabbed his adversary inside the office of the Justice of the Peñace while court proceedings were about to begin.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that the fight was personal and not intended as disrespect to the court.

Issue:Does committing a violent assault inside a court building or office dedicated to public authority constitute the aggravating circumstance under Article 14(5) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Committing a crime in a place where public authorities are engaged in the discharge of their duties constitutes the aggravating circumstance under Art. 14(5).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 5, RPC (Committed in a Place where Public Authorities are Discharging Duties). Applicability: Applicable because public buildings dedicated to the administration of justice demand special sanctity and respect under the law.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The stabbing occurred inside the courtroom premises while judicial authority was present. This desecration of a judicial hall constitutes the aggravating factor under Art. 14(5).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 14(5) RPC. DOCTRINE: Committing a violent crime inside a courtroom or public hall of justice is aggravating under Art. 14(5) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(5), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 187

People v. Pagal

CITATION Citation: 79 SCRA 570 (1977) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(6), 294(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the offenders deliberately delayed their attack to the dead of night to exploit the darkness for ambush and concealment.

Facts:Pagal and his co-accused waited until 2:00 AM in the pitch-black darkness to assault, rob, and kill the victim along an unlit road, using the darkness to conceal their identities and escape unnoticed.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that nighttime was merely accidental and not purposely sought.

Issue:When is Nighttime (Nocturnity) appreciated as an aggravating circumstance under Article 14(6) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NIGHTTIME PURPOSELY SOUGHT. Nighttime is aggravating when it is purposely sought by the culprits, or taken advantage of to facilitate the commission of the crime or ensure impunity.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 6, RPC (Nighttime / Nocturnity). Applicability: Applicable because the offenders deliberately delayed their attack to the dead of night to exploit the darkness for ambush and concealment.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The culprits specifically chose 2:00 AM in an unlit area to prevent identification and ensure safe escape. Nocturnity was deliberately exploited under Art. 14(6).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Nighttime under Art. 14(6) RPC. DOCTRINE: Deliberately choosing deep darkness to facilitate a robbery-killing is aggravating under Art. 14(6) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(6), 294(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 188

People v. Daniel

CITATION Citation: 86 SCRA 511 (1978) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(6), 335, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the isolated wilderness location was exploited to eliminate any possibility of the victim receiving assistance.

Facts:Daniel ambushed, raped, and killed a woman in a dense, remote forest trail located several kilometers from the nearest residential settlement, where help could not possibly arrive.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that the isolated location was incidental to where the victim happened to be walking.

Issue:Does committing a rape-homicide in an isolated forest trail constitute the aggravating circumstance of Uninhabited Place (Despoblado) under Article 14(6) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. An uninhabited place is aggravating when the crime is committed in an isolated area where there is no reasonable possibility of the victim receiving help or rescue.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 6, RPC (Uninhabited Place / Despoblado). Applicability: Applicable because the isolated wilderness location was exploited to eliminate any possibility of the victim receiving assistance.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The crime was perpetrated in deep forest terrain far from human habitation. Daniel purposely chose this wilderness location so the victim's screams could not be heard.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for RAPE WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Uninhabited Place under Art. 14(6) RPC. DOCTRINE: Committing a crime in a secluded area where assistance is impossible constitutes aggravating despoblado under Art. 14(6) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(6), 335, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 189

People v. Ambis

CITATION Citation: 68 Phil. 645 (1939) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(6), 294(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because five men, all carrying deadly weapons, acted together to overwhelm the victims.

Facts:Ambis and four other armed men, all carrying firearms and bolos, broke into a house, tied up the occupants, and murdered the owner before looting the property.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that the presence of multiple men was only incidental.

Issue:Does the commission of a crime by more than three armed malefactors constitute the aggravating circumstance of By a Band (En Cuadrilla) under Article 14(6) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Whenever more than three armed malefactors act together in the commission of an offense, it is deemed committed by a band under Article 14(6).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 6, RPC (By a Band / En Cuadrilla). Applicability: Applicable because five men, all carrying deadly weapons, acted together to overwhelm the victims.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The presence of five armed men working in concert fulfilled all statutory criteria of a band (more than 3 armed malefactors), aggravating the crime under Art. 14(6).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Band under Art. 14(6) RPC. DOCTRINE: An armed group of four or more malefactors committing a crime constitutes an aggravating band under Art. 14(6) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(6), 294(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 190

People v. Kalipayan

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 129815, 23 November 1999 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(7), 294(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because exploiting the vulnerability and chaos of a natural disaster to commit crime demonstrates extreme moral depravity.

Facts:During a massive flood caused by a typhoon when residents were frantically evacuating their homes, Kalipayan broke into an abandoned residence, looted valuables, and killed the elderly caretaker left behind.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that the typhoon was an independent natural occurrence not created by him.

Issue:Does committing robbery and murder on the occasion of a natural calamity or flood constitute the aggravating circumstance under Article 14(7) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Committing a felony on the occasion of a conflagration, shipwreck, earthquake, epidemic, or other calamity is an aggravating circumstance under Article 14(7).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 7, RPC (On the Occasion of a Calamity/Misfortune). Applicability: Applicable because exploiting the vulnerability and chaos of a natural disaster to commit crime demonstrates extreme moral depravity.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Kalipayan took advantage of the typhoon floodwaters and evacuation chaos to burglarize and kill. This directly satisfied the aggravating factor under Art. 14(7).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 14(7) RPC. DOCTRINE: Exploiting the helplessness of victims during a typhoon or natural calamity is aggravating under Art. 14(7) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(7), 294(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 191

People v. Verdad

CITATION Citation: 122 SCRA 239 (1983) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(8), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because armed guards preventing rescue increase the offender's physical advantage and ensure execution.

Facts:Verdad attacked the victim with a bolo while two armed companions stood guard with rifles, aiming their guns at bystanders to prevent anyone from assisting the victim.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that his companions did not strike the victim and their presence should not aggravate the crime.

Issue:Does the presence of armed companions standing guard to prevent rescue constitute the aggravating circumstance of With the Aid of Armed Men under Article 14(8) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The aggravating circumstance of with the aid of armed men is present when armed companions participate directly or indirectly to intimidate bystanders, secure the perimeter, or ensure impunity.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 8, RPC (Aid of Armed Men). Applicability: Applicable because armed guards preventing rescue increase the offender's physical advantage and ensure execution.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The armed riflemen secured the perimeter and prevented any aid to the victim. This satisfied the aggravating circumstance of aid of armed men under Art. 14(8).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 14(8) RPC. DOCTRINE: Armed guards standing by to prevent rescue constitute the aggravating circumstance of Aid of Armed Men under Art. 14(8) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(8), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 192

People v. Syou Hu

CITATION Citation: 65 Phil. 270 (1938) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(9), 308, 315, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because both Theft (Art. 308) and Estafa (Art. 315) are embraced in Title Ten (Crimes Against Property) of the Revised Penal Code.

Facts:Syou Hu was convicted of theft. The prosecution established that he had previously been convicted by final judgment of estafa (both crimes under Title Ten: Crimes Against Property).

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that theft and estafa are different crimes and recidivism should not apply.

Issue:Is an accused who was previously convicted of estafa a recidivist under Article 14(9) RPC when convicted of theft?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. A recidivist is one who, at the time of his trial for one crime, shall have been previously convicted by final judgment of another crime embraced in the same title of the Revised Penal Code.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 9, RPC (Recidivism / Reincidencia). Applicability: Applicable because both Theft (Art. 308) and Estafa (Art. 315) are embraced in Title Ten (Crimes Against Property) of the Revised Penal Code.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because both prior final conviction for estafa and current conviction for theft fall under Title Ten RPC, Syou Hu is a recidivist under Article 14(9).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for THEFT AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Recidivism under Art. 14(9) RPC. DOCTRINE: Prior final conviction for an offense under the same Title of the RPC establishes Recidivism under Art. 14(9) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(9), 308, 315, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 193

People v. Abrazaldo

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 124492, 4 February 2003 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(10), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because aggravating circumstances must be proved beyond reasonable doubt by competent documentary evidence.

Facts:Abrazaldo stabbed the victim to death. The prosecution attempted to prove habituality / reiteracion by alleging prior charges without presenting authenticated final judgments.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that prior arrests and pending charges cannot establish reiteracion or habituality.

Issue:Can reiteracion under Article 14(10) RPC be appreciated without certified copies of final judgments of conviction?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Reiteracion and recidivism must be proved by certified copies of final judgments of conviction; mere police records or pending charges do not suffice.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 10, RPC (Reiteracion / Habituality); Best Evidence Rule on Final Judgments. Applicability: Applicable because aggravating circumstances must be proved beyond reasonable doubt by competent documentary evidence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The prosecution failed to produce certified copies of final convictions showing that the accused had served sentences for prior offenses. Reiteracion could not be appreciated.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED without aggravating reiteracion. DOCTRINE: Reiteracion under Art. 14(10) RPC requires certified copies of final judgments proving prior conviction and service of sentence.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(10), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 194

People v. Bermas

CITATION Citation: 306 SCRA 135 (1999) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(11), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because contract killing for money corrupts the mercenary and the inducer, qualifying the crime to murder.

Facts:Bermas was hired by a mastermind to assassinate a political rival for the sum of P50,000. Bermas shot and killed the victim as agreed and received the payment.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed he was coerced by the mastermind into carrying out the shooting.

Issue:Does committing a murder for a monetary consideration qualify the crime to murder or constitute the aggravating circumstance of Price, Promise, or Reward under Article 14(11) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:QUALIFIES TO MURDER (Article 248) and AGGRAVATING (Article 14[11]). Commission of a crime for price, promise, or reward is a qualifying circumstance for murder as well as an inherent aggravating circumstance affecting both inducer and hitman.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 11; Art. 248, par. 2, RPC (Price, Promise, or Reward). Applicability: Applicable because contract killing for money corrupts the mercenary and the inducer, qualifying the crime to murder.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Bermas agreed to kill for P50,000. The monetary reward was the primary inducement, qualifying the killing to Murder under Art. 248.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with Death Penalty. DOCTRINE: Contract killing for money qualifies the homicide to Murder under Art. 248(2) and Art. 14(11) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(11), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 195

People v. Matbagon

CITATION Citation: 60 Phil. 887 (1934) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(12), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because fire was the chosen instrumentality to accomplish the murder.

Facts:Matbagon set fire to the victim's house while the victim was asleep inside, with the specific intent to kill the victim by burning him alive.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed he only intended to burn the house and that the killing was accidental.

Issue:When fire is used as the specific means to kill a person, is the crime Murder or Arson with Homicide?

•
[A] ANSWER:MURDER. When fire is employed as the deadly instrument and means to execute the killing of a person, the crime is Murder qualified by the use of fire under Article 248(3) and Article 14(12) RPC.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 12; Art. 248, par. 3, RPC (By Means of Inundation, Fire, Poison, Explosion). Applicability: Applicable because fire was the chosen instrumentality to accomplish the murder.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Matbagon used fire specifically to execute the victim. Under Article 248(3), the use of fire qualifies the killing to Murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Employing fire as the direct means to kill a person constitutes Murder qualified by fire under Art. 248(3) and Art. 14(12) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(12), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 196

People v. Arpa

CITATION Citation: 27 SCRA 1037 (1969) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(13), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the two-week surveillance and preparation proved prolonged, cool reflection and persistent criminal determination.

Facts:Arpa and companions stalked the victim for two weeks, purchased special knives, met repeatedly to assign roles, and executed the assassination as planned.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed the attack was a spontaneous response to a heated encounter.

Issue:What are the requisites of Evident Premeditation under Article 14(13) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:ALL REQUISITES PRESENT: (1) the time when the offender determined to commit the crime; (2) an act manifestly indicating that the culprit clung to his determination; and (3) a sufficient lapse of time between determination and execution to allow cool reflection.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 13; Art. 248, RPC (Evident Premeditation). Applicability: Applicable because the two-week surveillance and preparation proved prolonged, cool reflection and persistent criminal determination.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The two-week planning, weapon procurement, and execution proved cool reflection and persistent intent. Evident premeditation qualified the crime to murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Proof of determination to kill, persistent overt preparation, and sufficient time for cool reflection establish Evident Premeditation under Art. 14(13) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(13), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 197

People v. Manlolo

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 40778, 26 January 1989 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(14), 294, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because deceit and disguise were deliberately used to induce false security and gain entry into the home.

Facts:Manlolo wore a police uniform and displayed fake police badges to gain entry into the victim's residence under the guise of serving a search warrant. Once inside, they drew weapons and robbed the household.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that the disguise was harmless trickery that did not cause physical injury.

Issue:Does using a fake police uniform to gain entry into a home constitute the aggravating circumstance of Craft, Fraud, or Disguise under Article 14(14) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The use of a counterfeit police uniform and fake badges constituted craft, fraud, and disguise employed to lower the victim's defenses and facilitate entry.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 14; Art. 294, RPC (Craft, Fraud, or Disguise). Applicability: Applicable because deceit and disguise were deliberately used to induce false security and gain entry into the home.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Manlolo deceived the victims into opening their doors by impersonating police officers. This deception directly satisfied Article 14(14).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Craft/Disguise under Art. 14(14) RPC. DOCTRINE: Impersonating police officers to gain entry into a residence constitutes aggravating craft and disguise under Art. 14(14) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(14), 294, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 198

United States v. Rodriguez

CITATION Citation: 19 Phil. 150 (1911) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(15), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the marked disparity in age, strength, numbers, and weapons was deliberately exploited to execute the crime.

Facts:Three robust, armed young men overpowered, beat, and killed an elderly, frail, unarmed man who was alone in his store.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that the fight was mutual and superior strength was not purposely taken advantage of.

Issue:Does the simultaneous armed attack by three strong men against a frail elderly person constitute Abuse of Superior Strength under Article 14(15) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Abuse of superior strength exists when the assailants purposely use their physical superiority, number, and weapons to overpower and render the victim defenseless.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 15; Art. 248, RPC (Abuse of Superior Strength). Applicability: Applicable because the marked disparity in age, strength, numbers, and weapons was deliberately exploited to execute the crime.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Three armed young men attacking an elderly lone victim created a gross physical disparity that was purposely used to kill him without risk to themselves.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER qualified by Abuse of Superior Strength AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Exploiting marked physical disparity in numbers and weapons against a defenseless victim is aggravating under Art. 14(15) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(15), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 199

People v. Hipolito

CITATION Citation: 106 SCRA 610 (1981) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(16), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the sudden, surprise attack from behind completely deprived the victim of any defense, fulfilling all elements of treachery.

Facts:Hipolito approached the victim from behind while the victim was drinking coffee, drew a firearm, and shot him in the back of the head without warning.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed self-defense, asserting the victim made a threatening movement.

Issue:Does shooting an unsuspecting victim from behind without warning constitute Treachery (Alevosia) under Article 14(16) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Murder Qualified by Treachery). Shooting an unsuspecting victim from behind employs means, methods, or forms of execution that directly ensure the killing without risk to the assailant from any defense the victim might make.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 16; Art. 248, RPC (Treachery / Alevosia). Applicability: Applicable because the sudden, surprise attack from behind completely deprived the victim of any defense, fulfilling all elements of treachery.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Hipolito attacked from behind while the victim was drinking peacefully. The surprise execution afforded the victim no opportunity to defend himself, establishing treachery.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with Reclusion Perpetua. DOCTRINE: A sudden surprise attack from behind on an unsuspecting victim is Treachery (Alevosia) under Art. 14(16) & 248 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(16), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 200

People v. Nabual

CITATION Citation: 28 SCRA 747 (1969) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(17), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because stripping the victim in public deliberately subjected her to extreme moral degradation and public humiliation prior to her death.

Facts:Nabual and co-accused stripped the female victim naked in the public plaza, mocked and paraded her before bystanders, and then stabbed her to death.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that stripping the victim was merely incidental to the physical struggle.

Issue:Does stripping a female victim naked in public before killing her constitute the aggravating circumstance of Ignominy under Article 14(17) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Ignominy is an aggravating circumstance that adds moral disgrace, shame, and obloquy to the material injury of the crime.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 17; Art. 248, RPC (Ignominy). Applicability: Applicable because stripping the victim in public deliberately subjected her to extreme moral degradation and public humiliation prior to her death.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Publicly stripping the woman added extreme moral humiliation and shame to the killing, directly fulfilling the statutory definition of ignominy under Art. 14(17).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Ignominy under Art. 14(17) RPC. DOCTRINE: Deliberately subjecting a victim to moral degradation and public humiliation adds the aggravating circumstance of Ignominy under Art. 14(17) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(17), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 201

United States v. Manalinde

CITATION Citation: 14 Phil. 77 (1909) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(11), 14(13), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the agreement to kill for reward provided the premeditated determination, which persisted during days of travel.

Facts:Manalinde accepted an offer of money and goods from a datu to assassinate the first two Americans or Christians he encountered. He traveled for days, stalked a street in Cotabato, and hacked a Spanish merchant and an American officer to death with a kris.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed he had no personal grudge against the specific victims and only followed the datu's command.

Issue:Does contract assassination against indiscriminate victims constitute Evident Premeditation and Price, Promise, or Reward under Article 14(11) & (13) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Agreeing to kill for money and stalking for days establishes both Price/Reward and Evident Premeditation, even if the specific identity of the victims was not predetermined.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, pars. 11 & 13; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the agreement to kill for reward provided the premeditated determination, which persisted during days of travel.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Manalinde agreed to kill for reward and carried that lethal determination over days of stalking. This satisfied both qualifying price/reward and evident premeditation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with DEATH PENALTY. DOCTRINE: Contract killing for reward against indiscriminate targets establishes both Price/Reward and Evident Premeditation under Art. 14(11) & (13) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(11), 14(13), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 202

People v. Quiñanola

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 126148, 5 May 1999 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(18), 266-A, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because entering a dwelling through a window is an unlawful mode of ingress increasing vulnerability.

Facts:Quiñanola scaled a ladder, climbed through a second-story window not intended for ingress, entered the victim's bedroom, and raped her.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed the victim consented and let him in through the window.

Issue:Does climbing through a window to commit rape constitute the aggravating circumstance of Unlawful Entry under Article 14(18) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Unlawful entry is present when an entrance is effected by a way not intended for the purpose, such as a window.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 18; Art. 266-A, RPC (Unlawful Entry / Escalada). Applicability: Applicable because entering a dwelling through a window is an unlawful mode of ingress increasing vulnerability.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Scaling a ladder and entering through a bedroom window constituted unlawful entry, aggravating the rape under Article 14(18).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for RAPE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Unlawful Entry under Art. 14(18) RPC. DOCTRINE: Entering a dwelling through a window not intended for ingress constitutes aggravating Unlawful Entry under Art. 14(18) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(18), 266-A, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 203

United States v. Devela

CITATION Citation: 3 Phil. 625 (1904) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(19), 299, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because breaking physical structures to gain ingress demonstrates determined criminal destruction.

Facts:Devela cut and sawed a hole through the wooden floor of a store at night, crawled inside, and stole cash and goods.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that cutting the floor was part of the element of robbery and should not be separately aggravating.

Issue:Does breaking or cutting through a floor to enter a building constitute the aggravating circumstance under Article 14(19) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Inherent in Robbery under Art. 299, but Aggravating in other crimes). Breaking a wall, roof, floor, door, or window is an aggravating circumstance under Article 14(19) when not already an inherent element of the specific robbery charged.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 19; Art. 299, RPC (Breaking Wall, Roof, Floor). Applicability: Applicable because breaking physical structures to gain ingress demonstrates determined criminal destruction.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Sawing through the floor to gain access completed the statutory element of robbery by force upon things, and constitutes the aggravating factor under Art. 14(19).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY IN AN INHABITED HOUSE AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Breaking through a wall, roof, or floor is aggravating under Art. 14(19) RPC when not absorbed as an element.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(19), 299, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 204

People v. Sangalang

CITATION Citation: 58 SCRA 737 (1974) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(20), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the high-speed motorized boat was specifically used to land by surprise and make a rapid maritime escape.

Facts:Sangalang and armed companions used a motorized speed boat to land on a coastal island, kill their target, and immediately speed away into open sea to evade pursuit.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that using a motorized boat was merely their mode of ordinary transportation.

Issue:Does using a motorized watercraft to facilitate an ambush and swift escape constitute the aggravating circumstance under Article 14(20) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The use of a motor vehicle or motorized craft is aggravating when it is purposely utilized to facilitate the commission of the crime or ensure swift flight and escape.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 20, RPC (By Means of Motor Vehicles or Motorized Craft). Applicability: Applicable because the high-speed motorized boat was specifically used to land by surprise and make a rapid maritime escape.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The speedboat was essential to execute the coastal hit and elude police pursuit. This fulfilled the aggravating circumstance under Article 14(20).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE under Art. 14(20) RPC. DOCTRINE: Using a motor vehicle or motorized craft to facilitate the crime and ensure swift escape is aggravating under Art. 14(20) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(20), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 205

People v. Cañete

CITATION Citation: 44 Phil. 478 (1923) | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(21), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because slowly mutilating a conscious, bound victim deliberately inflicts unnecessary physical agony prior to death.

Facts:Cañete tied the victim to a tree, slowly cut off his ears and nose, gouged his eyes, and taunted him while he bled for hours before finally slitting his throat.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that the multiple mutilations occurred in a fit of uncontrollable rage.

Issue:Does deliberately prolonging the physical suffering of the victim before death constitute Cruelty (Ensañamiento) under Article 14(21) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Qualifies to Murder). Cruelty exists when the culprit deliberately and inhumanely augmented the suffering of the victim, causing unnecessary physical agony before death.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 21; Art. 248, par. 6, RPC (Cruelty / Ensañamiento). Applicability: Applicable because slowly mutilating a conscious, bound victim deliberately inflicts unnecessary physical agony prior to death.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Cañete deliberately tortured the victim for hours before the fatal blow. This deliberate augmentation of physical suffering established cruelty under Article 14(21).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with DEATH PENALTY. DOCTRINE: Deliberately augmenting physical pain by torturing and mutilating a conscious victim prior to death constitutes Cruelty under Art. 14(21) & 248 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(21), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 206

People v. Dela Cruz

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 175929, 16 December 2008 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(21), 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because cruelty requires a specific sadistic intent to prolong agony; rapid multiple wounds in a frenzy indicate rage, not deliberate torture.

Facts:Dela Cruz stabbed the victim 25 times in rapid succession during a violent frenzy. The prosecution alleged cruelty based purely on the large number of stab wounds.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that multiple stab wounds delivered rapidly in a frenzy do not establish deliberate cruelty.

Issue:Does the mere number of stab wounds establish the qualifying circumstance of Cruelty under Article 14(21) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The number of wounds alone does not prove cruelty; there must be positive proof that the accused deliberately and sadistically intended to prolong the victim's agony.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 21; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because cruelty requires a specific sadistic intent to prolong agony; rapid multiple wounds in a frenzy indicate rage, not deliberate torture.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The 25 stabs were delivered rapidly during a furious assault. Without evidence of deliberate torture or prolongation of suffering while alive, cruelty was not established.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED (Cruelty not appreciated). DOCTRINE: Mere multiplicity of wounds does not constitute Cruelty under Art. 14(21) RPC in the absence of proof of deliberate intent to prolong suffering.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(21), 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 207

People v. Monte

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 144317, 5 August 2003 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(16), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because shooting a sleeping person is the quintessential manifestation of treachery, affording the victim no defense.

Facts:Monte walked up to a sleeping fisherman lying on a bench, pointed a gun at his temple, and shot him dead.

Accused's Defense:Accused denied shooting the victim and presented alibi.

Issue:Does killing a sleeping victim constitute Treachery (Alevosia) under Article 14(16) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Killing a person who is asleep is treacherous because a sleeping victim is completely defenseless and unable to offer resistance or escape.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 16; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because shooting a sleeping person is the quintessential manifestation of treachery, affording the victim no defense.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victim was asleep and utterly helpless. Monte's execution of the sleeping man eliminated all risk to himself, establishing treachery.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with Reclusion Perpetua. DOCTRINE: Killing a sleeping, defenseless victim is Treachery (Alevosia) qualifying the crime to Murder under Art. 14(16) & 248 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(16), 248, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 208

People v. Torrefiel

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 115431, 18 April 1997 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(13), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because all three elements of evident premeditation were established by clear and convincing evidence.

Facts:Torrefiel publicly threatened to kill the victim in the morning. He spent the afternoon sharpening his bolo, waited along the victim's path at dusk, and hacked him to death.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed he acted on impulse during a chance encounter.

Issue:Does public threat followed by hours of weapon preparation and lying in wait prove Evident Premeditation under Article 14(13) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The morning threat proved determination, sharpening the weapon proved clinging to that determination, and the lapse of hours allowed cool reflection.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 13; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because all three elements of evident premeditation were established by clear and convincing evidence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Torrefiel harbored a premeditated design throughout the day and waited along the path. Evident premeditation qualified the killing to murder.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Morning threats followed by afternoon weapon preparation and evening ambush establish Evident Premeditation under Art. 14(13) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(13), 248, RPC.
•

CASE 209

People v. Alfanta

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 139194, 28 October 2002 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(15), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the attackers used numerical and weapon superiority to ensure the destruction of the victim.

Facts:Alfanta and two armed companions surrounded an unarmed farmer in his field and simultaneously attacked him with knives and clubs, killing him.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that they fought the farmer one-on-one.

Issue:Does a simultaneous assault by three armed men against one unarmed victim constitute Abuse of Superior Strength under Article 14(15) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Three armed men attacking an unarmed, lone farmer constitutes clear abuse of superior strength, overwhelming the victim's defenses.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 15; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the attackers used numerical and weapon superiority to ensure the destruction of the victim.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The three assailants exploited their combined physical force and weapons against a solitary unarmed victim, satisfying Article 14(15).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Three armed men simultaneously attacking a solitary unarmed person constitutes Abuse of Superior Strength under Art. 14(15) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(15), 248, RPC.

CASE 210

People v. Fuertes

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 104067, 29 January 1999 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(3), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the home is a sacred sanctuary; invading another's home to kill him demonstrates greater perversity.

Facts:Fuertes forced his way into the victim's house at night and stabbed the victim inside his living room without provocation.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that dwelling should not aggravate the crime because the quarrel began outside.

Issue:Does killing a person inside his own home without provocation constitute the aggravating circumstance of Dwelling (Morada) under Article 14(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Dwelling is aggravating in crimes against persons committed in the victim's sanctuary and home where the victim has not given provocation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 3; Art. 248, RPC (Dwelling / Morada). Applicability: Applicable because the home is a sacred sanctuary; invading another's home to kill him demonstrates greater perversity.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victim was inside his own home and gave no provocation. Fuertes invaded the residence, aggravating the homicide/murder under Art. 14(3).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Dwelling under Art. 14(3) RPC. DOCTRINE: Committing a murder inside the victim's dwelling without provocation is an aggravating circumstance under Art. 14(3) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(3), 248, RPC.

People v. Puda

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(6), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the accused exploited darkness to mount a surprise attack and facilitate immediate flight.

Facts:Puda waited in the darkness outside the victim's house, and when the victim opened the door at night, shot him dead and escaped into the dark.

•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 6, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because the accused exploited darkness to mount a surprise attack and facilitate immediate flight.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Puda used the cover of night to ambush the victim and avoid identification during escape, fulfilling Article 14(6).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Nighttime. DOCTRINE: Exploiting the cover of darkness to mount a surprise attack and escape is aggravating under Art. 14(6) RPC.

[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(6), 248, RPC.

People v. Bondoy

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(6), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because four armed malefactors acted in concert to execute the murder.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed that not all participants were armed.

•
[A] APPLICATION:All four attackers were armed with firearms. Their coordinated assault satisfied the statutory definition of a band.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Band under Art. 14(6) RPC. DOCTRINE: Four armed malefactors acting together constitute an aggravating band under Art. 14(6) RPC.

CASE 213

People v. Sitchon

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 134362, 27 February 2002 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(14), 294(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because artifice and intellectual trickery were used to disarm the victim's suspicions and gain entry.

Facts:Sitchon knocked on the victim's door asking for a glass of water. When the victim turned to get water, Sitchon entered, drew a knife, and stabbed the victim to rob the house.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed he was invited inside and did not use craft.

Issue:Does feigning thirst to induce the victim to open the door constitute the aggravating circumstance of Craft under Article 14(14) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Pretending to ask for water to lure the victim into lowering her guard and allowing entry constitutes aggravating Craft under Art. 14(14).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 14; Art. 294, RPC (Craft / Artificio). Applicability: Applicable because artifice and intellectual trickery were used to disarm the victim's suspicions and gain entry.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Sitchon used a feigned request for water as a ruse to enter the house and attack the unsuspecting victim. This was a classic application of craft.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH HOMICIDE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Craft under Art. 14(14) RPC. DOCTRINE: Feigning innocent requests to gain entry and disarm a victim constitutes aggravating Craft under Art. 14(14) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(14), 294(1), RPC.

CASE 214

People v. Fernandez

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 134762, 23 July 2002 | Topic: Aggravating Circumstances (All 21 Paragraphs)

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(16), 248, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because an attack on a sleeping person ensures execution without any defensive risk to the shooter.

Facts:Fernandez shot his brother-in-law in the head while the latter was lying asleep on a hammock inside their yard.

[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 14, par. 16; Art. 248, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because an attack on a sleeping person ensures execution without any defensive risk to the shooter.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The victim was asleep in a hammock and defenseless. Shooting him in the head was murder qualified by treachery under Art. 248.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED with Reclusion Perpetua. DOCTRINE: Shooting a sleeping victim is Murder qualified by Treachery under Art. 14(16) & 248 RPC.

[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 14(16), 248, RPC.

CASE 215

People v. Cortes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(4), 308, 310, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because domestic employment creates high trust and confidence, the betrayal of which qualifies the theft.

[A] APPLICATION:Cortes was entrusted with access to the master bedroom as a houseboy. Stealing the employer's valuables constituted grave abuse of confidence, qualifying the theft.

[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for QUALIFIED THEFT AFFIRMED with enhanced penalty. DOCTRINE: Theft committed by a domestic helper against an employer constitutes Qualified Theft under Art. 310 RPC through grave abuse of confidence.

CASE 216

People v. Bernabe

Statutory Anchor:Art. 14(17), 294(2), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because raping a spouse in front of her bound husband deliberately inflicts profound moral anguish and degradation.

[A] APPLICATION:The perpetrators deliberately augmented the shame of the sexual assault by forcing the husband to witness it. This satisfied the aggravating circumstance of ignominy.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for ROBBERY WITH RAPE AFFIRMED with AGGRAVATING CIRCUMSTANCE of Ignominy under Art. 14(17) RPC. DOCTRINE: Raping a woman in the presence of her bound husband constitutes aggravating Ignominy under Art. 14(17) RPC.

Topic: Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Article 15, Article 20, Article 247, Article 332, Revised Penal Code • Total Cases: 12Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors circumstances taken into consideration as either mitigating or aggravating according to the nature and effects of the crime (relationship, intoxication, degree of instruction), as well as absolute bars to criminal liability (absolutory causes) founded on marital honor or close family relationship in property crimes.

CASE 217

People v. Orilla

CITATION Citation: G.R. Nos. 148939-40, 13 February 2004 | Topic: Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 15, 266-A, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because in crimes against chastity, relationship is inherently aggravating as a breach of domestic guardianship.

Facts:Orilla raped his 10-year-old stepdaughter inside their home while the mother was away working.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that relationship as a stepfather should not be aggravating under Article 15.

Issue:Is relationship as a stepfather an aggravating alternative circumstance under Article 15 in the crime of rape?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. In crimes against chastity and rape, relationship (including stepfather) is always aggravating under Article 15 RPC because it represents a vile betrayal of parental trust.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 15; Art. 266-A, RPC (Alternative Circumstance of Relationship). Applicability: Applicable because in crimes against chastity, relationship is inherently aggravating as a breach of domestic guardianship.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Orilla stood in loco parentis over the 10-year-old child. Betraying that protective role to rape the child made relationship an aggravating circumstance.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for QUALIFIED RAPE AFFIRMED with Death Penalty (commuted to Reclusion Perpetua). DOCTRINE: In crimes against chastity (rape), relationship under Art. 15 RPC is always aggravating.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 15, 266-A, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 218

People v. Lomaque

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 189297, 5 June 2013 | Topic: Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 15, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 15 provides that intoxication is mitigating only when non-habitual and not intentional.

Facts:Lomaque was drinking liquor prior to stabbing a neighbor. He claimed he was drunk and should be given mitigating intoxication under Article 15.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed mitigating circumstance of non-habitual intoxication under Article 15 RPC.

Issue:What proof is required to appreciate intoxication as a mitigating alternative circumstance under Article 15 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:PROOF OF NON-HABITUALITY AND ABSENCE OF PREMEDITATED INTENT TO DRINK. The defense must prove that the intoxication was non-habitual, that the offender did not drink to bolster courage, and that liquor impaired his mental faculties.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 15, RPC (Alternative Circumstance of Intoxication). Applicability: Applicable because Article 15 provides that intoxication is mitigating only when non-habitual and not intentional.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Lomaque failed to prove that his drinking was non-habitual. In the absence of positive evidence, intoxication could not be appreciated.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for HOMICIDE AFFIRMED without mitigation of intoxication. DOCTRINE: Intoxication under Art. 15 RPC requires affirmative proof that it was non-habitual and not intentional.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 15, 249, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 219

People v. Macatanda

CITATION Citation: 109 SCRA 35 (1981) | Topic: Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 15, RPC; PD 533.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 15 allows degree of instruction to be appreciated as mitigating in exceptional circumstances where lack of literacy diminishes comprehension of special statutory decrees.

Facts:Macatanda, a member of an indigenous cultural community (Muslim Maranao), stole a carabao and was convicted of Cattle Rustling under PD 533. He pleaded that his lack of formal instruction and cultural background should mitigate his liability.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed mitigating degree of instruction / cultural minority under Article 15 RPC and customary law.

Issue:Can lack of education or membership in a cultural minority mitigate criminal liability in crimes against property (Cattle Rustling)?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (as to cultural minority / lack of education under proper circumstances). While illiteracy is generally not mitigating in crimes against property, the Supreme Court recognized the accused's cultural minority status and lack of instruction as mitigating under Art. 15 and special laws.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 15; Art. 13(10), RPC; PD 533. Applicability: Applicable because Article 15 allows degree of instruction to be appreciated as mitigating in exceptional circumstances where lack of literacy diminishes comprehension of special statutory decrees.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Macatanda was completely illiterate and belonged to a cultural minority. His lack of education was considered as mitigating in determining the penalty.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for Cattle Rustling AFFIRMED with MITIGATED PENALTY. DOCTRINE: Membership in a cultural minority and complete lack of instruction may be appreciated as mitigating under Art. 15 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 15, RPC; PD 533.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part V: Mitigating, Aggravating, Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes (Articles 13-15 RPC).
CASE 220

People v. Baltazar

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 129933, 26 February 2001 | Topic: Alternative Circumstances & Absolutory Causes

Statutory Anchor:Art. 15, 249, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 15 explicitly provides mitigation for non-habitual, non-intentional drunkenness.

Facts:Baltazar drank liquor with friends before engaging in a shooting. The defense presented evidence from barangay officials that Baltazar rarely drank and was not a habitual drunkard.

Accused's Defense:Accused claimed mitigating circumstance of non-habitual intoxication under Article 15 RPC.

Issue:Does credible proof that the accused is an occasional drinker entitle him to mitigating intoxication under Article 15 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. When the defense proves that the accused is not a habitual drinker, did not drink to commit the crime, and was intoxicated at the time of the offense, intoxication is mitigating under Art. 15.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 15, RPC (Intoxication as Mitigating). Applicability: Applicable because Article 15 explicitly provides mitigation for non-habitual, non-intentional drunkenness.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Testimony from community leaders established that Baltazar was an occasional drinker who did not plan the crime while drinking. Intoxication was properly mitigating.
•
