CASE 259

Bala v. Martinez

CITATION Citation: 181 SCRA 459 (1990) | Topic: Death Penalty, Complex Crimes, Continued Crimes, ISLAW, and Probation

Statutory Anchor:Sec. 11, 15, PD 968.- Applicability:Applicable because probation is a privilege subject to strict compliance with good behavior conditions; breach of condition justifies revocation upon summary hearing.

Facts:Bala was granted probation. During the probation period, he was arrested for committing another criminal offense. The trial court summarily revoked his probation and ordered him to serve the original sentence.

Accused's Defense:Probationer argued that probation could not be revoked until he was convicted by final judgment of the new offense.

Issue:Is final conviction of a subsequent offense required before a court can revoke probation for violation of probation conditions under PD 968?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The trial court may revoke probation upon summary hearing showing that the probationer violated any condition of probation; a final conviction for the new crime is not required.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:PD 968, Sec. 11 & 15 (Revocation of Probation). Applicability: Applicable because probation is a privilege subject to strict compliance with good behavior conditions; breach of condition justifies revocation upon summary hearing.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Bala violated the condition to be of good behavior and refrain from committing offenses. The summary hearing established the breach, justifying revocation.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Revocation of probation and commitment to prison AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Probation may be revoked upon summary hearing for violation of conditions under Sec. 15 of PD 968 without awaiting final conviction for a new crime.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Sec. 11, 15, PD 968.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VII: Penalties, Classification, Duration, Graduation & Indeterminate Sentence Law (Articles 21-88 RPC).
CASE 260

Salgado v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: 189 SCRA 304 (1990) | Topic: Death Penalty, Complex Crimes, Continued Crimes, ISLAW, and Probation

Statutory Anchor:Sec. 9(a), PD 968.- Applicability:Applicable because the disqualification threshold is determined strictly by the MAXIMUM term of the sentence imposed by the court.

Facts:Salgado was convicted of serious physical injuries and sentenced to an indeterminate penalty with a maximum term exceeding six years. He applied for probation.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that his minimum penalty was less than 6 years and should qualify him for probation.

Issue:Is an offender eligible for probation under PD 968 if the MAXIMUM term of imprisonment exceeds six years?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Under Section 9(a) of PD 968, an offender sentenced to a maximum term of imprisonment of more than six years is disqualified from probation.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:PD 968, Sec. 9(a) (Disqualified Offenders). Applicability: Applicable because the disqualification threshold is determined strictly by the MAXIMUM term of the sentence imposed by the court.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the maximum term imposed exceeded six years, Salgado was statutorily disqualified from probation under Section 9(a).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Denial of probation AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: An offender whose sentence carries a maximum term of imprisonment exceeding six years is disqualified from probation under Sec. 9(a) of PD 968.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Sec. 9(a), PD 968.
•

PART: VI. EXTINCTION OF CRIMINAL LIABILITY

Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Articles 89 through 99, Revised Penal Code; R.A. 10592 (Good Conduct Time Allowance); Rules on Executive Clemency • Total Cases: 8Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the legal grounds that completely wipe out criminal liability (death, amnesty, absolute pardon, prescription of crime/penalty) or partially reduce the penalty (conditional pardon, commutation, GCTA), delineating the survival of civil obligations.

CASE 261

People v. Bayotas

CITATION Citation: 236 SCRA 239 (1994) | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 89(1), RPC; Art. 1157, Civil Code.- Applicability:Applicable because criminal action and civil liability ex delicto are inextricably linked; without a final judgment of conviction, no civil liability ex delicto can survive.

Facts:Hermogenes Bayotas was convicted of rape. While his appeal was pending before the Supreme Court, Bayotas died in prison. The Solicitor General argued that his death extinguished only criminal liability, and that civil liability ex delicto survived against his estate.

Accused's Defense:Defense counsel moved to dismiss the appeal and extinguish all criminal and civil liability ex delicto arising from the crime.

Issue:Does the death of the accused pending appeal extinguish both criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto (arising from crime)?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Extinguished / Landmark Bayotas Rules). Death of the accused pending appeal totally extinguishes his criminal liability and the civil liability solely based on the crime (ex delicto).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 89, par. 1, RPC (Total Extinction of Criminal Liability by Death); Landmark Bayotas Rules. Applicability: Applicable because criminal action and civil liability ex delicto are inextricably linked; without a final judgment of conviction, no civil liability ex delicto can survive.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Under Article 89(1), death prior to final judgment extinguishes criminal liability and civil action ex delicto. Claimants may pursue separate civil actions founded on sources other than crime (law, contract, quasi-delict).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Criminal case and civil liability ex delicto DISMISSED and DECLARED EXTINGUISHED. DOCTRINE: Death of the accused pending appeal extinguishes both criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto under Art. 89(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 89(1), RPC; Art. 1157, Civil Code.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 262

People v. Dela Cruz

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 138990, 22 January 2003 | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 89(1), RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because death of the accused deprives the court of criminal jurisdiction over his person.

Facts:Dela Cruz died while his appeal from a murder conviction was pending before the Court of Appeals.

Accused's Defense:Defense counsel submitted a certified copy of the death certificate and moved for total dismissal.

Issue:Does the presentation of an authenticated death certificate pending appeal require immediate dismissal of the criminal case under Article 89(1) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Upon proof of death of the accused pending appeal, the criminal case is closed and all criminal and civil liability ex delicto is extinguished.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 89, par. 1, RPC; Bayotas Doctrine. Applicability: Applicable because death of the accused deprives the court of criminal jurisdiction over his person.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Upon submission of the official death certificate, the Supreme Court dismissed the criminal case and extinguished civil liability ex delicto pursuant to Article 89(1).
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Criminal case CLOSED and DISMISSED; criminal and civil liability ex delicto EXTINGUISHED. DOCTRINE: Proof of death of the accused pending appeal permanently extinguishes all criminal and civil liability ex delicto under Art. 89(1) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 89(1), RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 263

People v. Patriarca

CITATION Citation: 341 SCRA 464 (2000) | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 89(3), RPC; Proclamation No. 724.- Applicability:Applicable because Amnesty completely obliterates all legal memory and penal effects of the political offense.

Facts:Patriarca, a member of the New People's Army (NPA), was convicted of murder committed in furtherance of the communist insurgency. While his appeal was pending, he applied for and was granted Amnesty under Presidential Proclamation No. 724.

Accused's Defense:Accused moved to dismiss the appeal on the ground of Amnesty granted by the National Amnesty Commission and concurred in by Congress.

Issue:Does a grant of Amnesty concurred in by Congress completely extinguish the criminal liability and erase the crime under Article 89(3) RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES (Total Extinction by Amnesty). Amnesty is a public act of the sovereign power which obliterates the offense itself, treating the offender as if he had never committed the crime.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 89, par. 3, RPC (Amnesty as Total Extinction); 1987 Const. Art. VII, Sec. 19; Proclamation No. 724. Applicability: Applicable because Amnesty completely obliterates all legal memory and penal effects of the political offense.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Patriarca was granted official amnesty for political crimes committed in pursuit of the rebellion. Under Article 89(3), his criminal liability was totally extinguished.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Criminal case DISMISSED and accused DISCHARGED. DOCTRINE: Amnesty completely obliterates the crime and totally extinguishes criminal liability under Art. 89(3) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 89(3), RPC; Proclamation No. 724.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 264

People v. Casido

CITATION Citation: 269 SCRA 360 (1997) | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 89(3), 89(4), 94, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Amnesty requires proof that the crime was political in character and approved by the Amnesty Board.

Facts:Accused-appellants convicted of murder claimed they were covered by a general amnesty proclamation for political rebels.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that their crimes were committed in connection with insurgency and should be dismissed under amnesty.

Issue:What is the distinction between Amnesty (Art. 89[3]) and Executive Pardon (Art. 89[4] / Art. 94)?

•
[A] ANSWER:AMNESTY BLOTS OUT THE CRIME; PARDON REMITS THE PENALTY. Amnesty applies to political offenses, requires concurrence of Congress, is addressed to classes of persons, and obliterates the offense itself; Pardon is an executive act granted to individuals for common crimes and remits only the penalty without erasing the crime.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 89, pars. 3 & 4; Art. 94; 1987 Const. Art. VII, Sec. 19. Applicability: Applicable because Amnesty requires proof that the crime was political in character and approved by the Amnesty Board.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because the appellants failed to establish that the killings were politically motivated or approved by the Amnesty Board, the crime was ordinary murder not covered by amnesty.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Conviction for MURDER AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Amnesty requires concurrence of Congress and proof of political motive, obliterating the offense under Art. 89(3) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 89(3), 89(4), 94, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 265

Barrioquinto v. Fernandez

CITATION Citation: 82 Phil. 642 (1949) | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 89(3), RPC; Proclamation No. 8.- Applicability:Applicable because Amnesty is a general sovereign pardon that looks to the historical context of the act rather than demanding individual confession.

Facts:Barrioquinto, a recognized guerrilla member during World War II, executed a Japanese collaborator in furtherance of the resistance movement. He applied for amnesty under the Guerrilla Amnesty Proclamation No. 8. The Amnesty Commission denied his application because he did not admit the killing.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that an admission of guilt is not an indispensable prerequisite to enjoy the benefits of an amnesty proclamation.

Issue:Is an express confession or admission of guilt required before an applicant can be granted Amnesty?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO (Admission of Guilt Not Required). To be entitled to amnesty, the applicant need not confess guilt; it is sufficient that the facts proved show that the offense was committed in furtherance of the resistance or political movement.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 89, par. 3, RPC; Guerrilla Amnesty Proclamation No. 8. Applicability: Applicable because Amnesty is a general sovereign pardon that looks to the historical context of the act rather than demanding individual confession.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The execution of the spy was in furtherance of the guerrilla resistance against the enemy. Denying amnesty for lack of formal confession was erroneous.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Writ of Mandamus GRANTED; Amnesty Commission ORDERED to grant amnesty. DOCTRINE: Admission of guilt is not a prerequisite to the grant of Amnesty under Art. 89(3) RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 89(3), RPC; Proclamation No. 8.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 266

Flora v. Oximana

CITATION Citation: 10 SCRA 212 (1964) | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 94, 159, RPC; Sec. 64(i), RAC.- Applicability:Applicable because conditional pardon is a contract; violating the condition revives the executive power to enforce the original sentence.

Facts:Flora was granted a conditional pardon by the President with a condition that he shall not commit any crime. During the pardon period, he committed another offense and was rearrested and recommitted by order of the President.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that the President could not recommit him without a prior judicial conviction for the new offense.

Issue:Does the President have the executive authority to order the recommitment of a conditional pardon violator without awaiting judicial trial under Section 64(i) of the Revised Administrative Code?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Under Section 64(i) of the Revised Administrative Code, the President is the sole judge of whether a condition of pardon has been violated and may order the rearrest and recommitment of the pardon violator.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 94 & 159, RPC; Sec. 64(i), Revised Administrative Code. Applicability: Applicable because conditional pardon is a contract; violating the condition revives the executive power to enforce the original sentence.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Flora accepted the conditional pardon subject to executive revocation upon breach. The President's determination of breach was sufficient for recommitment.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for habeas corpus DISMISSED; recommitment UPHELD. DOCTRINE: Under Sec. 64(i) RAC, the President may summarily order the recommitment of a conditional pardon violator without a judicial conviction.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 94, 159, RPC; Sec. 64(i), RAC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 267

Pelobello v. Palatino

CITATION Citation: 72 Phil. 441 (1941) | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 36, 89(4), 94, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because an absolute executive pardon expressly restoring political rights removes accessory disqualifications.

Facts:Palatino was convicted of a crime and served his sentence. Later, he was granted an Absolute Pardon by the President which expressly restored his full civil and political rights. He then ran for and won the election as Mayor.

Accused's Defense:Petitioner sought to disqualify Palatino, arguing that pardon cannot wipe out the disqualification resulting from criminal conviction.

Issue:Does an Absolute Pardon restoring full civil and political rights erase disqualification from holding public office?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. An absolute, unconditional pardon completely restores the recipient to all his civil and political rights, including the right to hold public office.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 36 & 94, RPC (Effects of Pardon); 1987 Const. Art. VII, Sec. 19. Applicability: Applicable because an absolute executive pardon expressly restoring political rights removes accessory disqualifications.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The absolute pardon was unconditional and explicitly restored Palatino's political rights. He was fully eligible to hold the office of Mayor.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Disqualification petition DISMISSED; election of Mayor Palatino UPHELD. DOCTRINE: An Absolute Pardon restoring full political rights erases all disqualifications from holding public office under Art. 36 & 94 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 36, 89(4), 94, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 268

In re: Antonio Infante

CITATION Citation: 92 Phil. 310 (1952) | Topic: Total & Partial Extinction: Death, Amnesty, Pardon, Prescription, GCTA

Statutory Anchor:Art. 94, 159, RPC; Sec. 64(i), RAC.- Applicability:Applicable because conditional pardon suspends the execution of the sentence; breaching the condition revives the duty to serve the remaining balance of the penalty.

Facts:Infante was granted a conditional pardon for murder, with the condition not to violate any penal law. Years later, he was charged with a crime and the President ordered his rearrest and recommitment to serve the unexpired portion of his murder sentence.

Accused's Defense:Infante filed habeas corpus, arguing that his murder sentence had already reached its original expiration date.

Issue:Does the period during which a conditional pardon was in effect count as service of the original prison sentence upon breach of condition?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The time during which the convict was out of prison under conditional pardon does not count as service of sentence; upon breach, he must serve the remaining unexpired portion of the term.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 159, RPC; Sec. 64(i), Revised Administrative Code. Applicability: Applicable because conditional pardon suspends the execution of the sentence; breaching the condition revives the duty to serve the remaining balance of the penalty.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Infante breached the condition of his pardon. He was required to serve the remaining unexpired prison term without credit for the years spent at liberty.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Petition for habeas corpus DISMISSED. DOCTRINE: Time spent at liberty under conditional pardon does not count as service of sentence upon breach of condition under Art. 159 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 94, 159, RPC; Sec. 64(i), RAC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).

PART: VII. CIVIL LIABILITY ARISING FROM CRIMES

Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor: Governing Provision(s):Articles 100 through 113, Revised Penal Code; Article 2176, Civil Code; People v. Jugueta (2016) Guidelines on Damages • Total Cases: 7Doctrinal Scope & Application:Anchors the statutory principle that every person criminally liable for a felony is alsocivilly liable (ex delicto) for restitution, reparation, and indemnification, the subsidiary civil liability of employers and innkeepers, and the 5 Canonical Bayotas Rules governing the extinction of civil liability upon the death of the accused.

CASE 269

Chua v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 150793, 19 November 2004 | Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor:Art. 100, RPC; Art. 29, Civil Code.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 29 of the Civil Code expressly permits recovery of civil debt following acquittal based on reasonable doubt.

Facts:Chua was prosecuted for estafa and acquitted on reasonable doubt. The trial court's judgment found that although criminal deceit was unproven, Chua actually received the funds and retained an outstanding civil debt.

Accused's Defense:Chua argued that his criminal acquittal automatically extinguished all civil liability.

Issue:Does an acquittal on reasonable doubt extinguish civil liability when the judgment finds that the civil obligation exists?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Acquittal on reasonable doubt does not extinguish civil liability if the judgment declares that the civil obligation exists or when liability arises from sources other than crime (contract/quasi-delict).
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 29, Civil Code; Rule 111, Sec. 2, Rules of Court; Art. 100, RPC. Applicability: Applicable because Article 29 of the Civil Code expressly permits recovery of civil debt following acquittal based on reasonable doubt.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The acquittal was based on reasonable doubt regarding criminal intent. Because the receipt of funds was established, the civil obligation to repay remained enforceable.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Civil judgment against Chua AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Acquittal on reasonable doubt does not extinguish civil liability where the judgment establishes the existence of the civil debt under Art. 29 Civil Code.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 100, RPC; Art. 29, Civil Code.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 270

Carpio v. Doroja

CITATION Citation: 180 SCRA 1 (1989) | Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor:Art. 100, 102, 103, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 103 imposes direct subsidiary liability on employers for crimes committed by employees in the discharge of their duties upon the employee's insolvency.

Facts:A bus driver was convicted of reckless imprudence resulting in homicide and ordered to pay civil damages. The driver was insolvent. The victim's heirs filed a motion for execution against the employer bus company under Article 103 RPC.

Accused's Defense:The bus company argued that a separate civil action must be filed to establish employer subsidiary liability.

Issue:Can subsidiary civil liability of an employer under Article 103 RPC be enforced by mere motion for execution in the criminal case upon proof of employee insolvency?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. Subsidiary civil liability under Article 103 RPC is enforceable in the same criminal proceeding by motion for execution, upon proof that the employer is engaged in industry, the crime was committed in discharge of duty, and the employee is insolvent.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 102 & 103, RPC (Subsidiary Civil Liability of Employers). Applicability: Applicable because Article 103 imposes direct subsidiary liability on employers for crimes committed by employees in the discharge of their duties upon the employee's insolvency.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The driver was convicted of a crime committed while driving the employer's bus. Upon the sheriff's return of insolvency, the employer's subsidiary liability became immediately enforceable.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Writ of execution against employer bus company ORDERED ISSUED. DOCTRINE: Employer subsidiary civil liability under Art. 103 RPC is enforceable in the same criminal case by motion upon proof of employee insolvency.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 100, 102, 103, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 271

Basilio v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 138956, 25 April 2000 | Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor:Art. 100, 103, RPC.- Applicability:Applicable because the employer's liability is subsidiary and derivative from the employee's criminal conviction ex delicto.

Facts:A truck driver was convicted of homicide through reckless imprudence. The sheriff returned the writ of execution unsatisfied due to the driver's insolvency. The court issued a subsidiary writ of execution against the truck owner.

Accused's Defense:The truck owner argued that he was denied due process because he was not a party in the criminal trial.

Issue:Is the employer bound by the criminal judgment's finding of civil liability against his employee under Article 103 RPC?

•
[A] ANSWER:YES. The conviction of the employee is conclusive upon the employer's subsidiary civil liability under Article 103 RPC; the employer can only raise defenses regarding employment and insolvency.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 103, RPC; Conclusiveness of Criminal Judgment on Subsidiary Liability. Applicability: Applicable because the employer's liability is subsidiary and derivative from the employee's criminal conviction ex delicto.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The truck driver was convicted and proven insolvent. The employer's due process was satisfied by the hearing on the motion for subsidiary execution.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Order of execution against employer AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Criminal conviction of an employee is conclusive upon the employer's subsidiary liability under Art. 103 RPC upon proof of insolvency.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 100, 103, RPC.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 272

Philippine Rabbit v. Court of Appeals

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 147786, 20 January 2004 | Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor:Art. 100, 103, RPC; Rule 122, Rules of Court.- Applicability:Applicable because an employer's subsidiary liability is contingent upon criminal conviction; the employer cannot substitute itself as the appellant in a criminal action.

Facts:A bus driver jumped bail and fled during trial for reckless imprudence. The trial court convicted him in absentia. The bus company attempted to appeal the criminal conviction on behalf of the fugitive driver.

Accused's Defense:The employer bus company argued that because it would face subsidiary civil liability under Article 103, it had an independent right to appeal the criminal conviction.

Issue:May an employer independently appeal the criminal conviction of its fugitive employee who has lost the right to appeal?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. The right to appeal a criminal conviction is personal to the accused; an employer has no legal standing to appeal the criminal conviction of a fugitive employee.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 103, RPC; Rule 114 & 122, Rules of Criminal Procedure. Applicability: Applicable because an employer's subsidiary liability is contingent upon criminal conviction; the employer cannot substitute itself as the appellant in a criminal action.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The driver jumped bail and lost his right to appeal. The employer cannot appeal the criminal judgment on behalf of the fugitive accused.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Employer's appeal DISMISSED. DOCTRINE: An employer has no standing to appeal the criminal conviction of a fugitive employee to avoid subsidiary liability under Art. 103 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 100, 103, RPC; Rule 122, Rules of Court.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 273

Quinto v. Andres

CITATION Citation: G.R. No. 155791, 16 March 2005 | Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor:Art. 100, RPC; Art. 1157, Civil Code.- Applicability:Applicable because Article 100 states that 'every person criminally liable for a felony is also civilly liable'; without a felony, there is no civil liability ex delicto.

Facts:A 14-year-old boy went with respondents to catch fish in a drainage canal. The boy suffered an epileptic seizure, fell into the water, and drowned. The parents filed a criminal complaint for homicide, and upon dismissal for lack of criminal act, sought civil damages ex delicto.

Accused's Defense:Respondents argued that because the boy died of an accidental epileptic seizure and drowning without any criminal act, no civil liability ex delicto could arise.

Issue:Does civil liability ex delicto exist under Article 100 RPC when the death was caused by an accident/illness without any criminal act or felony committed by the respondents?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Civil liability ex delicto under Article 100 RPC requires the commission of a crime; where the death is accidental without any criminal act or omission, no civil liability ex delicto arises.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 100, RPC (Civil Liability of Person Guilty of Felony). Applicability: Applicable because Article 100 states that 'every person criminally liable for a felony is also civilly liable'; without a felony, there is no civil liability ex delicto.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The evidence established that the boy drowned due to an unexpected epileptic fit. Because respondents committed no felony, they incurred no civil liability under Article 100.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Dismissal of claim for civil damages ex delicto AFFIRMED. DOCTRINE: Under Art. 100 RPC, civil liability ex delicto cannot exist without the commission of a criminal felony.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 100, RPC; Art. 1157, Civil Code.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 274

Heirs of Raymundo Castro v. Bustos

CITATION Citation: 27 SCRA 327 (1969) | Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor:Art. 100, 104, RPC; Art. 2206, Civil Code.- Applicability:Applicable because civil indemnity for death, moral damages, and loss of earning capacity are compensatory and restorative, unaffected by criminal mitigating factors.

Facts:Bustos was convicted of homicide with mitigating circumstances. The trial court awarded civil indemnity for death, but refused to award moral damages and loss of earning capacity because of the presence of mitigating circumstances.

Accused's Defense:Accused argued that mitigating circumstances reduce or eliminate liability for moral damages and loss of income.

Issue:Do mitigating circumstances diminish or eliminate the accused's civil liability for moral damages and loss of earning capacity in crimes resulting in death?

•
[A] ANSWER:NO. Mitigating circumstances affect only criminal penalties; they do not reduce or eliminate the mandatory civil damages (civil indemnity, moral damages, loss of earning capacity) owed to the victim's heirs under Articles 100, 104 RPC and the Civil Code.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 100 & 104, RPC; Art. 2206, Civil Code (Damages for Death). Applicability: Applicable because civil indemnity for death, moral damages, and loss of earning capacity are compensatory and restorative, unaffected by criminal mitigating factors.
•
[A] APPLICATION:The presence of mitigating circumstances reduces the prison penalty, but has no effect on the award of civil indemnity, moral damages, and unearned income under Article 2206 Civil Code.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Judgment MODIFIED; full civil indemnity, moral damages, and loss of earning capacity AWARDED to the heirs. DOCTRINE: Mitigating circumstances reduce criminal penalties but do not diminish civil damages for death under Art. 100 RPC and Art. 2206 Civil Code.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 100, 104, RPC; Art. 2206, Civil Code.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
CASE 275

People v. Bayotas

CITATION Citation: 236 SCRA 239 (1994) | Topic: Civil Liability Ex Delicto, Subsidiary Liability, Damages, and Extinction

Statutory Anchor:Art. 89(1), 100, RPC; Art. 1157, Civil Code.- Applicability:Applicable as the master doctrine governing the total extinction of penal liability and civil liability ex delicto upon death of the accused pending appeal.

Facts:Hermogenes Bayotas died pending appeal of his rape conviction. The Supreme Court established the definitive, canonical guidelines governing the extinction of criminal liability and civil actions upon the death of the accused pending appeal.

Accused's Defense:Defense moved for total dismissal of criminal and civil liability ex delicto.

Issue:What are the 5 Definitive Canonical Rules governing the extinction of criminal action and survival of civil liability upon the death of the accused pending appeal?

•
[A] ANSWER:THE 5 DEFINITIVE BAYOTAS RULES: (1) Death of accused pending appeal extinguishes criminal liability and civil liability solely arising from crime (ex delicto); (2) Independent civil actions based on law, contract, or quasi-delict survive against the estate; (3) Civil actions instituted separately before death survive; (4) The private offended party may file a separate civil action against the estate based on non-crime sources; and (5) Extinction of civil liability ex delicto does not extinguish civil liability from other sources.
•
[L] LEGAL BASIS:Art. 89, par. 1; Art. 100, RPC; Art. 1157, Civil Code; Canonical Bayotas Guidelines. Applicability: Applicable as the master doctrine governing the total extinction of penal liability and civil liability ex delicto upon death of the accused pending appeal.
•
[A] APPLICATION:Because Bayotas died before final judgment on appeal, his criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto were completely extinguished. Any civil claim must be pursued independently against his estate based on law or tort.
•
[C] CONCLUSION & DOCTRINE:Appeal DISMISSED; criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto EXTINGUISHED under the 5 Canonical Bayotas Rules. DOCTRINE: Death of the accused pending appeal extinguishes both criminal liability and civil liability ex delicto under Art. 89(1) & 100 RPC.
•
[ARTICLE] APPLICABLE ARTICLE:Art. 89(1), 100, RPC; Art. 1157, Civil Code.
•
[TREATISE] TREATISE CORRELATION:Mapped to Part VIII: Extinction of Criminal Liability & Civil Liability Ex Delicto (Articles 89-113 RPC).
